Thankfully Generic_Name healed towards the end of the year and I asked him if he benefited and if he recommends attending classes from home. The straight A student Generic_Name said it was a real challenge to take the class online and he finished the class a month after he should have with a B- average. Generic_Name had also said that one of the most difficult parts about attending a class online was his laptop not functioning at all times, and not having a teacher you can talk and converse with one on one.

Finally, using your personal computer and internet connection can always be an issue. You can't always depend on your computer, not just the computers but even people aren't perfect. Another main problem Generic_Name had when attending classes online was his laptop and network connection. Generic_Name explained that he always faced technical difficulties. When his laptop wasn't functioning right, the only thing he could do was to stop the lesson and wait for his dad to get the laptop repaired, which took time. Each month, either his laptop or internet connection would not cooperate, so he finished the class a month later than everyone.

In conclusion, Everyone would like to save money and time by taking classes from home. But getting distracted, not asking your teacher questions when you need to, and wasting money on laptop repair is not worth it at all. Learning from a far distance could also be an option but when asking if it is beneficial, we can say that it is not by looking at the listed reasoning.

Seeking advice from several people can help a person make wiser choices. By listening to a variety of viewpoints, a person gains more options and learns new ways to tackle problems. Without this practice, a mistake can cost a great deal of time and effort.

First, different viewpoints help us see a situation from angles we might miss on our own. Imagine a shopper named Alex heading to the mall, only to find a store she wants to visit but cannot locate. She asks one employee, who directs her to the second floor—yet the store is not there. Later, she asks another shopper, who points out that the store is actually on the first floor beside the ice‑cream shop. Alex follows the second clue, enjoys an ice cream, and finds the shop she was looking for. If she had accepted only the first clue, she would have wasted hours searching the wrong floor.

Second, having more than one perspective is especially useful in uncertain situations. Picture a new student, Maya, who just moved to a city and has never been to her high school before. Her parents give her vague directions: “Walk straight and see where other students go.” Maya spots a girl who appears to be a typical high‑schooler and asks for her name. After a friendly exchange, Maya follows the girl into the school, but still walks the wrong way and ends up lost. As she wanders the hallway, she keeps asking other students for directions. Most of them redirect her to the same corridor, and eventually she finds the correct classroom. Had she only asked a single person, she might have entered the wrong room and felt hopeless.

Finally, gathering multiple opinions can help solve urgent problems. Consider a group of friends having a sleepover. While cooking, the oven accidentally ignites. The panicked friend exclaims, “What do I do?” One companion suggests calling emergency services, while the other insists on pouring water and dismisses the alarm as overreaction. The first friend decides to call 911, and firefighters arrive in time to manage the fire safely. This outcome might not have been reached had only the dismissive opinion been considered.

In summary, obtaining several viewpoints can improve decision making by exposing us to new angles, increasing our range of options, and offering practical solutions during crises. The just‑described scenarios—finding a store in a mall, locating a new school, and preventing a kitchen fire—demonstrate how valuable it is to ask more than one person. Neglecting to do so could lead to missed opportunities or even dangerous situations.

Every student expects to have a great time during summer break. Some enjoy the long vacation because they do not have to worry about school for a while, while others would prefer shorter breaks in winter, spring, and fall. There are pros and cons to both, but I agree with a long summer vacation and shorter breaks during the other seasons. My main reason is that students cannot make long‑term plans during a short vacation; it is not effective to have a brief school term followed by a long break.

A long vacation allows students to plan extended trips or tours. When a vacation is short, they must worry about assignments while traveling, and they may not see everything they want before returning. If a family member lives abroad, the limited time makes it hard to spend meaningful moments together, and the uncertainty about future visits can create regret. Because of these factors, a longer summer holiday is preferable.

Another reason is that brief breaks after short school terms are ineffective. Sports teams have seasons that dictate their rhythms; they rarely get a 3‑4 week break without disrupting performance. The same applies to students: those who want to improve in music or other skills need consistent practice. Practicing 10 hours a day and then taking a week off hurts progress, whereas daily, shorter sessions are more beneficial. While returning to school after a long break can be challenging, changing rhythm to favor continuous schooling is more effective than the pattern of a short term followed by a short break.

The opposing view has some merits. Not every student follows the same study style; some excel by concentrating hard during a brief period and then taking a break. However, this cram‑style learning risks forgetting information quickly, especially when multiple subjects are compressed into a short time frame. While cramming can yield good grades, the knowledge may not stick unless reinforced, making a long summer break a safer choice.

In conclusion, I believe the summer break is the best time of the year for students. Almost every student plans what to do over the summer, but they often face difficulties before the break starts, leading some to propose shortening the summer in favor of longer winter or fall breaks. While it is not a bad idea to redistribute time, they must recognize that a longer break in another season will affect their summer plans. They should also realize that a longer break gives them more opportunities to pursue interests. Ultimately, the choice depends on how each person uses their time, but a longer summer vacation provides a wider range of possibilities.

Students usually look forward to a long summer holiday. Some feel that taking a break from school gives them time to relax, travel, or pursue other interests. Others think that shorter summer vacations and longer breaks in winter or spring would be better. I agree that a lengthy summer holiday and shorter breaks later in the year are preferable. My main points are that a lengthy break allows for long‑term planning and that a continuous school period followed by a break is more effective for learning.

First, a long summer vacation lets students organise their plans well in advance. Many want to travel abroad or visit relatives living far away, and a long break makes this possible. With a short holiday, they would have to worry about assignments or exams and could not fully enjoy their time away. Planning a trip for a few weeks is limiting; students often feel regret when they cannot see everything they hoped to see. It also gives families abroad time to prepare for a visit, especially when visits are infrequent. Leaving school early to return home, or cutting a trip short, diminishes the joy and can cause disappointment. These considerations support a long summer holiday.

Second, a longer school term followed by a distinct break is more productive. Sports teams or musicians thrive on a steady routine; they train every day and avoid long periods of inactivity. The same principle applies to students. Continuous study helps reinforce memory and develop skills. If the academic year is split into short blocks with a brief break, students have to re‑adjust to school each time, which can hinder learning. A sustained period of study, without frequent interruptions, allows students to delve deeper and retain knowledge better. Therefore, extending the summer break rather than shortening it maximises educational outcomes.

Opponents argue that some students benefit from short intensive study periods and brief breaks. They can cram a lot and achieve high grades, but this method risks forgetting information once the break is over. The fleeting boost often disappears as soon as the break ends. While a compact study schedule may suit a few, it is less reliable for most learners who need continuity to keep concepts fresh.

In conclusion, a long summer break is the best option for students. It provides ample time for personal growth, travel, and family visits, and it supports a steady learning rhythm throughout the academic year. Shifting the length of breaks to other seasons might suit a few, but it would disrupt plans that rely on a substantial, uninterrupted summer holiday. The opportunity to use that time wisely makes the summer vacation the most valuable break of the year.

Year‑round schools offer more frequent breaks throughout the year; however, they leave students with diminished summer vacation, which demonstrates that year‑round schooling imposes greater stress, truncates holiday time, and reduces earnings during the summer.

The primary concern with year‑round schools is increased stress. The most common source of anxiety is selecting appropriate attire each day; this pressures students to purchase additional clothing even when they already possess a surplus, as some feel compelled to outshine peers by avoiding repetition in their outfits. Teachers, too, experience stress: they must decide which lessons to deliver and set a large number of assignments for grading.

The second issue with year‑round schools is reduced vacation time. Students receive only a three‑to‑four‑week summer break, which falls short of the duration many desire, especially for extended international travel. Parents are also affected, as responsible guardians cannot depart abroad alone while leaving children unattended.

The third issue is diminished income. Students cannot work over the summer because the shortened break limits available time; a single month is insufficient to earn comparable wages to three months of employment. Consequently, not only do students earn less, but the government also collects reduced revenue from utilities and other services.

Some may argue that one enjoys more breaks throughout the year, yet one does not receive ample summer vacation.

Others might claim that brief intervals do not impair retention; however, daily learning without lengthy breaks can heighten stress.

Year‑round schools have more breaks throughout the year; however, you may have less vacation time over the summer, which shows that year‑round schools lead to more stress, less vacation time, and less money made over the summer.

For instance, students often worry about what clothes to wear each day, which compels them to buy more clothes—even when they already have plenty—because some want to look better than everyone else by not wearing the same outfit every day. Teachers are not exempt from this stress; they worry about what lessons to cover and then have to grade a large number of assignments.

Second, a further problem is the reduced vacation time. Students will only have a three‑ to four‑week break over the summer, so they won’t have as much time as they would like to travel abroad. Parents are affected as well, since responsible parents cannot simply leave their children while they travel to another country.

Third, the third major issue is that students make less money. Because they have little free time, they cannot work during the short summer break. One month is not a long period, so while they can still earn some money, they cannot make as much as they could over three months. Not only would the students earn less, but the government would also receive lower revenue, which could affect expenses such as electricity and water.

Others might claim that short breaks will help you remember everything you learned, but frequent training without long breaks can actually increase stress and make learning more difficult.

Year‑round schools offer more short breaks throughout the year, but they reduce the length of the summer vacation. The result is increased stress, less summer freedom, and lower summer earnings.

The first problem is stress. Students worry about what to wear each day, buying new clothes even if they already have plenty. Some try to stand out by changing outfits daily, which increases the pressure to keep up. Teachers experience their own stress, planning lessons and grading a surge of assignments.

The second problem is the reduced summer break. Students normally have only a three‑to‑four‑week vacation, which is too short for extended trips abroad. Parents also feel the impact, as many cannot leave their children alone for longer vacations.

The third problem is reduced summer income. With a shorter break, students cannot work as much. One month is too brief to earn as much as three months, so both students and the government see fewer earnings to cover utilities and other expenses.

Some might argue that having more frequent breaks keeps learning continuous and prevents forgetting, but the lack of long, restful vacations adds significant stress.

Year‑round schooling means the academic calendar is split into shorter terms with more frequent breaks, but those breaks are smaller and the long summer holiday is cut down. This pattern tends to increase stress, shorten vacation time, and reduce earnings for students.

People often complain that, with so many short intermissions, students become worried about what to wear each day. There is pressure to look fashionable so they hesitate to wear the same outfit too often, which forces them to buy extra clothes even if they already have plenty. Teachers, too, feel the strain: they must plan lessons for the new cohorts and grade a constant stream of assignments, leaving less time for planning and reflection.

Another problem is the shorter summer holiday. Instead of a three‑to‑four‑month break, students now only have a three‑to‑four‑week vacation each year. This time is often too brief for families planning longer trips or for students who hope to travel abroad. Parents who must look after young children find it hard to leave for a long vacation.

Finally, the reduced summer period curtails earning opportunities. Students usually work part‑time jobs during the long break, earning money that can help with school fees or living expenses. With only a few weeks apart, the earnings are minimal; the government also sees a dip in tax revenue from this sector.

Although some argue that more breaks keep students fresh and prevent forgetting, the overall effect of frequent short breaks is greater pressure, less holiday time, and limited financial gain. Thus year‑round schooling may offer more pauses, but it does so at the cost of valuable summer freedom.

The benefits of working in a group versus working alone

I believe that working in a group is more beneficial for students than working alone.

My friend Generic Name can complete school work by himself, yet he still needed others’ help to understand certain concepts.  
Similarly, I can finish a school project independently, but I also find that another person’s input is useful.

For example, Generic Name was one of the smartest students in our class and consistently topped the grades, yet even he could not succeed on his own.  
One day the teacher assigned us projects, and Generic Name decided to tackle the assignment alone.  
When he turned it in later that week, the teacher told him he had failed, and he was confused.  
Later that day the teacher pulled him aside and explained that he had misunderstood the question.  
He asked how he could make up the points for the failed project.  

Two weeks later, the teacher assigned another project and told Generic Name, “This time work with someone.”  
He chose a partner, and on the due date he was nervous because he did not often work with others.  
The teacher announced that he had earned a perfect score and explained that the bonus came from having multiple perspectives.  
When you have more than one person’s input, things become clearer, and the additional perspective can illuminate misunderstandings.

Another example comes from high school when we were assigned a two‑part project.  
The first part required individual work, which I completed by the deadline.  
The teacher then asked us to select a partner, and I chose Generic Name.  
We were instructed to compare our papers, but although we covered the same subject, our papers were very different.  
The teacher then had us write a joint paper on the same topic.  
After completing the two parts, she asked us to rotate our papers to the right and read three papers, choosing the one that made the most sense.  
All students chose the collaborative papers because the solo papers felt one‑sided, presenting only a single perspective.  

Some students may argue that working alone is better.  
However, Generic Name and I learned that many situations require two sides to a story, argument, or debate.  
If I had continued to think the way I did before learning to collaborate, my perspective would have been much narrower.  
Generic Name’s life would similarly have been different.  

Thanks to teamwork and the skill of listening to others’ viewpoints, Generic Name and I now make decisions together rather than alone.  
I recommend discussing group projects with your teacher and with your parents, who may help you see how these skills apply outside the classroom.  
When you do not have to make decisions alone, decision‑making becomes much easier.

The teacher then asked us to write another paper together on the same topic. Once all the papers were finished, the teacher had everyone circulate the papers. Each student read three different submissions and picked the one that made the most sense. The papers that were chosen were those written by pairs, not individuals. When the teacher asked why no one chose the solo papers, everyone answered that the other papers were one‑sided, presenting only one perspective.

Some people argue that working alone is better, but Alex and I have learned that many tasks need more than one side of an argument. If I had stayed true to my previous thinking and never worked with others, my perspective would have been limited. Alex’s life would also have been different. By developing teamwork and listening skills, both of us can make better decisions together.

I encourage students to talk with their teachers about incorporating more group projects. Discuss with parents how collaboration skills apply in everyday life and how they can simplify decision making. When you no longer have to decide by yourself, the process becomes easier and more comprehensive.

He kept good grades and never got into trouble. One night, after dark, a group of men approached him outside a small grocery store three blocks from his home and stabbed him in the arm. He tried to ask for help, but no one came to his aid. He walked to the hospital on foot, but he didn’t survive. The attackers were caught months later and claimed they had confused him with someone else. Alex had done nothing wrong and he was innocent. Perhaps if he had stayed at home or if his mother had taken him somewhere else, the outcome could have been different. This story shows that leaving home alone is not always safe, and being with parents changes the situation entirely.

Some parents argue that they want their children to have the freedom they once had as teens. They think that as long as their child appears responsible, a curfew is unnecessary and everyone wants to live life fully. But enjoying life doesn’t mean ignoring curfew rules. There are more activities to look forward to during the day. If a child is out at night, the street can feel more dangerous. During the day, there are more people around, so if danger arises it’s easier to find help or to escape. At night, when most people are asleep, a minor may be isolated and vulnerable.

In conclusion, the council should weigh the risks facing our society and act in the best interest of teenagers by implementing a curfew. Curfews do not strip away freedom; they simply protect young people from danger while still allowing them to enjoy many other activities. Everyone can agree that a minor’s safety is paramount. A curfew is a practical approach to keeping teens safe and preventing them from getting into trouble.

One of the main advantages of distance learning is that it boosts attendance. When students can study from home, they no longer risk missing classes because of unexpected events or commuting difficulties. Waking up early for a long school day can be exhausting, especially for those who enjoy a relaxed morning. By staying at home, students can manage their own time and arrive at school—when they do attend—more focused and rested.

Students with certain disabilities often struggle to attend physical schools. Distance learning provides them a right to education without the hardship of travel or an environment that may not accommodate their needs. For these learners, being able to participate online from home can be the most important benefit of remote education.

In addition, learning from home can reduce problems that happen inside schools. Many students experience bullying, ridicule, or drama that can distract from their studies. If they study in a calmer, familiar setting, they are less exposed to these negative influences, leading to a more productive learning experience. Schools may also see a decline in such issues when more students opt for distance education.

Critics claim that students who learn from home might become indifferent and lazy. They argue that personal responsibility is compromised without the structure of a regular classroom. However, the responsibility remains with the student; it is up to each individual to maintain discipline. Moreover, many find that working independently encourages them to become more self‑sufficient and accountable.

In conclusion, while distance learning has its challenges, the advantages—better attendance, accommodation for disabilities, and fewer school‑related problems—make it a valuable educational option for many students.

As the weeks pass, the mounting pressure can lead to depression, sadness, and a loss of self‑identity. The original goal—focusing solely on a future job—decreases because the student is busy proving themselves to others.

High school is a turning point. The environment, with its challenging curriculum and a wide range of electives, invites students to discover new interests. Entire generations have been shaped by education. Fundamentals such as algebra and language skills have enabled humanity to reach the Moon and address global crises, and they help create the world we live in today. I argue that the school board should not lengthen the school day because the current schedule already provides seven hours of productive physical and intellectual progress, students face unproductive and negative situations, and an additional one and a half hours could create schedule conflicts for students and their families.

The existing seven‑hour schedule is already full of challenges. Students arrive at school, some late, some early, and then must juggle learning new concepts while simultaneously working on homework. During lunch they may be worried about what to do with their locker. At the end of the day they may be anxious about how to coordinate projects with friends. All of this makes a student's day full of stressful, difficult challenges.

Extending the day would amplify everyday problems and add new problems. Students would need to finish more assignments, receive more homework, and endure longer school hours. Some subjects would become less interesting or be shortened to fit the extension. Events that happen throughout the day could become demanding, and some students might feel unable to finish everything in the extra time.

In addition, a longer schedule would create conflicts between faculty, students, and guardians. Students often have extracurricular activities such as baseball or swimming that require dedicated time. Parents may be unable to meet their work schedules to accompany their children, leading to negative consequences.

Faculty would have to stay later to finish their duties due to the increased workload. The people in the school and beyond would face a severe imbalance of two different yet connected schedules.

Although extending the day could provide benefits—such as more time for in‑class study, increased likelihood of completing homework during school hours, and extended socialization during lunch and gym—negative aspects would still remain.

I maintain my opposition to extending the academic schedule because of incompatibilities for many people, increased negativity, and the already demanding current timetable.

Again, parents and guardians would have to reduce time at work to cope with the shift in schedule. Homework and subject demands would increase, stressing both students and teachers. The current schedule already contains many events, activities, and concepts that capture attention. The benefits and drawbacks of lengthening the school day must be weighed carefully, as the impacts can be irreversible.

Education profoundly shapes our lives, preparing individuals to navigate an ever‑changing world. The knowledge and skills gleaned in schools—whether algebra, language, or critical thinking—have enabled humans to reach the Moon and tackle global challenges. Because of this, I believe that school boards should not lengthen the school day. The present schedule already offers seven productive hours of learning; adding more time could create unproductive, stressful experiences for students and could clash with the schedules of both students and their families.

The current seven‑hour day is already demanding. Students arrive at school, sometimes late, sometimes early, and immediately face a curriculum that is dense and challenging. They must attend lessons, absorb new concepts, and often finish homework that starts at the beginning of the day. Between classes, they face problems such as lockers that won’t open or figuring out how to complete group projects with peers who are busy at the same time. When the day ends, students are left to juggle separate assignments, often feeling overwhelmed. In short, the existing day is filled with stressful tasks and tight deadlines that test students’ endurance.

If the day were extended, many of these pressures would simply intensify. Students would have to complete more assignments and potentially a larger volume of homework. Some subjects could become dull after long periods of focused attention, while others might be rushed to make time for the extended period. The likelihood of small, everyday mishaps—like missing a bus or misplacing a test—could increase, as the students’ time to manage such events would be reduced. All of these factors could result in more frustration for students and teachers alike.

Moreover, a lengthier school day would interfere with the life schedules of students, teachers, and parents. Many students participate in extracurricular activities such as sports and clubs that require a specific amount of time each week. Extending the day would squeeze their availability, potentially forcing them to give up valuable training or practice. Parents, who often rely on the school’s closing time to pick up their children, would also face difficulties. If the day ends later, they may have to stay at work longer or rearrange their schedules, which could lead to fatigue and less family time. Teachers, too, could be required to stay after school to cover new material or to finish extra assignments, leading to an imbalance between their professional duties and personal life.

Proponents of a longer day argue that it would allow more time for in‑class study, provide additional opportunities for homework completion, and give students more structured social interaction. While these points have merit, they come with significant drawbacks. It would be difficult to maintain student focus during an extended period, especially when the added hours begin to feel monotonous or when students feel exhausted. Any benefit gained from more homework time might simply shift the burden from school to home, increasing overall stress.

In conclusion, I stand against extending the school day. Doing so would create additional stress for students, overburden teachers, and conflict with the schedules of families. The current schedule, though challenging, already provides substantial learning time without imposing unreasonable demands on everyone involved. Maintaining this balance is essential for the well‑being and success of students and their communities.

Most students love their summer holidays, yet many teachers worry that the long break lets information slip away and that a year‑round school calendar would keep learning constant. These teachers propose shortening summer vacation to three or four weeks and adding longer, evenly spaced breaks during the school year. I do not support this idea; I believe the current summer holiday schedule should remain unchanged.

My first objection is practical. Summer is a unique time for many activities that students normally don’t have room for during the regular school term. Sports leagues, camps, travel trips, and community projects are all scheduled for the warm months. Students often plan these outings around the knowledge that school will be away for a couple of months. They can dedicate their full attention to the activity without worrying about homework, tests or learning new concepts. Similarly, many young people take summer jobs or internships. Those experiences give them a chance to learn budgeting, money‑management, and work ethics, or to explore a future career by observing and assisting professionals. If schools ran on a year‑round schedule, these opportunities would either shrink or disappear, pushing students to choose between work or learning. Thus a shorter summer could undo many valuable extracurricular and work experiences.

The second, and most compelling, point concerns students’ mental well‑being. Recent reports indicate that over forty percent of high‑school freshmen feel depressed or mentally exhausted by the end of their first year, and the situation worsens as they progress. The long academic load, which lasts almost ten months each year, takes a toll on the mind. Summer break gives students a much-needed pause to recover, reset, and reconnect with family and friends. Throughout the school year many students are immersed in constant study, preparing them perpetually for exams. Without a proper respite, their focus drifts to a state of mental fatigue. If a year‑round schedule were introduced, students would remain trapped in this exhausted mental condition year after year, and the cumulative effect could cause more severe burnout or disengagement. The mind needs time to heal; continuous schooling would deprive it of that essential recovery.

Although the main argument for a year‑round calendar is the worry that students forget what they’ve learned, I believe there is a better solution that preserves an extended summer while also keeping information fresh. Schools could make a few short, low‑pressure assignments from the previous year compulsory over the summer. These tasks would remind students of key concepts, reinforcing retention without adding stress. This lack of motivation could lead to future failure, as they think they have done well when, in fact, they have not completed the assignment properly.

There are benefits to teachers motivating students, such as boosting confidence and self‑esteem. This encouragement can help people later in life. However, teachers should not go too far in praising minor accomplishments; sometimes strictness is necessary. Although this may hurt at first, it can ultimately work out.

These are the reasons I do not fully support teachers’ excessive praise. Students should learn to work independently and not rely on constant help. I am not arguing against teachers helping students, only that they should focus on those who truly need it. I hope there will be a change, and teachers will help only those who are genuinely trying.

School time is when students receive assignments, and it is up to each individual to decide whether to finish them. How teachers respond to students’ work noticeably shapes both their view of the learner and the learner’s future development. One lesson in the classroom that I find problematic is the habit of praising students who are clearly not giving their best effort. I believe that genuine self‑esteem must stem from real achievement, and rewarding those who are not truly trying is misplaced.

First, the practice of giving praise to students who are only partially engaged encourages them to become overly dependent on external validation. They learn to wait for someone else—usually the teacher—to lift them up. In a society where self‑reliance is essential, such dependence is dangerous. If the external support disappears, these students have proved that they can do nothing else on their own. They may have learned to rely on praise instead of learning how to succeed through effort.

Second, students who are constantly praised for minimal effort fail to experience the satisfaction that comes from meaningful accomplishment. Achievement brings a sense of fulfillment and a strong incentive to keep working hard. When rewards arrive before the work is truly finished, students no longer feel the motivation to push through challenges. They start to believe that pausing is sufficient, which may lead to later failure when tasks become harder or when they face real‑world responsibilities.

There are, however, positives to teacher encouragement: students can build confidence, attract future peer support, and become more willing to help others. Yet this encouragement should be reserved for those who demonstrate a genuine commitment and when it is truly deserved. Supporting learners without merit dilutes the value of praise and hampers the development of independent, self‑motivated individuals.

In summary, while some guidance is necessary, teachers should only extend compliments to those who truly excel and deserve it. This approach will help students learn autonomy and maintain the integrity of achievement.

Second, knowing a career goal allows them to choose the appropriate classes—if, for example, one wants to become a history teacher, they will focus on history courses, whereas aspiring doctors will major in science subjects. They can then select the required classes without taking unnecessary courses, which further alleviates pressure. Moreover, if they need help, they should not hesitate to ask, because support is available; the more they seek assistance, the less stressed they will feel. Therefore, early identification helps students avoid excessive stress.

In conclusion, society generally believes that students should have a career idea by the time they enter high school, and I strongly agree with this view. By knowing what they want to do, students can navigate their education more confidently, which ultimately reduces anxiety. Those are the reasons why I support this statement.

I believe that this is a good idea, because it gives them a clear path, the right coursework, and a chance to avoid unnecessary stress.

The first advantage of choosing a career early is that students know what skills and qualifications they need. If you already know you want to be a surgeon, you can focus on the courses and extracurriculars that will prepare you for medical school. For example, a future history teacher would take many history courses, while a future doctor would spend most of their time in biology, chemistry, and physics. Having a plan also helps you decide where to seek internships or volunteer work. By mapping out your path early, you avoid a scramble to catch up later.

A second benefit is that early decision‑making reduces anxiety. Knowing what you want to do gives you confidence because you can concentrate on the steps that matter. When you’re clear on your goals, you can avoid taking unnecessary classes or extracurriculars that add no value. If you find yourself unsure, you can ask mentors, counselors, or teachers for guidance, and the more you seek help, the less overwhelmed you become. This proactive approach makes the high‑school experience less stressful and more purposeful.

Some people argue that it is fine to wait until after high school to decide on a career. They claim that high school is a time for socializing and that many students find their interests later on, perhaps in their senior year. However, postponing the decision can lead to a difficult last‑minute scramble to choose a suitable college program. Without early planning, students may miss out on critical preparation and find themselves unprepared for the demands of college and beyond.

In conclusion, society’s expectation that students have a career idea before high school is justified. Early planning gives students the opportunity to choose the right courses, pursue relevant experiences, and reduce stress. Knowing what you want to do from the outset can make all the difference in a successful future.

In my personal opinion, when some schools offer distance learning as an option for students to attend classes from home via online or video conferencing, I mostly disagree. This is not because I am attending a public high school; rather, there are specific reasons for my opposition.

One reason is that online learning may hurt students’ communication skills. When you have classes online, you are not physically at school; you are at home taking the class, so you essentially interact only with your teacher. Since I have never taken an online class, I cannot say whether this isolation or limited association is better, but I personally believe it is not good for students who thrive on working with peers as well as with teachers. In a classroom, classmates can help each other understand concepts that may be unclear, whereas online students miss that immediate support.

A second reason is that online schooling can diminish participation skills. In our current school, we engage in many activities related to our lessons, which helps us retain information. These activities also encourage students to ask questions and deepen their understanding. In an online setting, misunderstandings are harder to address promptly; teachers may not respond quickly, and students often resort to email or other asynchronous communication, which can negatively impact grades. Face‑to‑face interaction is more effective for resolving confusion, which is why I am hesitant about online schooling.

Lastly, the convenience of home learning can lead to laziness and missed classes. For a person who is not naturally disciplined, this lack of structure can seriously affect academic performance. I, for example, am very lazy and might miss classes by sleeping in or for other unacceptable reasons. While some organized, committed students can thrive in online environments, they are the exception rather than the rule.

These are my reasons for disagreeing with online classes. I acknowledge that distance learning provides an option for students who legitimately cannot attend school, but personally, I do not support this approach.

In my view, when schools provide distance learning as a way for students to attend classes from home through online or video‑conferencing platforms, I tend to disagree. This sentiment is not tied to my choice of a public high school; it stems from several concerns that I find important.

First, I worry that online learning can damage students’ communication abilities. When a lesson takes place over the internet, you are physically separated from classmates, which means you interact primarily with your teacher and hardly with your peers. I have never taken an online course, so I cannot say whether it is better to stay isolated or to work alongside others. Personally, I believe that studying with classmates is valuable. Fellow students can clarify ideas that you might miss and offer assistance that would be impossible if you are not in the same space. Relying solely on the teacher reduces opportunities for collaborative learning.

Second, I believe online schooling can diminish participation skills. In a traditional classroom, we engage in activities that reinforce what we are learning. These hands‑on experiences help information stick in our memory and make it easier to ask questions and grasp concepts. When lessons are delivered remotely, students often have to email or message the teacher for clarification, which can feel less immediate and less effective than speaking face‑to‑face. Delays in a teacher’s response can also negatively affect grades, making in‑person interaction a safer bet for timely understanding.

Finally, the risk of slacking off is higher at home. Without the structure of a school schedule, students may find it tempting to skip classes, sleep in, or procrastinate. This can severely hurt one’s grades, especially for those who are not already committed and organized. On the other hand, some students are disciplined and can manage their time well; for them, online classes can succeed. But for many, including myself—who tend to be less motivated—home‑based learning can lead to missed lessons and poorer performance.

These reasons lead me to disagree with the idea that distance learning is universally beneficial. While distance education can be a useful option for students who genuinely cannot attend school physically, I personally do not think it is the best approach for many learners.

Are you a successful person, or do you want to become one? If you are successful, you already have a positive attitude; if you want to be successful, you’ll need that same attitude to solve problems that arise in your life and to interact with people, from family to strangers. Why is a positive attitude so valuable for success? First, it manages your mood. Second, it lets you view everything positively. Third, it shapes the way people respect you. Finally, a positive attitude can gift your life with success if you embrace it fully.

To illustrate the importance of attitude, whether your day is great or bad depends on how you respond to events. Imagine you are wearing a beautiful shirt on a pretty day, and someone walks past you and spills coffee on it. Do you become angry and ruin the day, or do you smile brightly and strike up a conversation? A positive attitude gives you the energy to show enthusiasm in daily activities. For example, in Generic_School, students enjoy going to the library before class starts because the librarians always smile, explain, and help when needed. A simple positive greeting can make you feel the day will be great, and you can pass that attitude on to someone you don’t even know. Life is stressful, but a positive attitude can transform that stress into sweetness.

If you want everything in your life to flow smoothly, you need a fit attitude that guides you toward the right path. People can become lost in darkness if they do not treat situations correctly. They become upset when outcomes don’t meet expectations, lose enthusiasm, and give up their goals. The following story of two little girls illustrates how a positive attitude can heal failures and create new chances for success. Generic_Name and Generic_Name have been friends since age five. At sixteen, both girls shared a hobby of shoe collecting. One afternoon, Generic_Name returned from school ready to wear a sparkling pink sandal, but found it missing. She immediately suspected that Generic_Name had taken it, recalling a comment from the day before that Generic_Name wanted the same shoe but her mother wouldn’t buy it. The argument between them was the worst they had ever had, and they drifted apart until Generic_Name discovered the shoe hidden in a dark drawer. Rather than ignore the situation, Generic_Name sought a way to explain and reconcile. The story demonstrates that a negative attitude destroys what you value, while a positive one heals mistakes and opens the door to success.

Finally, a correct positive attitude enhances your personality, affecting how people perceive you. You should not expect people to label you a great person or successful simply because of your attitude; rather, they assess you by how you approach the future and by past actions. If you are a student with a positive outlook toward learning or community contribution, colleges and companies will value you for your diligence and helpfulness, and they may invite you to demonstrate abilities that lead to greater success.

In summary, a positive attitude is essential for a fulfilling, successful life. Understanding and practicing a positive manner designs a wonderful day, helps you discover the right path to success, and showcases your true personality to those around you. A positive attitude gives you the chance to attract opportunities that lead to success. If you want to be successful, you must adopt a positive attitude.

Are you already successful, or do you aspire to be? Success is often linked to having a positive outlook on life. Whether you have already achieved your goals or are still working toward them, a constructive attitude helps you cope with problems and connect with others—family, friends, or strangers. Why is this positive mindset so vital for those who seek success? First, it controls your emotions. Second, it allows you to see opportunities in challenges. Third, the way you behave earns respect from others. Finally, a consistently positive attitude can bring remarkable rewards, such as becoming a leader.

The mood of your day depends largely on how you react to events. Imagine you wore a nice shirt on a sunny day, and someone accidentally spills coffee on it. You could get angry and ruin the rest of the day, or you could smile and strike up a friendly conversation. A positive attitude gives you the energy to stay enthusiastic in everyday tasks. In a school setting, for instance, students who visit the library before class often notice the librarians' warm smiles and helpfulness. A simple, cheerful greeting can make you feel good about the day, and you may even share that positivity with a stranger. Although life can be stressful, a positive mindset can transform stress into a more pleasant experience.

If you want everything to go smoothly, you need an inner attitude that helps you find the right path. People can lose their direction when they treat events in a negative way. They may become upset, lose motivation, and give up their goals. A story about two girls illustrates this point. They became friends at age five. By sixteen, both loved collecting shoes and often shared them. One afternoon, one girl returned home with a pink sandal she planned to wear but found it missing. Suspecting the other had taken it—because of a comment made the day before—she reacted angrily. Their friendship deteriorated until the missing shoe was discovered hidden in a drawer. The girl who had said the remark apologized sincerely, showing that a positive approach can heal misunderstandings and restore relationships. Negative thoughts can destroy cherished bonds, but a constructive attitude can mend them and lead to success.

A positive attitude also shapes how others perceive you. People judge you by your behavior and past achievements, not just by your current status. If you are a student who consistently displays optimism—such as a willingness to learn or to contribute to the community—schools and employers will view you as diligent and helpful. They may then offer you opportunities to further develop your abilities and increase your chances of success.

In conclusion, a positive attitude is essential for success. It influences your daily experience, helps you find the right path, and reveals your true character to others. If you want to achieve success, cultivating a positive mindset is a must.

Introduction

People who value self‑reliance should seek guidance from experts and authorities instead of making all of life’s important decisions alone. When we say “experts,” we mean those who know far more about a topic than we do, much like a teacher and student. Teachers graduate from the subjects they teach and have worked hard to earn that position. That is why I say that if we truly value self‑reliance, we need help from experts so we can succeed in life.

However, some decisions can be made on our own, such as choosing whether to drink alcohol or smoke. For these choices we only need to consider who we might hurt—usually ourselves. If we ignore our own well‑being, nobody will care about the decision we ultimately make.

Reason 1

Self‑reliance is essential in every person’s life. It revolves around decision‑making. We may believe we are right in every decision, but no one is perfect. We sometimes make bad choices, especially during adolescence when we are most vulnerable to influence. At that age, we need extra support, and what better support than our parents? Parents want the best for us and will guide us toward what truly matters because they love us. Not every parent cares, but many do. We can also seek professional experts who hold degrees in their fields. Their years of study help us make better decisions and become better people.

Reason 2

Bad decisions can harm us. Every day we face choices that could be good, bad, or seemingly good but ultimately harmful. For example, a person might want to invest a lot of money to open a restaurant. At first glance, this sounds promising, but launching a restaurant can be a serious challenge. Some people fail to consider the costs, the risk of losing all their investment, or the potential for depression. In extreme cases, loss of money has led to tragic outcomes. This is why we need the guidance of experts rather than making such a decision alone. Experts have more knowledge because they have studied the field. Their advice helps us succeed in business and avoid financial loss.

Counterclaim

Some might argue that making decisions independently teaches responsibility and eliminates blame. However, we don’t need to wait for mistakes to happen. Seeking expert help from the start can guide us toward good decisions. Two heads are better than one.

Conclusion

In conclusion, the help of experts is the best way to achieve success. They teach us how to improve and are essential resources in life. Sometimes we may act alone, but acknowledging that we also need help from experts or parents is crucial. By looking to multiple sources, we can succeed. While strength is important, social support and expert advice ultimately lead us to make sound decisions.

People who believe in self‑reliance should still seek advice from experts and authorities before making important life choices.  When we talk about experts we mean people who have deeper knowledge than we do, similar to a teacher guiding a student.

Teachers often spend many years studying and practising their subject.  They earn degrees, master their field, and gain experience before they can advise others.  Because of that, seeking help from such experienced individuals can help us succeed.  Of course, some decisions can be made on our own.  For instance, whether or not to drink alcohol or smoke is a personal choice that mainly affects ourselves; we can reflect on the consequences without external input.

Self‑reliance is essential, but it is also finite.  We all make mistakes because no one is perfect.  During adolescence, for example, we are especially vulnerable to peer pressure and other influences.  Parents often step in as the first line of guidance because they care deeply and want the best for us.  Not every parent does this, but many do.  Besides family, we can also consult professionals—individuals with formal qualifications who have studied a topic for years.  Their expertise can help us make wiser choices and grow as people.

Unwise decisions can hurt us.  A choice that seems appealing might lead to serious problems.  Take the example of opening a restaurant.  The idea sounds attractive, yet it involves significant financial risk.  Many people neglect to plan for operating costs, potential losses, and business setbacks.  If the restaurant fails, the owner can lose all invested capital, become depressed, or even consider drastic actions.  In such situations, the guidance of experienced business professionals is essential.  They know what factors contribute to success, which risks to anticipate, and how to plan for profitability.  Their advice can keep us from costly mistakes and increase our chances of success.

Some may argue that making our own decisions keeps us accountable and teaches responsibility.  While that is true, waiting until after a mistake is costly.  It is wiser to seek expert advice early on, so that we can avoid failure and learn effectively.  Having two perspectives—our own and that of an experienced advisor—often leads to better outcomes than relying on one alone.

In conclusion, expert guidance is a valuable tool for anyone wishing to thrive.  They provide knowledge and experience that help us make sound decisions.  At the same time, we must recognize when our own judgment is sufficient and when to ask for help, whether from professionals or supportive family members.  By balancing independence with consultation, we can achieve personal growth and success.

In this essay we will examine the issues that arise when working in a group versus working alone. The focus will be on how these situations affect each person rather than the group as a whole. First, we will look at the differences between group dynamics and individual work, then explore the challenges that come with being part of a team. Finally, we will consider how these challenges can either benefit or hinder a person.

Do you remember the last time you had to complete a project? You probably thought about how to tackle it on your own or with others. Working alone means you are the sole person responsible for the task. In contrast, a group is made up of several people who come together with a common goal. A group’s structure, processes, and interpersonal relationships all influence how it functions. These concepts are important not only in academic settings but also throughout the workplace and other collective endeavors.

Group dynamics concerns the reasons why groups form and how they develop over time, and many theories attempt to explain that process. While there are many benefits to working in a team, there are also drawbacks. For example, individuals may feel that they have less control over the task compared to when they work alone. Dominant members can monopolise the discussion while others become passive, limiting the overall learning experience. Nevertheless, well‑coordinated teamwork can bring out a wider range of skills and deepen understanding through shared discussion.

Being part of a team also helps to build interpersonal abilities such as speaking, listening, leadership, and motivating others—skills that remain useful throughout one’s education and future career. To make the most of these advantages, effective group management is essential.

Technology has always acted as a compelling and mysterious field for me. My involvement and superior results in these events prove to show not only my interest in this field, but my capabilities as well. These experiences transfer directly over to the internship, allowing for a smooth transition without much confusion.

Therefore, I believe this internship is perfect for me.

Emerson’s claim that “unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow” resonates with me. It reminds us that everyone has the potential to strive for more in life. The passage invites people to think about their ambitions and whether they are willing to push beyond their comfort zone. I will explain why I find Emerson’s assertion convincing.

First, Emerson’s words inspire confidence in many readers. A strong message can awaken a sense of possibility, encouraging people to pursue higher goals and break through limits they never thought possible. They begin to believe that they can surpass their own expectations. Conversely, those who give up before trying often end up feeling unsure about what they truly want to accomplish.

Those who step beyond their boundaries experience a more successful way of living. They discover what they are capable of and learn how to achieve it fully. This creates a sense of empowerment: they feel prepared to tackle any task that comes their way. Some people describe the feeling as a “weight‑lifting” moment, realizing what they have been missing. It stops them from overthinking and self‑imposed obstacles that hold them back from meeting their goals.

Moreover, pushing past limits delivers more experience. When you take on new challenges, you grow more knowledgeable and ready to handle future demands. Experienced individuals can adapt to different roles with ease because they have already learned how to overcome diverse obstacles. This continual learning cycle means they are always ready for new work, and challenges no longer feel insurmountable.

In conclusion, Emerson’s statement carries a powerful lesson for us all. It serves as one of the most motivating quotes ever produced, encouraging people to value themselves more deeply and strive toward higher achievements. Those who keep their ambitions within their current skill set are, in fact, not fully growing. Many hesitate because they fear the unknown, but those who are willing to go beyond their comfort zones reap the benefits of a richer, more experience‑rich life.

Most high school students prefer to complete the standard four-year program, entering college after graduation and applying during their senior year with the help of counselors and teachers. Graduating early can be difficult for adolescents because learning speeds vary, and some may progress faster than others. School districts should allow students to decide whether to graduate early and give them more freedom to shape their future. Those who follow the traditional four-year plan can avoid the additional pressure and anxiety, yet still have the opportunity to choose elective classes.

Every student knows that passing courses and tracking credits is essential for graduation. Efforts to graduate early can heighten anxiety and pressure, potentially leading to mental health issues. Parents who constantly monitor grades may frustrate their children, often restricting privileges when performance falters, which can further stress adolescents.

Fear of falling behind and receiving low grades is common, yet this concern is diminished for students who stay on the traditional track. Teachers often recommend extra courses in the summer or evenings to advance academically. By staying in the four-year plan, students eliminate the need for additional work, allowing them to complete assignments without the urgency that accompanies early graduation.

The school offers opportunities to try new subjects through electives. When students graduate early, they may lose access to some electives, as the courses might not align with their accelerated schedule; otherwise, they can take as many as they wish to challenge themselves and deepen their knowledge.

In conclusion, completing the traditional four-year high school is a better option. Students can receive support from teachers and school resources while avoiding the distraction of extra pressure. Excessive time devoted to additional work undermines focus on core assignments. Elective classes, however, are valuable for learning new activities and providing a balanced academic experience.

High school students usually follow the standard four‑year track, finishing their diploma and then applying for college in their senior year. This traditional path offers several advantages that questioning the idea of early graduation would overlook.

People learn at different speeds, and many students would find an accelerated schedule stressful. The pressure to finish coursework in a shorter time can cause anxiety and mental distress. When grades are monitored closely by parents, it can create a tense atmosphere where students feel they must perform at every moment or risk losing privileges. The fear of falling behind or receiving lower grades is real, but for those who stay on the normal timeline this pressure is less intense.

Teachers often advise students who may want to graduate early to take extra courses during summer or evening sessions. While this can be helpful, it also adds to their workload. Students who stay the standard four years avoid the rush, having the same amount of time to complete assignments and study without constantly feeling hurried. Responsibility for learning remains the same, but the pacing is more manageable.

In a regular four‑year program, schools allow students to explore new subjects through electives. These courses give students a chance to discover interests outside of core requirements. Students who graduate early miss out on this flexibility because the focus is on completing credit requirements quickly, leaving little room for electives that would not directly help them finish early.

Overall, sticking to the traditional four‑year plan is a sensible choice. It offers reliable support from teachers and counselors and reduces the risk of burnout associated with accelerated schedules. While early graduation might seem attractive, the added pressure can distract students from learning and harm their well‑being.

Elective courses are valuable; they provide a way to broaden horizons and relieve stress by offering a break from mandatory classes. Keeping these options open within the four‑year framework benefits everyone.

Growing up in the Generic City area, I witnessed a lot of drugs, gangs, and violence. The image that these groups present is far from positive and the outcomes of such paths are often disastrous. I once had a friend whose father shot himself because of a poor choice; that tragedy made the friend reflect and, tragically, he thought that was the only solution.

On the other hand, many people choose to positively influence society. During my three years of high school, I saw students who helped others without being selfish; many volunteered for the community and hoped to inspire others to do the same. I had the chance to throw a kids’ Halloween party at a church; it was enjoyable and fun.

Honestly, I do not think I am either a good or a bad example. I make mistakes, and that was how I was taught to grow. I believe that learning comes from making mistakes, evaluating them, and then improving—only then can we truly help inspire others.  

In conclusion, I am hesitant about using examples as the only way to influence others because they can be negative when driven by poor choices. I think a better idea is to strive to be the best version of yourself, because at the end of the day there is only one of you among many, and it is best to remain unique.

Is modeling your own conduct the most effective way to influence others? Sometimes it can backfire, because people are not always displaying positive behavior. There are moments when someone is in a bad mood, acts recklessly, and engages in harmful activities; at other times, they may be charming, well‑mannered, and inspiring.

I grew up in the Generic_City area, where I witnessed a lot of drug use, gang activity, and violence. The example these groups set is far from commendable, and their path leads to terrible outcomes. I once knew a friend whose father committed suicide after making a poor decision that he believed was the only way out.

On the other hand, many individuals choose to impact society positively. During my three years of high school I saw classmates who worked hard for others, avoided selfishness, and often volunteered to help the community. They inspired those around them to take similar actions. I had the chance to host a children’s Halloween party at a church; it was a fun experience and taught me the value of giving back.

I don’t consider myself a perfect role model, nor do I see myself as a terrible one. I make mistakes because that is how I was raised. I was taught that the only way to learn is through error, evaluating those mistakes, and then using that insight to improve oneself and inspire others.

In conclusion, I believe that while setting an example can be powerful, it is not always positive because people can make harmful choices. It is better, in my view, to strive to be the best version of oneself, because each individual is unique and there are many of us in the world.

It is essential to show your true self in every situation; that is what makes life beautiful, because it allows us to connect with people who have different personalities. Unfortunately, the world today can be cruel and heartless. Bullying often arises from trivial differences such as clothes, shoes, or looks, and it can happen over almost anything. When people are targets, they may begin to hate themselves and try to pretend they are someone else.

I stopped wanting to go to school, and I rarely left my house or spoke to anyone. It was a very bleak period. Then one of my close friends asked why I wasn’t attending class, and I confessed everything. He told me plainly to ignore the hateful comments and to live life fully. Since that day, we have been inseparable; we have each other’s backs no matter what. A few weeks later I talked to my mother about it. We had a long conversation and she encouraged me to ignore the negativity because life is short and nothing should hold me back. That conversation shifted my perspective and taught me a powerful lesson about how to see life.

Living honestly in modern society is a challenge. Even something as simple as calling someone’s shoes unattractive can influence their self‑esteem. They may buy items they dislike or do things they do not want, simply to conform with better‑off peers who boast stylish clothes and shoes. The pressure to fit in prevents many people from being true to themselves, because fear of judgment is overwhelming.

More support should be available for those who are dealing with bullying and self‑doubt. Encouraging people to love who they are and to respect themselves would help every victim of harsh words. In extreme cases a hurtful remark can push a person toward self‑harm, so teaching empathy and respect is critical. Parents need to instill respect in children early on, so that societal pressure to care about the opinions of others is minimized. Everyone should live a life of authenticity.

Being real is the greatest achievement. When others say negative things, it can feel like they are trashing you, but these challenges are inevitable. Overcoming them only makes us stronger, shaping us into better human beings. The struggle motivates us to do great things, making ourselves and loved ones proud. Remaining true to who you are is the ultimate accomplishment in this world.

If you’re looking for enjoyable ways to spend time in a park, there are plenty of options. You can walk your dog, have a picnic with family or friends, spot animals, or ride a bike, skateboard, or scooter.

Walking your dog is a great choice because it gives both you and your pet physical activity and the chance to explore new places together. The park’s paths are safe and scenic, making it an ideal spot for a relaxed stroll. You’ll enjoy the fresh air, the chance to bond with your dog, and the opportunity to meet other pet owners.

Another fun activity is having a picnic. Bringing a blanket, snacks, and a bottle of water turns the park into a social gathering spot. You can chat with friends or family while enjoying a meal outdoors. Picnics are especially enjoyable on warm, sunny days. After eating, you can wander around the park, discovering new areas and maybe encouraging newcomers to visit again.

Some parks feature animal exhibits or farms, where you can observe creatures such as goats, chickens, pigs, or even fish and turtles. Watching these animals can be fascinating and educational. Signage or guides often explain each animal’s habits and diet, and some parks even allow visitors to offer food that the animals can eat.

Finally, the park is a perfect place for riding bikes, skateboards, or scooters. With wide, traffic‑free paths and ample space, you can practice safely. The scenery adds to the enjoyment, and riding with friends provides a fun, low‑risk alternative to busy streets.

Overall, a park offers many enjoyable activities that combine relaxation, exercise, and social interaction, making it a wonderful place to spend time with loved ones.

Later, as we get to know each other better, our view of the person and the person’s view of us can shift.

I remember the first time I met my boyfriend’s mother. I was shy and nervous, and I felt I was coming across as bored or uneasy. I was simply careful not to say or do anything that might upset her. Her opinion of me improved, showing that the first impression had changed.

As we spent more time together, I learned that she is a thoughtful, caring person. Choosing to complete high school in only three years and jump straight into college or the workforce feels thrilling at first—after all, all the effort seems to pay off. Yet the reality of accelerating the curriculum brings significant drawbacks that make such a plan ill‑advised.

First, students would have to attend classes during the summer or in the evenings. Many take up part‑time jobs over the break, and adding coursework would cut away that opportunity for earning income. Even if they manage to study during the week, the extra homework, test preparation, and project work would keep them locked into a demanding schedule, leaving little room for rest or recovery.

Second, finishing early limits the chance to enroll in elective courses. Core subjects—mathematics, science, language arts—must all fit into an already packed timetable. Because of that constraint, students often find themselves unable to take art, music, drama, or other enrichment activities. These electives are not only enjoyable but also critical for a well‑rounded education and a stronger college application.

Third, the added pressure can lead to high stress levels. Balancing coursework, assignments, quizzes, and presentations all at once is exhausting. Students may feel constantly behind, which erodes confidence and negatively impacts mental well‑health. There simply isn’t enough time for self‑care, social activities, or to pursue personal interests.

In short, while dropping a year might seem advantageous, the overload of summer and after‑school classes, the loss of elective opportunities, and the heightened stress make it an unwise choice. Schools should encourage students to finish the full four‑year program so they can enjoy a balanced, comprehensive education before moving on to college or the workforce.

I agree with Emerson’s assertion that some people never grow up. When a person behaves like a child, it is often difficult for them to change. Three main factors explain why – attitude, violence, and the way friends treat them.  

Many would argue that everyone can change, but this is not always true. People can refuse to alter their attitudes toward others, and they can also refuse to behave differently toward us. For instance, I have a habit of being very harsh toward my sister, who is three years younger. I often scold her when she asks me to do something, even though I know she is still very young. This kind of unyielding attitude is hard to change, both for her and for me.  

Violence is another obstacle to growth. Some people cannot stop being violent, even if they try to control it. In middle school I was normally calm and friendly, but after a bout of teasing from classmates, I began reacting with anger. I still try to keep my temper under control because I do not want to cause trouble, yet the urge to lash out can remain. Another example is my youngest sister, who becomes violent when she feels her older sister is angry with her. Even then, she makes a conscious effort to suppress that violence, just as I do.  

Friendship can also hinder personal development. Some individuals use friends for money or favors, paying only for what they want, while others behave kindly in front of us and later speak cruelly behind our backs. Watching a popular girl pretending to be friendly with a newcomer in a movie, only to gossip harshly after the newcomer leaves, is a clear illustration of this duplicity. Such behavior can make it difficult, or even impossible, for the person affected to trust or grow.  

In conclusion, growth is hard when one’s attitude is rigid, one's tendency toward violence is strong, and friends use or betray them. These factors make it likely that some people will never truly mature. I stand with Emerson’s view that certain individuals remain childlike because changing those traits is exceptionally challenging.

I believe that people in this world have the power to choose their own character, yet many also let outside influences shape them. Friendships, family, and even casual acquaintances can encourage habits that are either good or harmful. While some decisions stem from our own convictions, others are a by‑product of the company we keep. Those who remain true to their positive traits often find themselves on a path to success, whereas those who allow negative influences to dominate are more likely to stumble.

For instance, a child raised in a supportive family may develop confidence and kindness. Conversely, a child who grows up amid conflict or neglect can adopt distrust or anger as coping mechanisms. These early patterns can carry into adulthood, affecting how we act in relationships and at work. Even friendships that seem harmless can slowly erode self‑respect and lead us toward bad habits such as procrastination or dishonesty. On the other hand, close friends who practice honesty, discipline, and empathy can strengthen our own virtues.

The same dynamics play out in romantic relationships. A healthy partnership provides encouragement and groundedness, while a toxic one can leave lasting emotional wounds and negative outlooks. Arguments, blaming, and hurtful actions can leave scars that influence future decisions and how we treat others. A single relationship can tip the balance between maintaining a constructive character or falling into destructive patterns.

It is important to remember that not every person is unduly controlled by outside forces. Intelligent, self‑aware individuals often recognize that others may try to derail them, but they resist. They set boundaries, choose supportive companions, and stay focused on their goals. If you feel pulled in a negative direction, the best solution is to reflect on your core values and make a deliberate choice: cultivate those traits that align with success and well‑being, and steer clear of influences that would undermine them. In the end, your character is shaped by both your choices and the people around you; the key lies in deciding what kind of traits you will allow to guide you.

Can extending school hours really save energy? I believe that adding two extra hours to each weekday is not a wise choice. The plan would make life harder for students with commitments after school, and it would create difficulties for teachers as well.

Adding extra hours would burden students, especially those who hold part‑time jobs or participate in after‑school clubs and sports. They would already be tired when school ends, and the longer day would cut into the time they need to relax or meet friends. Families would also feel the strain: parents and guardians often have to pick up children or manage household chores on the same days.

Teachers would not be spared from the trouble either. Many educators live outside the school district and must leave school early to drive their children home. A longer day would force them to adjust their commutes or take longer vacations. The disruption to their personal schedules would make the system less attractive to skilled instructors.

There are few benefits that outweigh these problems. Proponents argue that longer days mean more projects can be finished, tests given in full, and homework reduced, allowing students to graduate faster. Unfortunately, this ideal picture ignores the reality that higher workload can lead to fatigue and burnout, not increased achievement.

Moreover, the argument that a longer school week could reduce overall travel or energy use is weak: students would still need to commute, and the extra classroom hours would consume additional electricity and heating. The savings, if any, would be marginal compared to the costs in time and well‑being.

In short, the proposal to extend school hours seems misguided. It disrupts daily routines, stresses both students and teachers, and offers limited practical benefits. Schools should look for other ways to conserve energy—such as reducing lighting or adjusting heating schedules—that do not interfere with people’s lives.
