All you have around you are textbooks but no image or notion of what your invention might be. If only you could envisage a novel device, perhaps you could construct something. Yet without imagination, how can you cultivate knowledge? I concur with Einstein's assertion. I believe imagination supersedes knowledge.

I agree with Einstein's quote because imagination has driven all our innovations to date. Without imagination, how were many of the items we possess conceived? Consider the telephone. It could not have emerged without someone visualizing a device that enables communication without leaving one's home. Imagination is essential for creating new things. Similarly, the camera: the inventor had to imagine a mechanism that captures moments almost instantaneously. Even as a student, I rely on imagination to generate compelling narrative openings for assignments like this one.

Moreover, I hold Einstein’s quote because, without imagination, knowledge becomes largely futile. For instance, when studying a new vocabulary list, you may know all the definitions yet cannot paraphrase them or deploy the words in varied contexts. Why? Because you cannot picture them. Another illustration is when reading a book; mastery of reading alone is insufficient for full comprehension. You must imagine the narrative, visualizing the story to grasp the book’s theme, setting, and tone.

Finally, I concur with Einstein’s statement because, absent imagination, our decisions would be made indiscriminately. For example, before speaking or acting, most of the time you anticipate the outcome of the action. Without this foresight, the result may be undesirable. Likewise, in an experiment, you hypothesize the expected outcome—an act that requires imagination. When signing a contract, you must envisage the ramifications of both signing and refusing. In other words, you need to envision contingencies before committing. Knowledge alone cannot guide decision-making.

In conclusion, Einstein’s observation resonates with me. Knowledge is not the paramount factor; imagination is the cornerstone of everything we undertake. We cannot fully grasp most concepts without visualizing them, nor can we invent without first conceiving. Similarly, sound decisions hinge on foreseeing outcomes. Ultimately, imagination enriches our existence. While knowledge is valuable, it does not impart the same depth of joy that imagination provides. It is the source of our long-standing contentment, our progress, and our resilience in this world.

The answer is no; simply standing or lying down at home will not bring results. However, when we stay busy and productive, we open many doors—learn new skills, meet people, and reach our goals.

Being productive lets us learn faster. When my mother enrolled me in a soccer team, I had no idea I would join or enjoy it. Yet I quickly learned to kick the ball, defend, and improve my speed. Another time, I faced an English vocabulary test and didn’t know half the words. I studied until I mastered them, which would not have happened if I had stayed idle.

Likewise, when I approached a new math teacher about a confusing equation, she clarified the problem and now supports me whenever I need help. These interactions would never have occurred if I had remained passive.

Imagine the possibilities when we are constantly doing something. Even when we think we don’t need help, asking for guidance can deepen our understanding instead of staying stuck in the same mindset.

Inactivity can also serve a purpose; perhaps they lack money or transportation to pursue opportunities. Yet simply doing nothing and hoping for good fortune will not produce results.

Are vacations a necessity to us and to our success? Why do we need them? While some say that inactivity gives us time to reinvent ourselves. Others believe that it instigates procrastination. Inactivity serves a purpose because it keeps us from giving up and it allows us time for new ideas.

In fact, students who take mental breaks during long testing periods score 31% higher than the ones who did not take any breaks. In conclusion, inactivity keeps us enthusiastic about our work.

I would like to begin this topic with an important question that no human being really thinks about: “How is technology impacting our health?” This is one of the most crucial questions that cannot be left unanswered.

Technology has rooted itself in our lives; from the moment we wake up until we go to bed, we interact with hundreds of devices, software programs, and tools. It allows people to complete many tasks without any contact with others: checking out books, shopping, and playing games can all be done online. The resulting limitation of human contact has had negative effects on people’s lives.

While some might argue that limiting human contact through technology has positive effects, most agree that the lack of personal interaction caused by technology is detrimental.

Consider two people: one who always uses technology to shop, check out books, play games, do homework, and even talk to friends or family; the other who prefers not to use technology at all, instead going to the store to buy a book, shopping for clothes in person, and visiting family members face‑to‑face. The technology‑dependent person is more likely to get sick, experience pain, or feel depressed sooner. This is because computers and devices encourage sedentary behavior, poor posture, neck strain, back problems, and hearing loss. Such habits can lead to chronic pain that is difficult to treat.

Having clarified the issue, let us return to the original question: “How is technology impacting our health?” If people truly thought about this question, they would see that technology is not positively affecting our health. It increases stress, worsens vision, causes back pain, leads to hearing loss, and produces many other negative outcomes. Another reason people feel depressed after extensive technology use is the lack of real‑world interaction; staying at home and doing everything on a device prevents forming friendships. Scientific studies show that everyone needs at least one or more friends to talk to when they feel down. This explains why many heavy technology users feel depressed and avoid interacting with others.

In conclusion, technology allows us to complete many tasks without contact, but the resulting limitation of human interaction has a negative effect on our lives. If people do not learn to control and manage their time and stop relying on technology at every opportunity, the next generation will be no different from us now. To improve the situation, people need to learn how to balance their time even when using technology; otherwise, the problem will worsen, leading many to suffer back pain, sickness, and depression from prolonged isolation and technology use.

The first thing I want to ask is one that most of us never pause to consider: “In what ways is technology affecting our health?” This question is crucial, yet it often goes unanswered.

Technology has become woven into our daily routine. From the moment we wake to the moment we go to bed, we interact with countless devices, applications, and tools. These gadgets let us accomplish tasks—reading, shopping, gaming—without touching another person. While this convenience is undeniable, the reduction in face‑to‑face interaction can have serious repercussions for our well‑being.

Some people argue that the decline in human contact brought about by technology is a net benefit. Others feel the opposite, believing that the lack of direct social interaction harms mental and physical health. Most people lean toward the latter view.

Consider two individuals. The first relies on technology for nearly everything: studying, shopping, communicating. The second prefers in‑person activities, such as visiting a bookstore, shopping in a physical store, or meeting family face‑to‑face instead of calling. The tech‑heavy person is more likely to develop health problems—pain, depression, or illness—earlier than the one who avoids excessive screen time. Devices and computers encourage a sedentary lifestyle, often leading to posture problems, neck strain, back pain, and even hearing loss. Over time, these habits can cause chronic discomfort that is difficult to treat.

Revisiting the initial question, “How is technology affecting our health?” we see that the evidence points to mostly negative outcomes. Technology can increase stress, worsen vision, cause back pain, and lower hearing acuity. Moreover, the scarcity of real‑life social interaction can trigger depression. Studies confirm that humans need at least one close friend to turn to when feeling low; the absence of such connections can worsen mental health.

In conclusion, technology enables us to perform many tasks without interacting with others, but this lack of human contact can erode our health. If we fail to learn how to manage our time and limit our reliance on digital devices, future generations may simply repeat the same patterns. The current trajectory seems irreversible; we live in a society where innovation dominates. The recovery lies in balancing technology use and fostering real social connections. Without intervention, we risk increasing back pain, illness, and depression in an increasingly isolated population.

For instance, if you’re struggling with weight, deciding to become fit means you might spend two hours a day at the gym or jog every morning. Over time, that commitment will likely let you lose weight and improve your physique. Determination also supports reaching broader goals. Suppose you’re a high‑school senior who wants to graduate but is falling behind in grades. By asking teachers for help, studying online, and practicing at home every day, you can raise your marks and finish the year on time.

Being determined also makes the time you spend more meaningful. When you finish a task, you feel proud and satisfied. Working consistently yields better results than sporadic effort, and the habit of persistence can strengthen your patience. It keeps you from giving up, even when faced with obstacles, and helps build a stronger character.

On the other hand, remaining idle while we have aspirations can feel futile. Without action, we risk ending up jobless, without money, and with little hope for the future. Imagine needing to buy a house but keeping all your time in idleness instead of searching for a job—that wasted time produces nothing for you. Furthermore, people may begin to see you as unreliable, especially when they are working hard and achieving while you simply sit around.

Deciding what to do isn’t difficult. Making a simple list of tasks helps; it breaks down what needs to be done, clarifies priorities, and boosts your sense of completion. By staying determined and organized, you set yourself on the path to success.

On the other hand, some people disagree with programs that allow early graduation. They believe students are not sufficiently prepared to graduate before the scheduled time and that students should complete all four years of high school to be ready for college or the workforce. Parents who oppose the program often view the summer or evening courses as additional pressure on their children. Some suggest that the better choice is for students to finish the full four years, even if it prolongs the time to graduate.

To conclude, pressure can be a tool that helps people excel in their projects and life in general. When people take risks and have the courage to pursue their goals, they will achieve them. The time invested in positive actions is essential for reaching those goals. The program offers essential support to students, helping them realize they have the capacity to achieve their goals. It is a great opportunity for growth and success; one year can make a big difference and bring us closer to that dream.

Some school districts now offer students the chance to finish high school in three years instead of the usual four, and I support this idea. I believe that an early completion allows students to enter college or the workforce sooner, giving them more time to explore their interests and make better informed decisions about their future careers. Although critics argue that an accelerated path can be stressful, the benefits of having an extra year to plan can outweigh these concerns.

When students are faced with major life choices, they often spend time weighing their options carefully. Completing high school a year early gives them that additional time to reflect on the subjects they enjoy most and to choose a college that feels like a good fit. A first‑year advantage can also let them pursue special programs or study abroad opportunities that they would otherwise miss. This extra time, while not a huge stretch, can be pivotal in shaping a thoughtful and purposeful academic trajectory.

Time invested wisely is an investment in oneself. Some parents, teachers, and students worry that early graduation will cut into leisure time and family moments. However, the reality can be quite the opposite: students often find themselves more focused and motivated, prioritizing their goals more effectively. I personally took an advanced English course during summer school in Generic City. Despite the long commute and early mornings, the experience accelerated my progress and brought me closer to graduation. Those who are willing to make a few extra efforts often reap extraordinary rewards.

Opponents of accelerated programs claim that students are not fully prepared to finish a year early and that four years of high school give them enough maturity. They worry that added summer or evening courses will place undue pressure on students and may even delay overall graduation. While these concerns are understandable, they overlook the opportunity that a “fast‑track” program offers students who are ready to take on more responsibility. Instead of postponing the inevitable, a focused plan can help students complete the necessary curriculum more efficiently.

In conclusion, pressure can be a catalyst for growth when used constructively. Students who embrace the challenge of an early graduation often discover new strengths and confidence in their abilities. The program provides essential support and signals to students that they have the capacity to achieve their goals ahead of schedule. A single additional year can make a significant difference, bringing them one step closer to realizing their dreams.

All schools have different educational activities, including playing an instrument. There are so many things you can do when you play an instrument. Everyone has seen marching bands doing all types of exciting things in the middle of a football game. Have you not seen the routines they make, those take hard work! Orchestras play classical music and make their sound flow in the room. Not only do they play classical music, but they also play loud and exciting music. Everything you can do while playing an instrument is enjoyable. Some things are more enjoyable than others like being able to listen to yourself making good music, going on fun field trips, and being able to find all different types of music.

While playing an instrument you play all different types of music, and all of the pieces of music are good. When you hear yourself play a song well you get a boost of confidence. Hearing your class play well makes you confident that your concert will sound great. It feels good to know that you're capable of playing music that others who aren't able to do. You get to enjoy the amazing sound your class makes. Whenever you play an instrument you normally audition for the class you want to get into and when you get into it, you are full of joy. It's always nice to know that you can achieve the level that you want to achieve. The opportunities you get while playing an instrument are endless.

When being in band or orchestra you get the opportunity to go on field trips. Schools don't normally go on field trips unless the students are in band or orchestra. They offer the field trips to people who play an instrument because of all their hard work they put into it. All the field trips you go on are enjoyable because of the people in your class. You always make friends whenever you join band or orchestra. Some schools know that the students want more fun, so they include more field trips than others. Every field trip is a gift to the students who play their instruments from the school. Some places that schools go to are Kings Dominion, Busch Gardens, Hershey Park, and many more exciting places. Those all have roller coasters, water activities, and carnival games, who wouldn't want to go there.

Every movie or show has a soundtrack which the classes can play. You can always search up the sheet music to any song you want to play. You can also make your own sheet music and play that yourself. You can play every song on an instrument. People enjoy playing the music they've wanted to play since they first started playing an instrument. There are movies that people love and the people who can play an instrument are able to play that movies theme song. Not a single song cannot be put in sheet music so, if anyone ever wanted to play their favorite song they could search it up and it would pop up. Even though some songs are harder to make sheet music for they're still possible to do.

When playing an instrument, practice does make perfect. Nothing about playing an instrument is easy, but everything about it is fun. The effort put into playing your instrument does pay off at the end. Playing well can make you so happy and proud of yourself. Not only are you proud of yourself, but others are proud of you. Being able to play an instrument is a privilege that not everybody gets. There is nothing that can stop someone from becoming a part of the music community. The friends you can make and go with to the exciting field trips. Play all the music you've ever wanted to play. Everything you can do in band is limitless.

Music making is an important part of many school programs.  
Every school has its own way of introducing students to an instrument, and the
activities that come with it are many and varied. You have probably seen
marching bands performing powerfully during a football game, or witnessed an
orchestra filling a hall with smooth, classical melodies. Whether playing soft
film music or loud, energetic pieces, the act of playing an instrument is
always enjoyable, and some experiences are more rewarding than others—listening
to your own good performance, going on fun trips, and discovering many styles
of music.

When you sit down to play, you encounter all kinds of music, and each piece
has something special. Hearing yourself play a song correctly boosts your
confidence. Seeing your classmates play well gives you hope that your own
concert will turn out great. Realising that you can create music that others
might not be able to is satisfying. Giving a class a good sound creates a
sense of pride that lasts when you move on to the next level. Knowing that you
can reach the level you aim for is a joy. The possibilities offered by
instrumental music are endless.

One of the biggest advantages of being in a band or orchestra is the chance
to go on field trips. Many schools only provide such trips for music
students because of the dedication they show. These excursions are fun, and
they build friendships that last. Some schools schedule more trips to give
students more enjoyment. The places we visit—theme parks like Kings
Dominion, Busch Gardens, Hershey Park—offer rides, water fun and games.
Everyone looks forward to these adventures.

Every movie or TV show has a soundtrack that a class can explore. You can
search for the score of any tune you like, or even create your own. Every
song can be played on an instrument, and people feel happiest when they can
perform the songs they love. There are countless songs that have been
transcribed to sheet music; if you want to play a favorite theme, you can
almost always find it. Even the more difficult arrangements can be
implemented.

Practice truly makes perfect. Nothing about playing an instrument is easy,
but everything makes sense and feels fun. The hard work you put in pays off
in the end. Playing well brings joy and pride—not only for you but also
for others. Having the ability to play an instrument is a privilege not every
person enjoys. Nothing stops someone from joining the musical community.
You will meet friends who will accompany you on exciting trips, and there
will always be new music to learn. The world of band and orchestra is
limitless.

What are the benefits of working with a group and working alone? I believe that working in groups helps you to have more ideas, more knowledge, because if you communicate with your group members, they'll think about different ideas to proceed the work that is getting done. Working alone sometimes helps you more than working with groups because you are responsible for your own work.

I rather work by myself because I've had bad experience working with groups. When I work in groups sometimes I'm the one that has to do all the work, and in my opinion if we are working in groups we have to help each other, communicate and share our thoughts because if we don't do that what's the point of working in groups. However, I think working in groups is important because you can come out of your comfort zone and be free to share your thoughts with your group members, and you can make friends too. For example, I'm a very shy person, it's rare the times I talk in class but when I'm in a group I have to talk, share my thoughts with my group members and communicate with them.

What are the benefits of working with a group versus working alone? I believe that group work can generate more ideas and knowledge, because communicating with teammates often leads to diverse perspectives that advance the project. However, working alone can be more advantageous for some, as it places full responsibility for the work on the individual.

I prefer working by myself because I have had negative experiences with group work. In past collaborations, I often ended up doing all the work. I feel that group work should involve mutual help, communication, and idea sharing; otherwise, the point of collaborating is lost. Yet, I also recognize that group work can push us out of our comfort zones, encourage sharing, and foster friendships. For example, I am a shy person who rarely speaks in class, but in a group I must contribute and communicate with others.

I prefer working alone for several reasons: I can focus better on my own tasks, I bear sole responsibility, I must ensure timely submission, and any poor grade reflects my performance. I am accountable for my own actions and must verify that everything is correct to receive full credit.

I dislike group work for similar reasons: teammates sometimes neglect their responsibilities, produce messy work that is hard to understand, waste time on trivial activities, or rely on their phones instead of contributing. When group members fail to complete their parts on time, we risk submitting late and losing credit.

In conclusion, group work can be beneficial, but its success largely depends on the participants. If collaborators are diligent and care about the work, group projects can thrive. Conversely, a partner who is indifferent or merely playing around can derail the effort, leading to poor outcomes unless the rest of the group compensates. Therefore, I find working alone to be more advantageous for me, as it allows focused effort and full responsibility for my academic success.

What are the advantages of working in a team versus working alone? In my view, group work can generate more ideas and expand knowledge, because when you discuss a task with others you are exposed to different viewpoints and strategies that you might not have thought of on your own. On the other hand, staying on your own can be advantageous because you are in full control of your work and are solely accountable for the outcome.

I generally prefer to work by myself, largely because my past experiences with teams have not always been positive. In group projects I often found myself carrying more of the workload than my teammates. I believe that a true group effort should involve everyone contributing, communicating, and sharing ideas; without that collaboration, the purpose of being together is lost. Nevertheless, I recognise that group work can push you out of your comfort zone: it forces you to voice your thoughts and can even help you make new friends. For example, as someone who is quite shy, I rarely speak up in class, but when I’m required to contribute in a group I am compelled to share my ideas and interact with others.

My reasons for preferring solitary work are simple. I can concentrate better on my tasks, I bear only my own responsibilities, and I am the one who must ensure the work is finished on time. If a grade is low, the blame falls on me alone rather than being diluted among a group. I am also entirely responsible for checking that everything is correct to secure the full credit.

The negatives of group work, in my experience, include members who are not accountable, who do their parts in a disorganized way where their handwriting or style is unclear, and who treat the sessions as free time, often distracted by phones. When teamwork is uneven, deadlines can be missed and the whole group may suffer a lower mark, while the least diligent members might still receive credit.

I believe that group work can be beneficial, but only when the participants are committed and care about the project. If you collaborate with people who are diligent and respectful of deadlines, the collective effort will be fruitful. If the group contains individuals who avoid responsibilities, the entire effort can stall and result in a poor outcome unless you step in to do the work alone.

In summary, I think that working alone offers more advantages for me than working in groups. It allows me to focus, take full responsibility, and ensure that my work meets the required standards. Ultimately, the choice depends on the specific situation and the people involved, but for me solo work is the most effective approach.

Being yourself brings out the best parts of a person. When you remain true to yourself, you do not need to change for anyone; you simply become a better version of who you already are. It can be good to adapt in life, but don’t lose the essence of what makes you distinct because that essence—your attitude and personality—sets you apart. Many people change because they want to improve or because they feel isolated and quiet. The way you present yourself reflects who you are, and attempting to revert to a person you no longer are can be difficult because you are, in fact, evolving.

First, being yourself means embracing your uniqueness. You do not need to transform yourself to impress others. Even when you are rude or harsh, such traits tend to persist; they are part of your character. Change often occurs after a significant loss, such as the death of someone close, or after enduring trauma, abuse, violence, or depression. These events can profoundly alter a person. By staying true to yourself while pushing for personal growth, you may surprise even your family, who have grown accustomed to your behavior. If you decide to become better, do it because you want it, not to satisfy anyone else. Being authentic means you no longer care overly about others’ opinions, because the real you cannot be altered by them.

Second, changing too much can cause you to lose your inner self. You might try to become someone you admire or respect, but if you do it only for friends, it will not last. Your essence reflects who you truly are, a quality that those who love you will appreciate. As my grandmother used to say, “Sweetie, be yourself; do not change for anyone, because no one will love you as deeply as your family does.” Keep your inner self safe; even if you are perceived as rude or annoying, you remain a cherished member of your family. Do not be changed by others’ perceptions of you; be yourself and let your hidden strengths surface. People may try to bring you down with words, but maintain your individuality and show others your true character.

Third, personality reveals character. Nobody wants to be friends with someone who claims superiority over everyone else; authenticity is far more attractive. Show where you come from, even if you are poor or lack material wealth. Demonstrate that you do not care about superficial judgments; people will recognize you for who you are. Avoid becoming the mean person you did not intend to be just because friends have suddenly cut you off. Likewise, do not abandon who you are due to someone’s advice, unless you genuinely believe it will help you become a better person. Stand out by being yourself, not by copying everyone else.

Fourth, returning to a former version of yourself can be difficult once you have moved beyond it. You may have pushed away the person you didn’t want to be. Trying to reclaim that old self can take so long that it feels impossible. Those who left because of your change may not return. The best strategy is to embrace the new you, loving the transformation that has happened. Let the person you aimed to become settle into your life, and celebrate the growth you have achieved.

Finally, continue to be yourself instead of molding yourself into someone else. Your authentic self can serve you well throughout life. In some moments, you may not act in full alignment with your core values, but do it only for yourself, not to please those who do not deserve your change. Strive to be unique and true, and others will admire you for it. By staying your own person, you will reflect the qualities you wish to embody as you grow older and leave your parents’ home.

Being yourself brings out the best in a person. When you remain true to who you are you are not becoming someone you are not. Sometimes change is useful, but it should not erase the qualities that make you unique. A person’s attitude and personality are what really define them, so losing the way you are only makes you worse. Many people change because they want to be better or because they feel stuck, but trying to become someone else can be hard because it means abandoning parts of yourself.

First, being yourself means respecting your own uniqueness. There is no need to pretend to fit someone else’s idea. Even if you have been rude or disrespectful, you cannot pretend to be anyone else without breaking your own identity. People often change when they lose someone dear or when they suffer from abuse, violence, or depression. These experiences can shift who you are. By staying true to yourself and pushing for improvement, you can influence your family and friends, who have learned to accept you for who you are. If you aim to become better, do it because you want to grow, not because you fear what others will say. Remember, those who love you will accept you as you are.

Secondly, changing too much can make you lose your inner self. When you try to become someone you admire, you start to forget who you really are. This change should be driven by your own desire, not by others. My grandmother used to tell me, “Sweetie, be yourself. Change only if you truly want to.” No matter how annoying or difficult you may seem, you are still loved by your family. No one should be forced to change just because they think you are not good enough. By showing your real self, you can reveal qualities you have hidden and undo the negativity that others have spread about you.

Thirdly, a person’s personality reflects their character. Nobody wants to be friends with someone who acts superior or pretends to be better than others. You should always be honest about where you come from, even if you come from modest surroundings. It shows that you are not worried about what people think. If a friend stops talking to you, do not become a mean person; that will only push them further away. Listening to advice about change is okay, but it should not become an excuse to lose yourself. Stand out for who you truly are instead of copying others.

Fourth, going back to the person you were before can be very difficult once you have moved on. The people who left you because of your previous habits may never return. The changes you made have become a part of you. Instead of trying to reclaim an old self, embrace the new and love the growth you have achieved. The person you become now will stand on your own strengths and experiences.

Finally, always be yourself and do not attempt to become someone you are not. The way you behave now will shape the rest of your life. You do not need to be everyone’s favorite, but you should be true to yourself for those who deserve to see your genuine self. Strive to be unique and authentic, and everyone will appreciate the real you.

Technology, the 21st century’s most remarkable creation, captivates nearly everyone. Is it truly that magnificent? When I was a child, people warned that “technology will erode our social lives.” I dismissed that notion then, yet today I recognize the meaning behind their caution.

Primarily, technology’s objective is to streamline certain tasks, not to render us antisocial or unhealthy. In my view, technology boasts immense potential, yet we underutilize it. Instead of preparing our own meals, we now order from restaurants that are far less nutritious. Another significant issue is that people structure their lives around technology; the loss of that technology feels fatal. Everyone relies on social apps on their phones, and this reliance largely explains why many prefer digital interaction over face‑to‑face conversation.

Secondly, technology has its advantages just as it has its disadvantages. One key benefit is the reduction of time wasted on routine errands. Previously, communications via mail took hours to reach their destination; now that process can be completed in a minute or two. Moreover, technology enables us to design zero‑waste homes, cars, and aircraft by operating on electricity instead of fossil fuels that harm the planet. We capture electrical energy through solar panels, wind turbines, and hydroelectric generators. A further advantage of energy harvesting is its virtually limitless supply—unless a catastrophic event vaporizes water, blocks the sun, or halts the wind. Until such disasters occur, we can rely on clean energy.

Thirdly, I believe technology is a monumental invention for humankind. Although it has numerous adverse effects, remedies are straightforward. By ceasing to build our lives around social media or technology and treating it merely as a supplementary communication tool, we can mitigate its harms. Technology has advanced far from its humble beginnings; once it powered only a light bulb, it now energizes cars, homes, phones, and entire cities—every human‑made structure incorporates some form of technology.

Finally, these brilliant inventions and dazzling innovations divert our attention and isolate us from one another. Technology is a brilliant tool yet also a detrimental one to our social fabric. Humans are inherently social; if something obstructs that fundamental aspect, the consequences are dire. For millennia, we have evolved in a particular social context, and now we attempt to alter it... What I’m stressing is that technology is a beneficial element of our lives, but social interaction is not one of them.

Do people who have mastered something grow, even if they do not try anything else? Some believe that mastering one skill is enough. They think they can be content with what they know, and they assume they will never grow in any other area if they do not try. If someone decides to focus only on one area, that is fine, but their knowledge will increase only in that domain and nothing else. Growth stalls when a person’s mindset is locked into past mastery and does not expand.

For example, Ms. Generic_Name, a beautiful woman, ran a plant store and taught others about plants. One day she told a group of children that plants do not grow on their own and that people must help them. She led the kids to the back of the store where she showed them an apple seed. Ms. Generic_Name told the children that she had taken care of the seed, but she stopped because she thought that once the plant grew enough, she would no longer need to tend it. She watched the plant stand there, convinced her work was done, and did not care for it further, unaware that it would never grow more. This is exactly what happens with people who master something and then do not attempt anything else; they become stagnant and cannot grow. Thus, if people believe they are satisfied with what they have mastered and do not try anything new, they will not grow.

Knowledge is central to growth. Ms. Generic_Name initially knew little about plants and did not realize she had to nurture them until they were strong enough. After years of experience, she gained deep knowledge and did not content herself with what she already knew. She enrolled in a college program to study plant species from around the world. Thanks to her enthusiasm, Estency Generic_Name became one of the world’s leading plant specialists. No one should be comfortable knowing only what they wish to know; people should continually seek more knowledge, just as Ms. Generic_Name did.

Some argue that mastering one field is sufficient because one can pursue a passion. For instance, Generic_Name entered college with the dream of becoming a constructor and graduated, but his work does not match his original aspirations. He could have become an architect but chose a lesser role. Yet people should seek knowledge beyond a single master and continue learning new things every day.

In conclusion, people will never grow if they do not try new things. A person’s knowledge increases with time and interest. Growth is largely driven by knowledge, so it is better to remain open to learning more.

Can someone who has mastered a skill still grow if they never try anything else? Many people think that once you have excelled in one area, you can be satisfied with that and stop learning more. They believe that a specialist will never expand beyond their existing expertise unless they deliberately search for new knowledge. However, if people fixate only on what they already know, their growth will be stagnant.

Take the example of Ms. A, a well‑known plant expert who runs a small shop and teaches others about gardening. One afternoon she explained to a group of children that plants do not grow by themselves; humans must nurture them. She brought out an apple seed and told the children that she had stopped caring for it once it grew enough, thinking that the plant would have to take care of itself from that point onward. She overlooked that the plant needed continual attention, and its growth stalled. Her story mirrors what happens when a person masters a discipline but refuses to expand beyond it: they become comfortable and cease to develop further.

Knowledge is the foundation of growth. Ms. A began with a limited understanding of plants and only then realized she had to keep learning. After years of practice she gained extensive knowledge and decided to study botany at university, traveling abroad to learn about diverse species. Her curiosity turned her into a leading specialist in her field. No one should settle for a narrow view of the world; individuals must keep pursuing new knowledge, just as Ms. A did.

Some may argue that mastering one thing is enough if it aligns with one’s passion. For instance, Generic B studied construction in college, pursued a career in that field, and found satisfaction. Yet even he had to learn new techniques, regulatory changes, and innovative materials to stay relevant. If one only clings to the initial mastery, they risk becoming obsolete. Continuous learning keeps skills fresh and minds active.

In summary, growth comes from continual effort and curiosity. Relying solely on a single mastery limits a person’s potential. By embracing new challenges and seeking additional knowledge, anyone can keep growing.

Students work hard; there is no doubt about that. They juggle schoolwork, homework, extracurricular activities, and sometimes part‑time jobs, all of which add stress to their lives. That is why it is important for them to get a break from time to time. I believe that students should enjoy a long summer holiday instead of a continuous year‑round school calendar. The reasons are: summer offers many activities that keep the mind active, it protects students’ health, and it benefits school staff as well.

Everyone needs a pause from their everyday routine to relax, enjoy life, and perhaps discover new interests. While formal education is essential for future success, outside experiences help students develop real‑world skills. During summer break a student can participate in sports, summer camps, internships, or other projects. These activities keep both the mind and body busy. Even though they are not studying academic subjects, students are forced to think critically, work cooperatively, and remain open to new ideas—all skills that are useful in real life. For instance, a camp might group a student with four strangers to solve a problem that requires teamwork, analysis, and creative solutions. Such experiences mirror the collaborative environment of school, so the student’s mind stays sharp during the break.

Not every student will choose activities, but everyone benefits from a mental respite. The academic year is long, and the cumulative demands can become overwhelming. Teen depression has risen in recent years; while many factors contribute, academic pressure plays a significant role. Chronic stress harms physical health, raising blood pressure, leading to weight loss, and increasing cortisol levels. Excess cortisol impairs thinking and reaction times—skills essential for school work. Without a break, students’ grades may slip because they cannot think clearly, further worsening their mental well‑being.

Finally, the long summer holiday is also essential for teachers, administrators, and counselors. Schools exist to educate, but it is the staff who make education possible. Those same arguments that apply to students also apply to them. A lengthy break allows teachers to plan lessons thoughtfully, reflect on their teaching, and spend quality time with family and friends. Teachers, like everyone else, need rest and personal fulfillment to perform their demanding roles effectively.

In conclusion, students should be granted a substantial summer break rather than a nonstop school year. The break keeps their minds active through varied experiences, reduces mental and physical stress, and provides necessary downtime for educators as well.

Some people might have heard this before: “The greater danger for most of us lies not in setting our aim too high and falling short, but in setting our aim too low, and achieving our mark.” This is what the great artist Michelangelo said. Though not everyone agrees, setting higher aims is ultimately better. By aiming high, people can achieve bigger goals, and such aims inspire more unique thoughts than those who set them too low. Consequently, many significant possibilities open in various directions.

First, by setting your aim high, you can explore a wider array of possibilities. Many people decide their aims before they even consider their options. For example, which path will offer more job prospects: simply applying for a dish‑washing job because it is easy, or applying to every field you could possibly work in? The same logic applies to education. Consider a student unsure of their future: choosing to enlist in the military or going to college, which offers many opportunities. Attending college can broaden job prospects, potentially leading to a better career than the military.

Furthermore, setting our aim high encourages people to conceive more unique and authentic thoughts than those who set their aims too low. For instance, people with low aims are more likely to conceal or be unaware of their true aspirations. Because they do not challenge themselves with difficult goals, they miss opportunities for growth. Conversely, those who aim high pursue harder tasks and think more deeply, thereby developing their minds and fostering unique perspectives. Famous artists, who produced significant works, would likely have remained mediocre if they had imposed limits on their creativity. Their groundbreaking ideas and art exist precisely because they aimed high.

In addition, aiming high allows you to achieve larger goals than settling for a lower aim, even if it seems more plausible. For example, why submit only the minimum requirement for an assignment when you could tackle the maximum? The answer is obvious: working to the maximum yields a better grade. If your aim is low, you may give up before completing a crucial task; if your aim is high, you persevere and succeed. Thus, higher aims are preferable to merely doing the easiest thing you can.

Some people argue that setting too high an aim can cause suffering. While this can be true, it does not justify aiming too low. What is important is to strike a balance. Childhood advice to “eat a balanced meal” mirrors how we should balance our ambitions. Understand your abilities and set aims that you can possibly achieve, rather than aiming for something easy. Others claim that low aims reduce stress, yet not all stress is detrimental—some stress can be motivating. For example, I once hated school in Japan, felt too lazy to work, and the resulting stress pushed me to stay home indefinitely. That did not alleviate my stress; instead, it made me feel worse. I eventually chose to return to school, learning that moderate stress can propel growth.

Finally, the core point is that running away from challenge and choosing the easy path is not the best decision. Although aiming low may seem safer, the real danger is forgetting to aim high and believing you cannot achieve great things. The best choice is to decide on an aim that will not lead to regret, thereby making the most of your short life. No one has to be perfect, but everyone should strive to reach their best potential to leave no regret behind.

First impressions vary from person to person. When someone sees something for the first time, their initial reaction is shaped by their own attitude and expectations. However, as we learn more about the person or situation, our views can shift. Understanding this shift is key because the first reaction often sets the tone for future interactions.

Consider a classroom: on the first day it may seem dull, so a student might develop a negative impression. By the second day, the teacher introduces engaging activities, and the student’s perception can turn completely positive. This example shows that a bad initial feeling does not have to stay forever; it can change once we have more information. Of course, if someone approaches a situation with a negative mindset, their first impression will naturally be negative as well. In such cases, the initial reaction can reveal a lot about that person’s character.

On the other hand, some first impressions are stubborn and hard to alter. Many people hold onto their initial judgments even when new facts come to light. This resistance can make it difficult to form accurate opinions about others.

When we have a favorable opinion of someone, a single bad action can bruise that perception and change our thoughts. Likewise, if we think a workplace looks easy and enjoyable, we might feel comfortable and make friends. Yet, if the next day we discover that the boss treats us poorly, our view of the job can quickly shift, and the once‑pleasant atmosphere feels tainted.

In short, first impressions are powerful but not immutable. They rely on both personal attitudes and the information we gather over time. It would be problematic if we never allowed our opinions to evolve, as we might miss out on understanding people deeply. Getting to know someone—not just judging them at first glance—helps us create better relationships and avoid unfairly dismissing others.

Many schools now give students the option to study from home through online courses or video conferencing. Others believe that learning in a physical classroom is superior and therefore do not offer distance learning. I disagree with schools that refuse to provide remote study because, in my view, it can be an effective way for many learners.

Firstly, distance learning allows students to access lessons at times that fit their individual schedules, something that is especially helpful for those who must work or care for family members. For instance, parents who are juggling a job and a child can study from home, avoiding the commute and the time constraints of a traditional timetable. When the students who have this responsibility are able to attend class virtually they can still achieve their goals, provided they stay motivated.

Secondly, although some argue that learning best occurs in a face‑to‑face environment, the absence of a teacher in a virtual setting does not mean that help cannot be obtained. Online platforms now offer chat functions, discussion boards, and live Q&A sessions where students can request clarification. These digital tools can replicate the immediacy of classroom help, especially when teachers are available during set hours.

Thirdly, remote instruction can be particularly valuable for international students or those who have recently moved to a country where they still need to acquire a new language. For these learners, attending school in person may be difficult due to financial constraints or family commitments. Distance learning provides a flexible alternative that enables them to continue their education while adapting to new surroundings.

It is also true that home environments can present distractions such as electronic gadgets, family members, or other responsibilities. However, this speaks more to the need for better time‑management skills than to a fundamental flaw in distance learning. With the right self‑discipline, students can effectively balance study with personal life.

Finally, the core of learning is motivation and persistence. Whether a student attends classes in person or online, success hinges on their willingness to engage, to ask questions, and to persevere. By offering remote options, schools widen access to education without sacrificing quality. Therefore, schools should not dismiss distance learning outright; instead, they should support it as a legitimate and potentially transformative mode of instruction.

To conserve energy and resources, some businesses have adopted a four‑day work week, with each day consisting of ten hours. Some schools have considered extending the school day by two hours to follow this model. I do not agree. Extending the day would impose two more hours of school, which I believe would be very stressful for students and would leave them insufficient time to complete homework after school. This change would also create significant problems for schools.

First, many students have responsibilities outside of school. For example, I have a job after school and must be there at 4 p.m. If the school adopted this model, the day would finish two hours later, making it impossible for me to keep my job. This illustrates that the extended schedule would affect not only me but also other students who also work after school.

Second, two additional hours of school would be stressful. Classes would be longer than usual, tiring students and reducing their concentration. They would also have less time to do homework because they would arrive home very late and exhausted. Consequently, their grades could suffer, as they might fail to submit assignments on time.

Some argue that extending the day would negatively impact attendance. If students are tired from an extended day the previous day, they may skip classes. Attendance is crucial, and poor attendance can jeopardize a student’s ability to pass the academic year.

In conclusion, this routine would not be easy for students to manage, even if the school only offers a few days per week. As a student, I would find it difficult to maintain my daily routine. The additional hours would make classes more stressful, reduce attendance, and ultimately hurt academic performance.

Many companies have begun to use a four‑day work week, with each day lasting ten hours, as a way to save energy and cut costs. Some people propose that schools adopt a similar schedule by adding two extra hours to the school day. I do not agree with this idea. Extending the day would be too tiring for students and would make it harder for them to complete homework. It would also cause problems for schools and the community.

First, students who have other responsibilities after school would be negatively affected. I myself work a part‑time job that starts at four o’clock. If the school day were extended by two hours, I would miss my shift and lose my income. Other students who need to help their families or have part‑time jobs would face the same difficulty. A longer day would clash with their outside commitments and make it impossible to balance work and study.

Second, two additional hours mean that lessons would become longer and more exhausting. Students would easily become fatigued and would have trouble following the teacher. Their concentration would drop during class, and they would feel too tired afterward to do their homework. As a result, assignments might be turned in late or not at all, which would hurt their grades. The extra fatigue would also raise absenteeism. If students arrive back home exhausted, they may skip school on the next day, leading to a cycle of missed learning opportunities.

Finally, school attendance is a crucial indicator of success. Dropping the attendance rate would threaten a student’s ability to graduate and could negatively affect school rankings and funding. Extending the school day would undermine this key metric.

In conclusion, adding two extra hours to the school day is not a good idea. It would create stress for students, interfere with their after‑school responsibilities, lower their academic performance, and diminish attendance. Therefore, my school should not adopt this model.

Failure plays a huge part in becoming successful. By failing, people learn how not to make the same mistakes again. For example, let’s say that I was trying to become a professional soccer player. Now this is the part where enthusiasm plays a role. I can either stop playing soccer and choose a different route or I can pick myself up and try again. Why should we let your character take control of us when we have most of the control through the actions we take? For example, if your parents were very abusive, you might think you will be that way, too. But that can make you stronger and build your character up more than it was before. We have a choice to shape our character; some people will say, “Oh, she’s mean,” or “Why won’t she share?” And it isn’t her character—it might be her personality. You yourself build up your character, and no one else has to like it except you, because at the end of the day all you have is yourself, not anyone else; that’s better than having someone judge you. No one can really know for sure what makes up their character just by saying, “I’ve done it before.” Let’s say someone in your family died because of their sickness and you spend those days being depressed and in denial that they are gone. Guess what? You are going to build yourself up and make them proud of the child they raised and the person who stood by their side. Each day you’ll try to make every second count so they can see how great you are handling everything, even if sometimes you might get sad here and there. But you’re still pushing through, which makes your character stronger than you realize. But when you realize what you’ve accomplished, the world doesn’t seem as scary anymore. That doesn’t get you through life; it just brings you down. You know your character isn’t meant for that. It’s meant to push you and help you get through all the brick walls that life throws at you. Only you can knock them down. So don’t stop yourself from making a choice you know is right. Go with your gut and let your heart show you the way. Don’t let anything in life stop you because what people think is impossible is possible. Stand out; make your character stand out because you are different, no matter what.

John Lubbock, a well‑known English naturalist and politician, once said, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make.” This idea raises a question: to what extent is our character shaped by the past versus our own decisions? I believe that while our history can influence us, ultimately we control how we respond and grow.

Consider a child raised by abusive parents. Many might say that such a background determines that the child will become abusive too. But this is not inevitable. In fact, a painful upbringing can provide a powerful motivation to break the cycle. The child can choose to become resilient, to work hard, and to practice kindness. In this way, he is constructing his own character rather than simply echoing what he has seen.

People often judge others on surface traits: “She’s mean” or “She won’t share.” These judgments reflect the observer’s interpretations, not the person’s true character. We have the right to define ourselves. Only we can decide what kind of adult we wish to become. No external approval is required to validate that choice. When someone truly gets to know us, the “cover” falls away and they see the story behind us. A strong character can leave a quiet legacy, inspiring others with questions such as, “How did she become so independent?” or “What made her so resilient?” The answer lies in the choices we make and the perseverance we demonstrate.

It is difficult to pinpoint exactly what builds character simply by looking at past actions. For example, after a family member dies, a person may feel deep sorrow and denial. Yet over time, that grief can become a catalyst for growth. By choosing to honor the lost relative, by supporting friends, by staying present in each day, that person develops a stronger sense of purpose. Although sadness may still surface, the overall trajectory of character becomes stronger and more compassionate.

Many people doubt themselves when confronted with challenges, believing they are incapable. The brain often tries to convince us that success is impossible. Instead of buying into that negativity, we should focus on our character’s purpose: to push through the obstacles life throws our way. Each small victory demonstrates that we can overcome seemingly insurmountable walls. The confidence that grows from these experiences reinforces the character we are building.

In life there is no universal prescription; we must decide what feels right and fits our values. By embracing the idea that “your character will be what you choose to make,” we can enjoy the journey and actively shape our personalities. Every decision, even difficult ones, helps sculpt the person we will become. Let your heart guide you and your actions speak louder than anyone’s doubts. The result will be a distinctive character that stands out because it is uniquely yours.

Showing our real selves to others is the most meaningful experiment we can undertake. Right now, many people still find it difficult to be authentic around others. Some mock those who simply act as they are, while others don’t care or pay attention to what people do. This should not be the case. Today we see more acceptance of people who are gay, transgender, bisexual, or otherwise different. Although it can sometimes be confusing, the fact that they are honest about who they are is important.

When I was 16, a friend of mine always bragged that she was rich, which was not true. She used this lie to make friends, but I rejected invitations that involved partying, drinking or smoking. Eventually, the people who had thought she was wealthy discovered the truth, and I realized that pretending to be someone else and lying about our circumstances can damage friendships. We need to be honest with each other.

For these reasons I always encourage people to be themselves no matter how difficult it may seem. The best thing we can do is be true to ourselves. People must learn to accept others for who they truly are and stop keeping two different faces. In today’s world, most people are liberated to be who they wish to be and do not care as much about what others do. When we let others see our authentic selves, we create a sense of comfort and respect between us.

People can make their own decisions because they can pursue anything they desire, something they have longed for. Nobody likes to do something they do not want; they have their own chosen path of life decisions regarding what they wish to become or to accomplish.

However, some of the decisions they may face are difficult or easy. The difficult route requires strenuous effort: study diligently to achieve high grades and work hard. The easy route involves investing effort or money at the outset of their future plans; it is a shortcut but truly demanding, and not everyone can make that choice depending on whether they desire it. It also depends on where they are in life. For example, people with abundant finances can make their future decisions more quickly because they do not worry about finances, taxes, or payments, whereas people with fewer resources must take longer to initiate their future plans because they must worry about finances, taxes, payments, paying for a car, etc., and they have to work even harder to secure their decisions. I met a friend who attended school while working. He was about to graduate from high school and attend college but made a poor decision. He stopped school and told me, “Working earns more money than going to school.” He abandoned his studies. His job is as a nail technician, which sometimes pays well and sometimes does not, and he does not wish to try harder. He could have gone to college, later secured a better-paying job, but he missed that opportunity and it changed his life forever; he cannot undo it. My brother was similar: he attended college for two years, then decided he did not want to continue. If he had persisted, he might have obtained a better career. Thus, people must consider what will happen in the future and choose what they will become, relying on what they currently possess and what they anticipate acquiring. People can decide for themselves but sometimes need assistance so others can support their life choices. Unfortunately, many people do not know what they will do in the future, what occupations interest them, so they are stalled; they need help choosing endeavors that may interest them later on.

Their choices and all that happens around them shape their future decisions, and all the support from those around them or from family can improve their decisions. They must design their own lives, work hard to secure a good future, and do anything they want. If people work hard enough, later their children will find it easier to decide their own lives.

Dear Principal,

Introducing a healthier lunch into the cafeteria is a commendable initiative. The new menu will feature fresh options, a greater variety of nutritious dishes, and flavors that many students have never experienced before. As a student, I wholeheartedly support this plan because it will provide wholesome choices for all of us.

Implementing a new lunch selection is likely to delight many students, especially those who are weary of the repetitive fare offered almost daily. However, it could also influence students who thrive on familiar meals and may not feel a rush of novelty. In such a scenario, it would be prudent for you, as Principal, to consult with the cafeteria manager and request a compilation of the most popular items among students. This data will enable you and your team to decide whether to modify the menu, and if necessary, remove the least favored dishes and replace them with appealing alternatives.

Students are inclined to appreciate thoughtful revisions, especially when the changes honor their preferences while introducing exciting new options. Experiencing diverse menus sets our school apart from others and may inspire nearby institutions to follow suit. Regional schools observing our initiative may adopt similar reforms. This not only benefits our own students but also assists parents, sparing them the expense of purchasing meals outside the school when students lose interest in the cafeteria’s offerings.

Moreover, by offering a broader range of nutritious dishes, we reduce the temptation for students to miss classes in pursuit of food elsewhere, thereby minimizing disruptions and safeguarding both student health and the school's reputation.

Tasting diverse cuisines is something many of us cherish; I cite myself as an example. Some students relish trying unfamiliar foods. Unfortunately, the cafeteria’s current balance between indulgent and healthy options is skewed, necessitating change. A broader selection of nourishing meals would accommodate dietary restrictions and reduce allergic reactions, ensuring that students aren’t compelled to eat solely at home.

In conclusion, if you gather data on students’ favorite and least favorite items, you can confidently reshape the menu to satisfy most preferences, preventing class absences for external food purchases, alleviating parental worry, and reducing health risks. A healthier menu augments our well‑being with essential nutrients—enhancing energy, supporting muscle growth, and fostering overall vitality. Parents will also benefit from savings on external meal purchases.

Changing the school’s menu is a visionary step that will resonate with most students, and those initially hesitant will soon adapt. This transformative approach will attract positive attention from the broader community and encourage other schools to emulate our success. A healthier lifestyle with diminished risks marks a brighter future. I sincerely hope the Principal will consider these student perspectives to make decisions that benefit all.

Thank you.

Dear Principal,

Changing the cafeteria lunch to include a healthier menu is a good idea. There will be new foods, healthier options, and different varieties that other students have never tasted before. As a student, I really like this idea because there will be healthy food for all of us.

A new lunch menu, therefore, is going to make many students happy because some are getting tired of eating the same lunch almost every day. However, it could also affect other students who enjoy the current menu and never get tired of it. In this case, it would be better if you, as the principal, talk to the cafeteria manager and ask her for a list of the foods that students favor most. Then, you and your team can decide whether to change the menu or not. As a student, I also think it would be wise to see which foods students like the most, remove the ones that are eaten the least, and replace them with new options.

Students might be happier, because you would not be discarding the foods they love and instead you would be bringing a new, appealing menu. By trying different options, we also differentiate ourselves from other schools, and they will see our school as an example. Consequently, they may follow suit, which is a very good thing, since not only our students are getting tired of the cafeteria menu, but students in other schools are facing similar issues.

Other schools from different states might observe us and adopt the same idea. This change will not only benefit the students; it will also help parents save money, because students who no longer like the menu are less likely to tell their parents to buy food outside—an expense that many parents cannot afford. Moreover, students will be less inclined to skip classes to get food from outside, which in turn will do good for the students, their parents, and the school's reputation.

Tasting different types of menu items, trying new foods, is something many students also love, as I have personally experienced. Although the cafeteria currently has both bad and healthy food, the options are not balanced. We need more healthy choices, as some students are allergic to items currently offered, which means they suffer from illness because they can only eat at home. Bringing a healthy and varied lunch menu will allow us to taste new, healthier foods and prevent students from leaving class to buy food elsewhere. This is safer for students who skip classes and for the parents, because the school will no longer have to explain to parents that their children are absent.

My conclusion is that students will be happier if you simply ask the cafeteria manager for a list of which foods are loved the most and which are least liked. This approach will help all students adapt to the changes you intend to make. Students will have their favorite foods, they will not need to skip class to buy food, parents will no longer worry, and students will not risk getting sick from eating limited options. Healthy food can benefit us in many ways, such as improving our bodies, reducing excess fat, and providing more protein.

Therefore, changing the school menu is a great idea that most students will understand, even those who initially resist will eventually get used to it. This will help every student, and observers outside the school will see the positive changes and inspire other schools to do the same for their students, promoting a healthier life with fewer risks.

This is my sincere opinion, and I hope the Principal takes into account what the students think and what is best for all of us.

Thank you!

People should make their own decisions, because doing so builds self‑confidence and ultimately allows them to be happier in life. Consequently, when people take charge of their choices, they are more likely to experience personal victories, even if those victories come in small, point‑based increments. Moreover, should they face challenging moments, they will be better prepared, since the difficulty of decision‑making actually strengthens their resilience.

Conversely, people who do not make their own decisions often lead easier lives, since they are not burdened by the need to think critically. However, even in those circumstances, it is ultimately better for individuals to take control and decide for themselves.

People should make their own decisions because it builds self‑confidence. When people decide for themselves, they are more likely to be happy in life. Facing challenging moments also helps them grow. Those who never make their own choices may live an easy life, but they miss the opportunity to develop confidence and truly succeed.

People should be empowered to make their own decisions. When we choose for ourselves, we develop self‑confidence, because the act of deciding forces us to weigh options, consider consequences, and commit to a course of action.

Deciding for ourselves also brings greater happiness. Life is largely shaped by the choices we make, and taking responsibility for those decisions gives us a sense of control and satisfaction that is hard to achieve when others dictate our path.

Moreover, facing difficult moments is a natural part of life. Making our own choices helps us learn how to handle challenges. Even when a decision turns out poorly, the experience teaches us resilience and grows our problem‑solving skills.

In contrast, when people let others decide for them, they may enjoy an easier life in the short term because they avoid thinking about difficult choices. However, this ease can come at the cost of personal growth and fulfillment.

For these reasons—building confidence, finding real happiness, and learning from life’s challenges—people should always strive to make their own decisions.

In my opinion, students who attend classes from home via online or video conferencing do not benefit.  

First, at home students face more distractions. While watching videos and using other devices, many students pause the class and work on other tasks. Schools need to address this by offering alternative options. In contrast, learning in the classroom provides a focused environment, with a teacher directly present to guide students. This focused setting is more effective.  

Second, I believe that distance learning is not a good alternative. As an example, in my own household I have three brothers and one sister, and the noise level makes home learning particularly distracting.  

Finally, I think that distance learning is a less effective option. Learning through video conferencing is more beneficial when scheduled for the morning, when students are energetic, rather than in the evening. Nonetheless, I do not find that attending classes from home offers the same benefits.  

In conclusion, students learn better when they attend school in person rather than from home or via distance learning. Parents share my view because the classroom setting proves far more effective than remote schooling.

In my opinion, students should not attend classes from home through online or video‑conferencing. I believe that learning at home does not provide the same advantages as attending school in person.

Firstly, the home environment is full of distractions. Screens, music, and other household activities interfere with focus. When teachers are present in a classroom, they can give immediate attention, correct mistakes quickly, and provide a structured learning atmosphere that is hard to replicate online.

Secondly, distance learning is not practical for many families. In my own house, I have three brothers and a sister, and we always find it difficult to study together. The noise and lack of a dedicated study space make it hard to concentrate, whereas at school students have a quiet place specifically designed for learning.

Finally, the timing of online sessions can be inconvenient. Watching lectures in the evening after a long day leaves students tired and less able to absorb information. In contrast, morning classes give students energy and better memory retention.

Consequently, I think that classroom learning remains essential. Parents share my view because they see that in‑school education is more effective, while distance learning does not offer the same benefits for students.

If we are always busy, we tend to achieve more. The people who keep working create new technology such as radios, televisions, and later computers. Those who do not invest time and effort into research and development are left behind when it comes to new inventions. Technology improves through continuous work and refinement, and it is the main driver for creating jobs and shaping modern life. When more people are active in research, the world changes, and our everyday experience improves.

A good example is the radio. Early radio engineers struggled with tuning and signal quality, yet their perseverance paid off. The radio quickly became an essential household item, demonstrating that hard work and determined improvement lead to widespread acceptance. This success inspired further innovation and opened up new employment opportunities in related industries.

Television followed as another breakthrough. Unlike films, which were silent, television combined sound and moving images, completely transforming entertainment. The production of the first television sets required skilled workers to tackle engineering challenges. As more people pursued better models, television became common in homes, expanding the market for TV manufacturers and advertisers. The first televised elections also illustrated how this technology could reach a massive audience, reinforcing the idea that diligent work creates powerful tools for society.

Later, computers emerged. Early machines were silent, purely mechanical calculators. Engineers worked to add sound, display, and programming capabilities, turning the computer into a versatile device. Their relentless refinement made computers affordable enough for widespread adoption, providing new jobs and enabling complex tasks such as solar tests and more.

In every case, continuous effort produced valuable technology, created jobs, improved daily life, and, ultimately, changed the world.

In cases such as a car accident or a family emergency, a child can quickly inform authorities or relatives without delay. Phones may be used during lunch periods, and in hallways only for authentic emergencies or to summon a nurse if a student faints. This balanced approach keeps the classroom environment focused while still providing a necessary safety net for students.

Technology allows people to complete many tasks without direct contact with others. For example, one can check out a book, shop, or play games without speaking to another person. This reliance on technology limits human contact, which is a biological need that humanity has sought to satisfy for centuries.  

Despite the conveniences, we are increasingly dependent on technology and therefore miss out on valuable in‑person interactions. That is why it is important to take a break from screens and speak to new people.  

Kids now use tablets before they even can walk, and we see them wandering through schools or malls, glued to their phones instead of engaging with classmates. This trend reduces face‑to‑face interaction and hinders the formation of new friendships.

Technology lets people finish many tasks without talking to others. For example, you can borrow a book, buy something, or play a game all online. While this convenience is useful, it also restricts real human interaction.

Humans have always valued face‑to‑face contact. For centuries, we have built communities and relationships by meeting people in person. Because of this, it is important to pause from screens and spend time with others. Face‑to‑face conversations help us grow socially and emotionally.

Even though online ordering and virtual games make life easier, we must remember that we need social connections. Kids today grow up with tablets and phones before they can even walk. They are comfortable with digital communication but rarely practice talking with classmates or friends in real life. This can leave them isolated and less capable of forming new friendships when the real world requires it.

In short, while technology is handy for convenience, it should not replace the essential human interaction we need for healthy development. We should balance digital life with time spent in person.
