Do you agree with “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm,” yes or no? I agree with Churchill’s statement because we cannot win or make everything perfect all the time. For example, when I took my English test last year in class, I studied a lot and aimed for an A+ or perhaps a B+, but I failed the test. I was very disappointed; however, my teacher told me I had a second chance. So I tried again and this time I passed with an A−, and I was thrilled. Failing the test taught me that it doesn’t matter how many times we fail in pursuit of our goals; we only need to remain strong and attempt as much as possible for success. Moreover, this year my aunt tried to travel to El Salvador, but when she called the airline to buy a ticket, the prices were too steep and she didn’t have enough money, so she decided to wait a few months. In conclusion, to achieve success we must experience failures in life, as I did with my test and as my aunt did. This teaches everyone to become stronger and never lose enthusiasm for success.

In conclusion, achieving success requires us to experience failure, as my test and my aunt’s experience have shown. These stories teach everyone to become stronger and never lose their enthusiasm for success.

I agree with Winston Churchill’s idea that “success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” The truth is that life rarely goes as planned, and we must keep our spirits high even when things don’t turn out as expected.

Last year, I studied hard for an English exam hoping to achieve an A+. Although I had practiced extensively, I only passed with a modest score. I was disappointed, but my teacher offered me a second chance. When I retook the test, I did much better and earned an A‑. This experience taught me that the result of a single failure does not define us; perseverance and a positive attitude are more important.

Another example is my aunt’s attempt to travel to El Salvador. She initially postponed her trip because the flight tickets were expensive and she didn’t have enough money. After waiting, ticket prices increased again, and she decided to buy them, only to find out her ID had expired. She could not purchase the ticket until she renewed her documents, which now takes at least three months. Though she is still waiting, she remains excited about the upcoming trip and the chance to visit her grandmother. Her story shows that setbacks can be temporary, and enthusiasm can survive even when plans are delayed.

Many people disagree, claiming that repeated failures turn a person into a loser or a failure. I believe that losing enthusiasm and giving up is what truly weakens us. The real challenge is staying motivated and learning from each setback.

In conclusion, success is not about never failing; it is about learning from failures, moving forward, and keeping a hopeful outlook. Whether it’s a test, travel plans, or any other goal, embracing failure without losing enthusiasm makes us stronger and more resilient.

For instance, I want to graduate and pursue further studies, but I find it difficult to complete homework and quiz preparations because I have no spare time. I also need to work to buy necessities and pay for housing and a car. Online classes give me the flexibility to study and work, allowing me to dedicate time to both.

The second reason is that students can complete better work and earn higher grades. With more time, they can produce thorough assignments and projects that incorporate detailed information. When students are focused on their homework and projects, they invest effort and use the internet to gather resources. In a traditional school setting, they must wake early and juggle many classes, which can be tiring. Online learning is less demanding in that regard.

Some people argue that online classes waste students' time, leading them to do nothing while at home. For example, students might play on their phones or use other distractions instead of studying. However, online learning can also foster family bonding, allowing students to spend a fun day with loved ones, play football, watch a movie, visit a cinema, or enjoy other preferred activities.

In conclusion, online classes are beneficial because they enable students to learn more, produce better work, and have more time for family. This advantage allows students to accomplish many things they wish to achieve. If students take online classes, they gain many benefits, enabling them to work and study simultaneously while pursuing goals such as securing a good job and completing their education.

Some schools should offer the option for students to learn from home through distance education or video conferences. Many people agree that online classes can be more advantageous for students because they can learn more, produce higher quality work, and spend more time with family. If students can study remotely, they gain new opportunities, can chase their dreams, and achieve the goals they set for themselves.

One major advantage of online learning is the flexibility it gives students. Being at home lets them manage their time better and prepare the materials they need. For example, a student who wants to graduate but struggles with time can still complete homework and study for quizzes while also working to pay rent or a car loan. Distance learning allows such a student to balance work and study, giving them extra time that would otherwise be taken up by commuting or early wake‑ups. Consequently, they can focus more on their education and achieve more.

A second benefit is that students can produce better quality work and earn higher grades. With the freedom of an online environment, they have more time to research, write, and refine assignments. They can take advantage of online resources and ask questions to teachers when needed. Because they are not rushed by the physical constraints of a classroom, they can submit well‑thought‑out projects that reflect their best effort. At school, the early start and heavy workload may leave students exhausted, making it harder to complete assignments with the same depth. In contrast, a distance learning schedule can be paced to allow deeper learning.

Critics argue that online learning can waste time, as students may be distracted by phones or other household activities. They claim that without the structure of a classroom, students might do nothing productive. However, remote learning still provides a framework of lessons and deadlines that keep students focused. Moreover, home learning can strengthen family bonds: students can share a day of learning and then spend time playing sports, watching movies, or visiting their favourite places together. The combination of educational and family activities can create a more balanced and fulfilling routine.

In conclusion, distance learning offers significant benefits, mainly the flexibility to study from home, the chance to produce higher quality work, and the opportunity to spend more time with loved ones. These advantages help students pursue employment, complete education, and meet their aspirations. Therefore, schools should consider incorporating online classes as a valuable option for students.

"Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm." Although failure is the lack of success, it also means losing the ability to work normally. As humans, we all know that instead of improving, we sometimes lose the capacity to start over and pursue what we want, just as Winston Churchill once warned: "Do not lose the enthusiasm."

From the outset, humans fail constantly. Every chapter of our lives contains failures, sometimes occurring at the most significant moments. We might wonder why failure happens when matters feel most important, assuming it is because we did something wrong or didn’t try hard enough for a job, a test, or to solve our problems. Yet why does failure play such a big role in our daily lives?

The reality of failure is not merely to endure disappointment; it is to learn from mistakes, to understand that failure can be constructive, and to avoid repeating past errors. Each failure is also an experience and a lesson toward success.

For example, scientists conduct many experiments, often failing repeatedly, but eventually discover new insights beyond their original goal. This demonstrates that no matter how many times we fail, we can still find answers and uncover new horizons.

Staying positive becomes a challenge for many people. We all try every day to remain optimistic and view mistakes in a positive light, but stress often intensifies after a setback.

It is important to recognize that feeling stress or insecurity is normal and can strengthen us. Unfortunately, many people feel depressed after a failure, lose hope, and give up on their goals, becoming tired and hopeless.

Consider a book students at Generic School read last year, "The Life of an Indian." It tells of a poor boy in a reservation who finds hope when a teacher introduces him to a broader world. After countless failures, he perseveres and overcomes his circumstances. His story shows that staying positive after failures is not impossible, even for a poor boy.

Clearly, not everyone can follow that path, but we all desire happiness. Failure can become a powerful ally in that pursuit.

In conclusion, embracing our mistakes is the best way to succeed and improve in life. Every failure offers a new experience and lesson. No matter how many times you fail, an answer lies ahead.

I completely agree with Winston Churchill: maintaining enthusiasm for what comes next in our lives is more exciting than we often realize. If we believe in ourselves, stay positive, and understand that failure is part of daily life, we become more successful, learning how life truly works and discovering that life need not be as hard as we think.

Success is the art of moving from one setback to another while keeping your fire alive. Even though failure means we are not where we want to be, it is also a signal that we have a chance to learn and correct our path. As Winston Churchill once said, “Never lose enthusiasm,” a reminder that excitement is essential to progress.

From the moment we are born, failure accompanies us. Every project, exam, or relationship contains moments of disappointment. We are conditioned to see failure as a flaw, guessing that it must be due to our own shortcomings or insufficient effort. But this view ignores the true purpose of failure.

Failure is not merely a bad outcome—it is a feedback mechanism. It tells us where we went wrong and points the way to improvement. Each failure is a stepping stone toward mastery, an opportunity to refine our skills and strategies. Even the most talented individuals face repeated setbacks before they achieve success.

Scientists illustrate this idea vividly. In laboratories, countless experiments end in failure, yet each one contributes to a body of knowledge that ultimately leads to breakthroughs. A single successful result often builds on a series of negatives. Thus, failure is an unavoidable element of discovery, and perseverance is rewarded with new insights.

Moreover, the capacity to stay hopeful after a failure is a significant challenge for many. While we are encouraged to maintain a positive mindset, the reality of repeated setbacks can produce stress, uncertainty, and even depression. These feelings are natural and, to a degree, beneficial, because they push us to adapt. When we confront these emotions calmly, we become stronger and more resilient.

Consider the story of a young boy from an impoverished reservation in India. He faced countless hardships, yet he refused to give up. Each failure drove him forward instead of pulling him back. Through determination, he eventually entered a world of opportunities that helped him realize his potential. This narrative shows that even under extreme adversity, cultivating optimism can lead to transformation.

In summary, learning from mistakes is the most reliable route to success. Every failure carries a lesson and propels us toward improvement. No amount of adversity is permanent; the key lies in maintaining enthusiasm, believing in ourselves, and treating each setback as a chance to grow.

I wholeheartedly agree with Churchill’s sentiment. Keeping our excitement alive as we confront new challenges is vital. By embracing failure as part of the journey, we build the confidence and knowledge necessary to navigate life’s complexities and ultimately achieve contentment.

The most frequent debate today is whether schools should conserve energy and resources, especially now that some businesses have adopted a four‑day work week with ten‑hour days. Should our school follow this model by extending the day by two hours? Some people argue that longer days would actually use more energy—increased electricity for lights, computers, the electronic blackboard, and water, because students often forget to turn off the tap. I believe we should extend the school day by two hours, but only if we take steps to conserve energy and resources, because the extra time can also be used to promote a better world.

One reason for the extension is that by saving energy for the future we can teach students about responsible consumption. The school could instruct each student on how to reduce their energy use at home and offer practical tips for lowering electricity bills.

Another reason is the potential to save water. Students use the bathroom almost twice as often as it comes to the hallway, and many forget to turn off the tap. Posters could be made to illustrate the importance of water conservation. Similarly, the school could reduce plastic and paper waste by purchasing fewer supplies and encouraging students to be more careful with resources.

Finally, if we extend the day by two hours, teachers and students will have more time to undertake projects that promote environmental stewardship. For example, they could create public awareness campaigns showing how the community can prevent climate change and care for the planet. An online page could also be established where students share tips with others at school and beyond.

As you have read, I think the school should add two extra hours per day, because everyone in the school will have more opportunity to develop a conscience for conserving energy and resources, and ultimately for saving our world. Only by taking conscious action can we create a better world.

The debate that dominates our schools today is whether extending the school day would help conserve energy and resources. Some argue that keeping the day longer would actually increase consumption of electricity, light, computer power, and even water because more time on campus means more usage. I believe, however, that adding two extra hours to each school day is a worthwhile experiment if we combine it with a strong emphasis on conservation.

First, a longer school day would give teachers a larger window to educate students about energy efficiency. Lessons could include practical advice on how to use lights and electronics wisely at home, or how to reduce heating and cooling. Students would then carry that knowledge beyond the classroom, potentially lowering their households’ utility bills and encouraging a broader community focus on conservation.

Second, water use is another area where schools can make a difference. In many halls, students use the bathroom more than twice during the day and often leave taps running. By adding a two‑hour period that includes a mandatory workshop on water savings, students could create posters and campaigns that remind everyone to turn off taps. Alongside this, recycling programs for paper and plastic can be intensified, saving both resources and money that can fund further improvements.

Finally, the added time could be used for environmental projects that raise awareness of global climate change. Students might organize informational booths, produce short videos, or run a school website that shares tips for living sustainably. Teachers would benefit by having extra time to develop these projects, fostering a culture of responsibility and proactive problem‑solving.

In conclusion, while extending the day could initially raise consumption, the educational opportunities it provides can lead to long‑term savings and a more environmentally conscious school community. By using the extra time to teach, engage, and inspire, we can help students become better stewards of the planet.

Some schools offer distance learning as a way for students to attend classes from home through online video conferencing. Is it a good idea to take classes online or not?

In my opinion, enrolling in online classes is a great idea because it fits students’ schedules. Students who work different hours, have family responsibilities, or face transportation challenges can attend classes from home after finishing work, which helps them relax.

When students are tired from work, focusing in a classroom is difficult. Online classes allow them time to eat, rest, and concentrate. They also free up time for other activities, such as sports or social events.

Health and transportation are also concerns. If a student is sick, going to school can spread illness and they may need a car and parking, which sometimes costs money. Good weather facilitates physical attendance, whereas bad weather does not. Online classes reduce the risk of spreading sickness and eliminate the need for travel and parking costs.

Family responsibilities benefit greatly from online learning. Many students have children or care for disabled family members. For example, a disabled student may not be able to go to school independently; online classes enable them to manage health issues and take breaks when needed. Parents who are students find it easy to care for their children while studying, which reduces stress and prevents missed classes. The flexibility of online learning allows both students and parents to spend time with their children and keep track of their academic progress.

Ultimately, technology has made life easier and more efficient. It saves time, ensures punctuality, and provides a practical solution for those who are always busy.

Online learning is a good idea because it fits students’ schedules and reduces many problems that arise when they are forced to attend classes in person.  

One of the biggest advantages is the flexibility it offers. Students who have part‑time jobs or other commitments can finish their work first and then attend their classes from home. After a long day at a job, they are more relaxed and better able to focus on the lessons compared with coming back to school tired and distracted.  

Distance learning also gives students extra time for other activities. While a traditional student may have to rush from one class to another, an online student can schedule breaks to eat, do some exercise or spend time with friends. This helps maintain a balanced lifestyle.  

Health is another important factor. If a student is sick, they can stay at home and avoid spreading illness to classmates. This is especially useful when many people are carrying colds or flu. Additionally, students do not have to worry about transportation, expensive parking fees, or unreliable bus routes, which can be a real hardship, especially in the winter or during bad weather.  

Online classes are also helpful for families. Many students are parents or have children who cannot travel to a school. The ability to learn from home means they can care for their families without missing out on education. This reduces stress and lets them allocate time to their homes while still receiving a quality education. For students with disabilities, technology can provide a more accessible learning environment that might be otherwise difficult to reach.  

Finally, all of these benefits are made possible by technology. Modern internet and communication tools allow students to join live lectures, submit assignments, and ask questions just as they would on campus. Students save time and energy, making the most of it for both learning and life. For those who are constantly busy, online education offers a practical and reliable solution.

Education is a lifelong process that grows the mind and expands our knowledge of new things; this chance may come only once, but it doesn’t matter when it appears.

I disagree with the idea that phones are harmless, because they can have a negative impact on our lives, especially by cutting us off from real communication.

First, phones can remove the need to go out and do simple errands. When I was still in my home country, I would cycle or walk to the shop for groceries. After moving to the United States, I hardly leave the house for shopping because my mother can call the store and have items delivered right to our door. This convenience limits our interaction with the people who run those shops and with the street environment.

Second, mobile gaming replaces traditional outdoor play. Last week I asked a friend back home if he still plays soccer in the street. He told me he no longer does so; instead, he spends his time playing popular games on his phone. As a result, kids who used to chase each other around the park now prefer the screen.

Third, young children become overly attached to devices. My two‑year‑old brother loves watching videos on his phone. When my mother takes the phone away, he cries; he no longer wants to play with his older brother or engage in other activities. The phone has become his only source of entertainment.

Fourth, even when we visit family or new places, the phone becomes a constant distraction. Every time we visit my relatives, I find myself staring at my phone instead of enjoying the reunion. While exploring new cities, I instinctively pull out my camera, but the phone keeps my attention focused on capturing pictures rather than experiencing the surroundings.

Finally, constant use of phones can lead to addiction. I have a classmate who keeps his phone glued to him during lessons. Sometimes he plays games, other times he watches videos. Has the limitation of human contact due to the use of technology had positive or negative effects on people's lives?  

I believe it does in many ways, and it does not in others. It depends on the person.  

Technology has positive effects. It can help people who feel lonely entertain themselves. For example, reading a book, shopping, playing games, listening to music on your favorite app, Pandora, or watching a show on YouTube or Netflix can be a positive way to use technology.  

However, nothing is perfect. As my grandfather used to say, “There have to be bad things so that there can be good things.” Every positive thing has its negative counterpart.  

It also has negative effects. With the use of phones and other technology, people lose interest in normal things, such as family reunions. I personally never cared much about that, preferring to spend time with my cousins and childhood friends at home talking about boring things. Now, though, you can’t have a simple conversation with someone because they’re usually on their phone doing who-knows-what. To me, that shows a lack of care about what I’m saying, and that can make people dislike you.  

Technology is one of the greatest inventions. It makes communication easier, provides entertainment, informs us about everything happening in the world and even in space, and we don’t have to read an entire book to find an answer. It has made almost everything easier: you can shop without leaving your house or order food with a few taps.  

But this convenience can also make people lazy. They may ask themselves, “Why should I do this when my phone can do it for me?” or “Why should I date someone when I can talk to my phone?” They may keep asking these questions until there is no one by their side.  

In conclusion, technology is very good if you use it only when you need it and do not let it dominate your mind.

The question of whether technology’s reduction of face‑to‑face contact is good or bad is not black and white. It really depends on the individual, and that’s my view.

On the positive side, technology gives people who feel lonely an outlet to stay engaged. For those who might otherwise feel isolated, being able to read a book, shop online, play games, listen to music on Pandora, or watch favourite shows on YouTube and Netflix can be a healthy way to pass time. It allows them to have companionship without having to go out, and that can prevent them from falling into bad habits or despair.

However, technology also has its downsides. Many people now become more interested in virtual interactions than in real, everyday activities. I can’t even say I care much about family gatherings, but I used to prefer hanging out with cousins or childhood friends instead of staying in the house. Now, when I try to have a simple conversation, the other person is often looking at their phone, distracted and possibly unimportant about what I’m saying. It feels like a sign that they don’t care, and over time this can create dislike or distance.

The inventions of technology are undeniable – communication is easier, entertainment is abundant, the news is instantly available, and we can shop or order food without leaving the house. These conveniences make life easier, but they also encourage laziness. People ask themselves: “Why should I leave the house if my phone can do it? Why should I date someone when I can chat through my device? Why spend time with a real person when my screen offers endless distraction?” Such questions may lead to a future in which no one is nearby to share life with.

In conclusion, technology can be very useful if we use it carefully and only when we need it. We must avoid letting it consume our thoughts and force us into isolation.

In summary, students should take art classes to feel refreshed after a tired day of two or three consecutive blocks, helping them recharge and improve their learning abilities. These classes also foster motivation and reduce pressure. However, art classes should remain elective so that students who are truly interested can participate without wasting time in a block that does not engage them.

In recent years schools have expanded their curricula to include courses that nurture students’ natural talents, particularly in the arts. Allowing students who are passionate about music, drama or visual arts to enroll in such classes lets them discover their strengths while also giving them an outlet to relieve the pressure that builds after a few hours of academic work. For those who find no value in practicing art, the time spent in these classes can feel wasted, but for many learners it is a welcome break.

Today’s high‑school experience is increasingly boring. Many students struggle to see where they fit and what excites them within the rigid structure of the classroom. Introducing engaging extracurricular options—such as a school band, a drama group, or a painting workshop—provides a constructive way to relax and re‑energise. When students are allowed to choose these activities, they often find new motivation that spills over into their regular studies.

Joining an art class helps clear the mind, making it easier to absorb the material that follows. After an intensive lesson, engaging in singing, acting or sketching can soothe the brain, allowing it to reset and ready itself for new information. The effectiveness of this reset depends partly on the student’s preferred form of entertainment, whether it’s music, theatre or drawing; each activity offers a different path to relaxation.

It is essential that all students have the opportunity to participate in the arts, but this should be voluntary rather than compulsory. If a class is forced upon a student who has no interest or aptitude for music, drama or visual art, it can create discomfort and distraction for others. A restless, unimpressed participant can disrupt the learning environment and diminish the benefits for the whole group.

In conclusion, arts classes are a valuable tool for refreshing students after long sequences of academic work, boosting motivation, and reducing stress. However, they must remain elective choices so that interested students can benefit without forcing others to spend time on activities they do not enjoy. This balance ensures that the arts remain a source of genuine enrichment rather than an unnecessary burden.

Those who start a career early can bring their plans to fruition, and students who do so can seek advice from their counselors. Early career choices can also waste time. Children may spend more time playing video games than pursuing a career. They often think that a career is simply another school assignment, and when confronted with the choice of a career, they may write “don’t know” and return to their hobbies. Thus, it is essential to make a plan first before pursuing a career at a young age.

Choosing a career at the age of twelve or younger is careless because it can cause overthinking, lead students to abandon courses, and create negative attitudes towards their studies. In many communities, students are asked to decide on a future job as soon as they get to high school. Some people think that the earlier a student commits, the better, because they can pursue higher education, secure employment right after graduation, and avoid uncertainty later. However, I believe choosing a career so early can be counterproductive for several reasons.

First, it often leads to dropping out of courses. Students who begin a specific career plan often find that after a few weeks of learning the basics they lose interest and stop attending class. Without steady attendance, keeping up with the curriculum becomes difficult, and the chance of abandoning the goal increases. It is therefore wiser to step back and evaluate the choice more thoroughly before committing full time.

Second, early career planning can cause prolonged indecision. Adults normally spend years contemplating the right profession, and they usually prioritize earning a salary before feeling ready to settle. Teens are eager to explore many interests, and insisting on a single path too soon can create endless ruminations and confusion. A balanced period of exploration is necessary to make an informed decision.

Finally, an early focus on a specific job may waste valuable time. Children and teenagers often have more energy for leisure—playing games or enjoying hobbies—than for shaping a life plan. By forcing them to decide at a very young age, we risk making them feel pressured and ultimately withdrawing from their academic duties. Before deciding on a career, students should develop a clear plan, but doing so after experiencing a variety of subjects and activities leads to better outcomes.

Online classes and video conferencing have become one of the most valuable solutions for students who cannot afford a traditional campus experience and for older adults who want to continue their studies but are restricted by financial constraints. In today’s society, many students face the dilemma of paying for tuition, housing, and other living expenses. Those who live on campus often struggle with costs, while those who live off campus must balance rent, food, and transportation. As a result, a significant number of students find themselves either dropping out or working extra hours to support their education. Juggling work and school creates considerable stress, making it hard for learners to stay organized and meet deadlines.

Transport and parking are additional obstacles that push students to consider online learning. University campuses that occupy large areas frequently lack sufficient parking spots, and many pupils do not own a car at all. Commuting can cause late arrivals, missed lectures, and added fatigue after a tiring day. By attending classes from home, students gain flexibility to start lessons at their convenience, thereby reducing the pressure of commuting and allowing them to manage their time more effectively.

The benefits of remote learning are clear. Students often complete assignments more efficiently because the home environment offers fewer interruptions. With better concentration, learners absorb the material more thoroughly and become more engaged. Moreover, the ability to ask questions online or revisit recorded lectures enhances comprehension. Instructors can also moderate their workload, allowing them to design more focused assignments for remote students and ensuring that learning remains constructive.

Ultimately, online education provides a practical way for many to fulfill their educational dreams. It enables students who would otherwise be confined by financial or logistical hurdles to attend classes, effectively leveling the playing field. By removing commuting barriers and reducing costs, remote learning promotes better time management and a more organized approach to both studies and personal responsibilities. This flexibility empowers learners to balance their academic ambitions with life’s everyday demands.

I see honesty as central to my personality; as people grow smarter, honesty remains a constant in my life from the start.

Another reason honesty matters to me is that I believe it prevents failure on tests and protects me from future bullying. However, sometimes honesty can backfire, and people who trusted me might become angry. They may learn not to trust me again, which would be sad if I had assured them of honesty while secretly hoping to avoid negative outcomes. After a negative experience with honesty, a friend or family member might disagree with me and never trust me again, or they might later apologize when they realize they could not rely on me.

If a better friend or family member decides to trust someone else, we might have a heated debate that could last forever. It would be better to avoid a huge argument, meet face to face, and talk calmly so no one’s feelings are hurt. By gathering people who value honesty, we can help friends and family avoid stress and avoid dangerous thoughts such as suicide or self‑harm. Even if someone cannot trust me, I will not think of death; I will stand by my honesty, even when some people have been disappointed.

Honesty is not a failure; it remains my most important personality trait. When I think I might fail a test, I honestly say I will do my best, study hard, and pass, rather than blame the test or others. If I forget to study, the fault lies with me, not with honesty. If I ever doubt honesty or think I don’t need it, I will still use it when I truly need it to succeed.

I would want everyone to regard honesty as their number one trait because it helps solve conflicts that cannot be resolved in one attempt. Many people disagree with continuous honesty, saying it should not be their primary trait. They claim that people must learn the true meaning of honesty and how it helps them succeed. Some believe that very smart people have the best honesty and others do not. That is wrong; honesty does not depend on intelligence. Even less‑smart people can grow and become honest, while smart people can also lose their honesty if they are not taught to stay true.

The people who can relearn honesty after it is lost are mainly family members and teachers, not friends. Friends may tempt me into a different world, causing everyone to wonder why I can no longer be trusted. When friends and family see that I have changed, they will be surprised: “How did they change?" They may later tell everyone about the person who has transformed. That illustrates why honesty is essential in everyone’s life.

I believe that honesty should be practiced at all times. When I am truthful, I am not deceiving anyone, and this builds trust. People are more likely to rely on me when they ask for help or advice, even if they are not perfectly honest themselves. Honesty is a cornerstone of my character; it stays with me from the beginning and grows with me as I mature.

Being honest also gives me confidence that I will succeed. If I speak plainly, I am less likely to be caught off guard by a surprise exam or to become a target of bullying. However, truthfulness can sometimes backfire. Some people might react angrily when I tell them the inconvenient truth, and they might decide never to trust me again. This is painful, especially if I have said something blunt only to please a friend or family member, ignoring the possible negative fallout. If a relationship suffers due to my honesty, the other person may disagree with me and refuse to trust me in the future. Over time, they may even blame me for everything that is wrong. Yet, if we work through that conflict, we can rebuild the bond. By meeting face to face and discussing the issue calmly, we avoid a prolonged argument and protect each other’s feelings.

It is also valuable to gather a supportive circle of honest people. With a network of trustworthy friends and family, misunderstandings can be resolved more easily and individuals can focus on positive relationships rather than negative ones. When someone loses trust in me, I do not resort to harmful thoughts; instead, I stand firm in my commitment to honesty, even if it means disappointment from those I’ve let down. My integrity remains intact—I will always strive to be honest throughout my life.

Adopting honesty as a primary trait benefits everyone. It helps solve difficult conflicts that might not be resolved in a single attempt. Some people claim that honesty is not essential because they are not naturally truthful, but this view is incorrect. Honesty can be learned and cultivated by anyone, whether they are currently intelligent or not. Even highly intelligent people may lapse into deceit if they lack guidance. Therefore, parents, teachers, and mentors play a key role in teaching those who have lost their moral footing to return to honesty.

Ultimately, honesty is a vital quality that fosters trust and success. When people understand and practice it, they can navigate life’s challenges with confidence and integrity.

Working with a group or working by yourself.

There is nothing more beneficial than working as part of a team, especially when you collaborate with people you like and who know what to do; this can be one of the best experiences you’ll ever have. Working alone, on the other hand, offers benefits such as preventing others from stealing your ideas or copying your work—a common problem in teams.

Teamwork often feels like people do less, because when you’re in a group you tend not to take on all the tasks yourself; everyone helps each other, which can reinforce a lack of confidence and a constant need for support.

Although I enjoy collaborating with friends, I notice they often copy my ideas, which is frustrating. It makes me feel like I am the only one who can do well, and I’m saddened that they rely so heavily on teamwork to succeed when they aren’t always the ones doing the work.

I prefer to work alone rather than in a team; it isn’t that I dislike others, it’s simply how I function. When I collaborate, I often feel that it doesn’t benefit me because the other person may cheat or not contribute, whereas working by myself is more authentically me. It allows me to keep going without worrying about others and to think that I can accomplish more on my own.

Through these experiences I have learned to put myself first, to think about my own needs, and to support myself. In my view, teamwork is something that should only happen when it truly adds value, because you should never feel useless or dependent on others at the expense of yourself.

Working alone is far more rewarding than collaborating in a group. When you team up with others, you often find that the work gets divided and everyone relies on each other. This can make people feel less confident because they expect help to finish tasks. For me, that sense of dependence is uncomfortable—being dependent on others feels like a weakness.

Another problem with group projects is that ideas and effort get diluted. My classmates frequently reproduce the work I do, and sometimes they submit my ideas as their own. This not only steals credit but also diminishes the personal satisfaction that comes from creating something on your own. I dislike watching others benefit from my hard work without contributing equally. It feels unfair, especially when some team members do little of the actual labor and still get the same grade.

I have tried working in groups with friends before; the experience was largely negative. I felt that my friends would only succeed if I carried the load. The fear that they will not achieve success without my help makes the group dynamic uneasy. A truly collaborative team should be evenly split, yet that condition rarely happens in practice.

In contrast, working by myself gives me complete control over my goals and methods. I can progress at my own pace, focus on my strengths, and choose the best tools without negotiating with others. It also protects me from the temptation to cut corners and ensures I am responsible for every part of the work. When I stay alone, I feel motivated and in charge of my learning process. I no longer worry about the expectations of my peers or about being unintentionally cheated upon.

Through experience in various situations, I have learned the importance of prioritising my own needs above others. The feeling of being useful is tied to what I am personally achieving rather than what others contribute. I have come to believe that relying on oneself is the best way to preserve self-efficacy and avoid feeling let down by group dynamics that often overlook individual effort.

Therefore, I continue to prefer working alone. For me, collaboration can dilute creative output, invite unfair sharing, and trigger feelings of insecurity. By focusing on my own work I protect my ideas, preserve a strong sense of self, and climb higher in my personal and professional development.

I believe that students would benefit greatly from the possibility of attending classes from home. This option allows them to arrive more prepared, widens their focus, and reduces the anxiety that many feel in a traditional classroom setting.

One reason is that some students feel embarrassed about showing their best work in front of their classmates. They might fear that others will see them as less capable or worry that they will not speak English well. By studying from home, they can practice freely, watch lessons again if they miss a point, and build confidence before presenting. This can help them meet their goals without the added pressure of a public setting.

For example, a student who is alone at home may have many questions about what he is supposed to do. Instead of waiting for a teacher, he can search online or explore different learning platforms to find solutions. If he is hungry after a long study session, he can simply make a quick snack in his kitchen and return to work, a convenience that is impossible at school. Any doubt can be cleared by texting a teacher or asking a classmate for help, which is quick and less intimidating.

Home learning also suits shy students and those who need individual attention. A female student who is pregnant, for instance, might find it extremely difficult to travel to campus and cope with the physical demands of class attendance. I once met a pregnant girl who, despite extreme tiredness, attended every school day. When her baby was born she still tried to keep up, but the discomfort and the constant interruptions from crying or feeding made it almost impossible. If she had been able to attend online, she could have studied at her own pace and shared a classroom with her baby if she chose.

Another benefit is flexibility with morning schedules. Some students prefer to sleep in and begin studying later. At night, without the need to be on time for school, they can review materials or finish assignments at their own rhythm. This flexibility can also help students who need to take part-time jobs to support their families. Working a few hours a day and studying online afterwards can be more manageable than trying to keep up with a full classroom schedule while earning money.

Of course, there are challenges. Not all families have the financial resources to access reliable internet or a suitable device. A student who also needs to work may find it hard to juggle both responsibilities. Schools must therefore provide subsidies, loaner equipment, and flexible deadlines so that every student can participate. Despite these obstacles, the pros often outweigh the cons, especially when we consider the support that can be offered: online tutoring, discussion boards, and recorded lectures.

In conclusion, attending classes from home can be a practical and empowering alternative to the traditional school environment. It removes logistical barriers, allows for self‑paced learning, supports vulnerable students, and can help those who must work while studying. Of course, for this model to succeed schools need to address technological and economic disparities, but with careful planning and support, students can thrive in an online setting and achieve their academic goals.

Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote, “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow.” This is a true fact, and you should try to be a better human or person in life and become someone that people can look up to.

I believe that, as Ralph Waldo Emerson said, if we never try to go beyond what we already know, we will never grow. In my seventeen years of life, I have found this to be true. When we stay in our comfort zone, nothing changes; we wish everything were easy and we stop striving to become the best version of ourselves.

Being comfortable can keep us safe, but it also wastes time and effort that could make us better people. By continually challenging ourselves, we can improve and share our knowledge with others. Everybody should aim to be the best they can be, because simply staying the same is not the best path forward.

Some may argue that constant effort is unnecessary once a person feels they have reached their peak. They might believe that learning more is impossible or that they have mastered all they need. This view is mistaken. Human beings can always learn something new, whether we are parents, teachers, friends, or strangers. We should not settle for mediocrity or simply “okay”; we must continue to push ourselves.

I think that learning a bit each day, asking for help when needed, and offering help to others strengthens our community. Curiosity and open conversation cannot harm more than they can help.

Ultimately, Emerson’s observation is correct: if we do not challenge ourselves to do something beyond what we have already mastered, we will never grow. By striving for improvement, we become role models for those around us.

Have you ever wondered why people graduate at such a young age? Some might argue that graduating early is a bad idea, but in reality it can be a good one because it allows students to become more mature and take full responsibility for themselves.

The first reason is that graduating early helps students become more mature for the real world. Many people today do not understand how the real world works. For instance, many teenagers are unaware of the consequences of their actions. Teenagers who drink and drive, for example, can cause accidents that hurt themselves and others, yet they may not think about how they would cope if their parents could no longer bail them out or if they were not so lucky. These young people often assume that someone will always be there to take care of them. If a teenager finishes school at 18, they have a chance to learn what they should and should not do in real life.

Another example concerns parental support. Some parents pay for their children’s car insurance only if they break the law, defending their child and saying “my child is innocent.” Parents sometimes convince themselves they are doing the right thing, which can delay learning from mistakes. When teens graduate early, they learn to take responsibility for the money they spend, such as paying for insurance or other bills.

The second reason is that teenagers who graduate early become fully responsible for their own expenses. They can pay rent, utility bills, and other costs. For example, I used to forget to pay my phone bill. My mother had to pay it, which made me realize how important it is to keep track of money. Similarly, if I tend to waste electricity or water, the price increases; my mother had to cover those expenses. These experiences show that when a teen can manage utility bills, they become more responsible.

Some critics argue that graduating early means missing out on life, that you have no opportunity to enjoy the moment as a teenager, or that you will be stressed and miss out on fun. They might say that early graduation means forgoing the pleasures of adolescence.

However, at the end of the day, graduating early can be a good idea. It encourages greater maturity and personal accountability, and it prepares you for the responsibilities that life will lay out before you.

Have you ever wondered why some people finish university so early? It isn’t because they are smarter; it’s because they feel ready to face the real world. Although some people disagree and think leaving school early is a mistake, I believe that graduating after only three years can be a very good idea because it helps students become more mature and take full responsibility for themselves.

The first reason is that early graduation can help students mature. Many young people don’t understand how the real world works. For instance, it is not uncommon for teenagers who stay in school to drink and drive or get into other risky situations. If their parents are always ready to solve the problem, the student may think that nothing will happen to them. When a person leaves school early, they do not have the safety net of their parents. As a result, they learn the consequences of their actions much faster and begin to behave more responsibly.

Another example is that parents may cover the costs of a car or a phone bill for their teenage children. Because the child is not responsible for paying, they may use these services without thinking. An early graduate will have to pay for these expenses themselves and will therefore become more aware of how their choices affect their finances. They will learn to keep track of bills and avoid wasteful spending.

The second benefit of early graduation is self‑reliance. Once a student leaves school, they no longer receive the help of their parents to pay for a phone or a light bill; they must pay for everything on their own. This forces them to understand where every dollar comes from, how to budget, and how to avoid overspending. Understanding how to manage a bill for electricity, water, or cable is a critical life skill that some teenagers simply do not learn until later in life.

Some people claim that it is a mistake to leave school early because you miss out on important life experiences. They argue that a teenager’s time should be spent enjoying the moment rather than worrying about money or responsibilities. I agree that experience is valuable, and that “fun” is an important part of education. However, I believe that early graduation does not prevent enjoyment. Instead, it forces students into the real world sooner, so they can learn to combine work, study, and leisure in a balanced way. They will develop a sense of happiness from achieving independence rather than feeling dependent on parents.

In conclusion, I think that graduating after only three years is an excellent idea. It allows students to mature quickly and become completely responsible for their own lives. When teenagers handle their bills, manage money, and learn how the world works, they gain the confidence they need to succeed.

Thomas Jefferson wrote, “It is wonderful how much may be done if we are doing.” What this means is that you should always be working, both for society and for yourself. Do we accomplish more when we are constantly engaged, or does inactivity also serve a purpose? Some claim that inactivity is beneficial because it provides rest to regain strength and sustain future work. Others argue that continual effort is preferable, as diligent effort leads to achieving goals and contributing productively to society.

Millions of people rise each morning to give their all at work, but what about those who do not work? Even if you cannot find a job, you can still contribute to society or to your personal development. You can engage in volunteer work or assist others, remaining an active individual. It is important to recognize that everyone needs rest, but excessive rest prevents you from reaching your dreams and ambitions.

Consistently doing something is advantageous if you are engaged in worthwhile activities, working hard, and passionate about what you do. Every person who works does so for a reason. Some aim to achieve goals, some must earn to meet responsibilities, and some merely love their work or wish to support their families. All work with intent, and that motivates them. My mother always tells me, “If you want something, pursue it; make it happen.” All of us need a promising future, so continual action is essential. This is why doing something is preferable to doing nothing.

Let us consider society’s perspective. In society, you must act, whether you have a specific dream or not, because you need to eat, secure housing, pay bills and taxes, and satisfy other necessities. Thus, you must have employment. And beyond a job, you can perform other activities that keep you engaged—such as helping others, which fosters personal growth. Whether remunerated or not, if you love what you do, you contribute meaningfully to society.

Doing something is vital to humanity because it propels the world forward. Dreams and goals drive people to act. Consider whether you are a productive individual or if inactivity might alter your perspective. In conclusion, the president Thomas Jefferson offered these words to inspire reflection on what we do or should do in life. It is wise to take a break, but never forget that you have goals and dreams that must become reality.

**Four‑Day School**

The debate over the advantages and disadvantages of a four‑day school week focuses on whether students who normally attend school five days a week should have their schedules shortened. Many argue that a four‑day week can be beneficial, but the proposal must be carefully considered by both business workers and schools—high schools and higher‑education institutions alike.

A typical four‑day week would reduce the school day by about ten hours per week. Those lost hours can be offset by extending the remaining school days by two hours. This extension increases the attention span and time available for each class, allowing students to complete projects and assignments more thoroughly. The extra time also offers opportunities for peer and teacher support when someone is struggling in a subject.

Students could use the additional two‑hour slot on the fourth day for activities such as library study, which helps those who love reading, or for sports and other extracurriculars. The fifth day, if retained, could be reserved for medical appointments or other health needs. Parents can write notes to excuse absences, and having a day off during the regular school period can reduce the number of missed classes.

Teachers, who are also parents, would benefit from an extra day to spend with their families and to manage their personal responsibilities. Sophomores and seniors, who face significant decisions about college or the workforce, would gain time to weigh options and complete necessary applications. Freshmen, transitioning from middle school, would also appreciate a break from routine to adjust to high school demands.

A free Friday or Monday could be used for community service, with parental permission and adult supervision. Students might help clean streets and rivers or assist local charities. Schools could partner with large companies to provide job‑search assistance, allowing students to explore part‑time positions on the free day.

Key considerations:

- A four‑day school week eliminates the fifth school day, making the full academic period available on the remaining four days.
- Three free days per week would let students devote time to family, friends, or personal interests.
- Parents could adjust the schedule so that Friday or Monday mornings are off, giving students an opportunity to rest and complete responsibilities.
- Students with part‑time jobs may find the longer school days challenging, but the free day could serve as a full‑time working day to earn money.

Balancing two activities per day can be exhausting. However, with a four‑day schedule, students can rest after school, finish homework, and dedicate the additional days to work or other commitments.

While disadvantages exist, the solutions—extended hours, more free time, and flexible scheduling—outweigh them for a majority of students. After reviewing all benefits, drawbacks, and solutions, I conclude that every student deserves three free days and four school days, even if a student’s situation requires a different use of the free day. With collective support, we can advocate for this new right for high‑school and college students.

Four‑Day School

The idea of switching from a five‑day to a four‑day school week has both supporters and opponents. Many argue that the benefits of a shortened week outweigh the drawbacks, and that schools, businesses, and families should seriously consider this change.

A four‑day schedule means students would lose ten hours of classroom time each week. However, those hours could be recovered by extending each day by about two hours. Increasing the length of each class would allow students to focus better, finish projects and assignments, and spend extra time with peers and teachers who might need additional help.

The extra two hours could also be used to enrich students’ experiences. On the fourth day, students could attend the library for independent reading, participate in sports, or take part in other extracurricular activities that are often cut short in a regular five‑day schedule.

Moreover, the shortened schedule could benefit those who need to attend medical appointments or manage health issues. Instead of writing excuses for missing class, teachers could allow students to use the extended day to attend appointments, reducing absenteeism during regular school days.

Teachers, who are often parents themselves, would also appreciate the extra day. It would give them more time for family commitments and personal responsibilities, which is often jeopardized by a long week.

High‑school seniors face a particularly stressful period, deciding on colleges and preparing for their futures. A longer school day combined with a day off could give them time to explore options, meet with college counselors, or even start part‑time work. Freshmen, coming from middle school, might also benefit from the chance to adjust their routines in a less pressured environment.

Frequent‑free days could be used for community service. With parental permission and adult supervision, students could volunteer to clean streets, support local charities, or help maintain parks. Schools could also partner with local businesses to offer part‑time job opportunities on the free day, giving students practical experience.

Consider the practical aspects: a four‑day school week means the five‑day schedule is replaced by four full days, with an extra day off. Students would have three days each week to spend with family, friends, or pursue other interests. No need to wake up on Friday or Monday morning—depending on which day is chosen for the break—allowing students to rest and finish responsibilities.

Some concerns remain for students who work part‑time jobs. Extending the school day could reduce their available hours, but with the fifth day free, those who can work full‑time might compensate in other weeks. Balancing school, work, and rest can be exhausting, yet a four‑day week could still provide sufficient downtime after school for rest and homework, while the remaining days work or rest as needed.

While disadvantages exist, solutions exist as well. The overall benefits—better focus, more extracurricular options, reduced absenteeism, and additional family time—appear to outweigh the drawbacks for the majority of students. In conclusion, a four‑day school week offers a more balanced life for students, teachers, and families alike. Everyone deserves a three‑day break, and together we can advocate for this change in high school and college schedules.

When motivation disappears, a student is likely to quit, missing out on the necessary credits to graduate high school. Without a high‑school diploma, college admission becomes difficult, which in turn limits employment opportunities. Employers often prefer candidates with a solid academic record. A jobless graduate may even face homelessness. These consequences show why students must choose courses that truly interest them.

The future can be full of challenges, but having the right skills helps students navigate obstacles. Knowing one’s strengths enables a student to dream bigger and direct their energies toward a future they genuinely desire.

Some people argue against mandatory electives, saying that students might lack the motivation or simply see them as “kiddie” courses. Author Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” In our lives, our accomplishments, actions, and attitudes speak volumes about who we are and how we are perceived. Around the world, many people view those who stay true to themselves as humble and admirable. For example, in your career, in your field of work, or in school, when you volunteer for tasks that are not part of your responsibilities, those gestures reveal a big heart and a commitment to authenticity.

I agree with Emerson, because when you are your true self, others notice something special about you. You may start by learning new things on your first try—mistakes are inevitable, but perseverance distinguishes you from those who remain unchanged. There are three reasons why staying true to yourself is essential.

First, by being authentic you influence those around you. When you consistently go the extra mile—helping a classmate solve a difficult math problem even though it is not your job—you become a role model. Others notice your willingness to support, and they may follow your example.

Second, being yourself makes you an inspiration. Whether at home, in the neighborhood, at school, or in a church, your actions can motivate others. If a neighbor sees you cutting the grass or cleaning a shared space, they may feel encouraged to do the same. Your commitment to a better community can spread throughout the entire area.

Third, your true accomplishments can shift the mindset of those around you. When people observe you progressing in life, they ask, “How did you do that?” You can share your methods, leaving a lasting message that others can replicate. In a family setting, for instance, one sibling may have a modest job while another runs a successful business. When the latter gives advice and encouragement, the entire family feels a boost of hope and confidence.

In conclusion, Emerson reminds us that we constantly strive for greater achievements and positive impact. More than half of the world seeks to help others because they see both the personal and collective benefits. By staying true to ourselves, we become examples for those around us, inspiring countless people and creating a ripple effect of kindness and progress.

My talent is drawing. When I draw, I like to sketch stars, the moon, woods, and oceans. Drawing lets me express myself in many artistic styles. My favorite type is free-style drawing, where I can create anything I want and fix mistakes as needed. I also enjoy painting because it lets me channel my emotions—sadness, happiness, anger, or excitement—into color. Art is my favorite pursuit; I can create anything, and people are willing to pay large sums for beautiful works, regardless of cost.  

Many people possess artistic talent, and some are so skilled that they doubt their worth and consider giving their work away. They fail to realize that others will appreciate and purchase it. Art can be expensive, yet some artists choose not to sell their pieces because they cherish the memories or want to display them for family. Others may sell them, but usually not for millions—they keep them for loved ones. Sometimes artists leave errors untouched, hoping that collectors will appreciate the authenticity.  

I believe artists should try to sell their work because they can earn significant income from paintings and drawings. Art is a demanding job that requires patience. Mistakes are common, but artists can transform them into something beautiful. Often, a perceived flaw becomes an unexpected source of interest.  

Some people find art boring, yet those who love it see it as a joy, not a chore. The exhilaration of painting can release inhibition; I sometimes let my body take over, creating spontaneously, and it feels truly liberating.  

Others feel stressed when their creations don’t match their vision. I experience that frustration too, but I remind myself that patience is essential. Art is challenging, but with regular practice, the difficulty lessens. I am good at art, yet I continue to learn and push myself, knowing that consistent practice is the best teacher.

I think my greatest talent is drawing. I enjoy sketching stars, the moon, forests, and oceans. Drawing allows me to express myself in many artistic ways. My favorite style is freehand drawing, where I can create anything I imagine, and if I make a mistake I can simply erase or adjust it. I also love painting because it lets me translate my emotions—be they sadness, joy, anger, or excitement—into color.

Art is one of my biggest passions. I can create whatever I wish, and people are often willing to pay large sums for a piece, no matter how expensive it is. Many people have this gift, and some are so good that they doubt their own work and consider giving it away. But they overlook that other people will appreciate and purchase it. Some artists keep their art for memories or for family, selling not for millions but for the joy it brings. Others leave unsent errors on paper, hoping that a wealthy collector might one day purchase them.

I believe artists should try to sell their work. Even though creating art is challenging and requires patience—mistakes may mean starting over—these errors can become unique features of a piece. Art is not a dull task; those who love it find it thrilling. When I pour myself into a painting, I sometimes lose control of the outcome, which feels liberating. Yet stress can arise when a piece doesn’t look as imagined, but learning to be patient and practicing consistently turns the difficult into manageable. Through perseverance, even a skilled artist keeps growing.

Does the student truly benefit from being able to attend classes from home? Students would not gain from remote attendance because, as I once observed with a friend who took advantage of it, she neglected her responsibilities, opting instead to fulfill other tasks she deemed necessary. She did not benefit at all. Students would not benefit from being able to attend classes remotely because they exploit the arrangement, fail to fulfill their obligations, and acquire no substantive learning.

First of all, students exploit the flexibility of attending classes from home to attend to other matters. For example, they might submit assignments late when due dates are extended. Not all students who attend remotely exploit this leniency, but those who do do so merely for amusement, deferring their academic work. Moreover, they will continually concoct excuses for why they failed to complete assigned tasks. They capitalize on their free time to socialize with friends, party, and engage in nonacademic pursuits.

Most importantly, they neglect their duties. When an assignment or project is assigned, they act indolently, knowing little will prompt them—teachers cannot constantly remind them, after all. Consequently, they spend most of their time on leisure activities instead of completing required tasks. Students devote more energy to partying and hanging with friends instead of engaging in academically valuable work that would benefit them later. Many students simply know the material yet prefer not to exert effort because they lack motivation.

Finally, students learn nothing by attending classes from home. All they do is party, hang out with friends and partners. They ignore assignments, resorting to copying others or searching the internet for answers. Those who remotely attend use it as a leisure opportunity rather than a learning one; they literally absorb no knowledge because all they indulge in is frivolity while they should be studying seriously.

In closing, students do not truly benefit from remote attendance because they exploit it to pursue other activities, ignore their responsibilities, and acquire no knowledge—all they do is party, socialize, and disregard the tasks they are assigned.

Does a student really benefit from being able to attend classes from home? In my opinion, students would not benefit because, as an example, I once had a friend who attended remotely and never completed her assignments; she treated the arrangement as an advantage and spent her time on other things, ultimately deriving no benefit.

First of all, students often take advantage of virtual attendance to do unrelated tasks. For instance, many submit late work simply because the deadline became less stringent; while not every remote learner abuses this flexibility, those who do tend to do so just to have fun and avoid obligatory work. Moreover, they frequently concoct excuses for missing assignments, claiming reasons such as “I was busy” or “I needed to go out with friends.” Thus, they prioritize social activities over academic responsibilities.

Does a student really benefit from being able to attend classes from home? I once had a friend who, when she could join classes remotely, never did what she was supposed to do and instead used the arrangement as an excuse to pursue other things. From that experience I concluded that remote attendance does not help students at all.

First, many students use the flexibility of home attendance to get things done at the last minute and to prioritize non‑academic activities. For instance, they may submit assignments late or “borrow” the extra time to hang out with friends, party, or spend more time with a boyfriend. Those who do take advantage this way usually do so for enjoyment rather than responsibility.

Second, remote learning often leads to a lack of motivation. When an assignment or project is assigned, some students simply act lazy because they know that teachers cannot monitor them closely. Consequently, they spend most of the time on leisure activities instead of completing the required work. Even students who understand the material often choose not to engage because they feel unmotivated.

Third, without the accountability that a physical classroom provides, students tend to cheat or copy answers from the internet. They view remote learning as a chance to relax and party all day, ignoring the seriousness of their studies and the tasks they are assigned.

In closing, students do not benefit from attending classes from home. They exploit the arrangement to do other things, they neglect their responsibilities, and they learn nothing while they party, hang out with friends, and ignore their coursework.

Students do not really benefit from attending classes from home. From my own experience, I know people who used remote learning as a loophole to avoid their responsibilities. They claimed the convenience allowed them to get things done, but in reality it only gave them an excuse to neglect schoolwork.

Firstly, many students see remote class as a perk. They might miss deadlines or submit late work because they feel less pressure at home. They find themselves more likely to use the extra time to wander online, chat with friends, or even spend the evening with a boyfriend instead of staying focused on homework. Even those who do turn in assignments often do so after last‑minute cramming, rather than through steady effort.

Secondly, the lack of constant supervision leads to laziness. If a teacher cannot spot a student in the physical classroom, it feels easier to postpone a project or forget a due date. Some students make up excuses, blaming technical problems or "just a bad day." They end up spending most of their time on social media or games, rather than on the assignments that are essential for later success. Their knowledge grows only as far as they are comfortable, and many choose to skip tasks altogether.

Finally, the learning that actually occurs in a remote setting is limited. Instead of deeply engaging with course material, students often copy answers from the internet or relay late‑night messages from classmates. They treat remote class as a break—a chance to party or relax—rather than a serious academic commitment. The result: important concepts are missed and the opportunity to develop independent study habits is lost.

In summary, attending classes from home does not benefit students. It offers them a loophole to procrastinate, leads them to neglect their responsibilities, and ultimately prevents meaningful learning. Their time is better spent taking the challenges at hand seriously rather than turning every lesson into a casual excuse.

Therefore, I do not agree with Churchill’s statement about the importance of failure in the pursuit of success. No one has lived without experiencing failure at least once, yet some people achieve success by working hard, fighting for what they want, and never losing enthusiasm. Enthusiasm is something that people should never forget.

First, everyone has failed at least once in their life. In this world, many people have made mistakes, experienced failure, or been disappointed. For example, they may miss out on a job, receive poor grades, or fail to achieve a goal. No one is perfect, and mistakes are inevitable. Failure does not always relate to personal achievements; you can fail your family or friends by lying to them or disappointing them. Perhaps only a small percentage, around 1 %, have never failed. I say this because my cousin has never disappointed her parents; she earned good grades, graduated with a scholarship, and is now at Virginia Tech University.

To reach your goal or dream, you must work hard. If you have failed once or more, do not become sad or depressed; you are strong enough to handle it. Life always offers another opportunity or chance. Work hard, never give up easily, and fight for what you want to achieve. Life is not easy, and no one claims it is; if you don’t get something the first time, you can get back up. If you fail at one thing, make other plans. There are many opportunities to explore, and you may find something that you enjoy.

People should never lose their enthusiasm. If you have enthusiasm for something, go for it; do not let others dictate your path. Enthusiasm is worth appreciating and working hard for. Not everyone has it; some people lack that strong interest and warmth that drives them to pursue their passions. Be proud if you are enthusiastic for something. Those without enthusiasm often feel indifferent about their lives or future and accept what they receive without giving it their feeling. For instance, when I was a child I excelled in school and was among the best students, but when I moved to the US I had to start over because I didn’t know English. To succeed with my English, I had to work hard.

In conclusion, I do not agree with Churchill’s statement. Success does not have to consist of going from failure to failure. You may fail many times, but if you do not give up and work hard, you can achieve your goals and dreams. Keep the enthusiasm you have—its warmth and inspiration will carry you forward. Always work hard for what you want, and you will succeed. Life is not easy, but with effort, it can be achieved.

Success should not be defined as a series of failures. Winston Churchill once said that “success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” I disagree with this idea. While setbacks are inevitable, the crucial factor is perseverance, hard work, and maintaining a positive spirit, not merely enduring failure.

First, everyone experiences failure at least once. In life we make mistakes, receive bad grades, lose jobs, or disappoint people we care about. No person is perfect. My own cousin, for example, never let herself fail her parents or her studies; she earned high grades and a scholarship, and now attends Virginia Tech. Her story shows that failure is not a prerequisite for success; it is simply a common experience. Understanding this helps us accept that a single failure does not define us.

Second, achieving a goal requires effort and resilience. If you fall short once or twice, do not give in. Life will offer new chances—different projects, alternative paths, or improved strategies. For instance, when I moved to the United States, I had to learn English from scratch. I did not let that failure stop me; I studied hard and eventually became proficient. By sticking with my objective and adjusting my approach, I turned a setback into a chance to grow. This demonstrates that success is built on hard work, not repeated failures.

Finally, enthusiasm is essential. Passion fuels motivation and keeps us pushing forward when obstacles appear. People who are enthusiastic about something are willing to invest time and energy into it. Those who lack this spark often settle for mediocrity; they may accept whatever comes their way without striving for more. In my childhood, I was a top student because I loved learning. When I arrived in the U.S., my enthusiasm drove me to master English despite the difficulty. That drive made the difference between giving up and succeeding.

In conclusion, I do not share Churchill’s view that success is simply a series of failures. While failure is a natural part of life, what matters more is persistence, hard work, and maintaining enthusiasm. If we keep trying, learn from our mistakes, and stay passionate, we can achieve our goals and realize our dreams. Failure may be inevitable, but it should not define our journey to success.
