Reading out loud is one skill I rely on because it helps me understand what I am reading. Hearing the words in my head solidifies the material, so I can explain it more clearly afterward. It also assists when I need to write an essay about the text.

When I read aloud, I grasp the content better. It feels good to hear myself read, and I can immediately notice if I’m pausing incorrectly or mispronouncing a word. If a word slips across my mind, I can say it out loud to ensure I understand its meaning.

Reading out loud also lets me describe the events of a story more effectively. By vocalizing the narrative, I retain more detail in my memory and am less likely to forget what I’ve read. Others can understand the text better when they hear it too.

Before writing an essay, I review the material aloud. I can note a lot of points and decide what to include while the story is still fresh in my mind. Knowing exactly where the book takes me lets me write confidently, without fear of missing something important. The process also helps me check whether my writing stays true to what the book is telling me.

Conclusion: Reading out loud lets me understand the book, write more effectively, and remember what I read.

Reading aloud is one of the strongest skills I have developed. Whenever I read a text out loud, I find it easier to understand the message. The act of speaking the words forces me to slow down and examine each sentence, which helps me retain the information more vividly in my mind. When I later need to write an essay or explain the material, the ideas stay fresh because I have already rehearsed them verbally.

The process also gives me instant feedback on my reading. I can hear myself pause at difficult words or stumble over phrases. By correcting these habits right away, I improve my pronunciation and fluency. Moreover, hearing the text gives me a clearer picture of the story’s events and characters, allowing me to describe scenes with richer detail.

When I write, I find that reading aloud beforehand saves time and reduces anxiety. I have a ready-made outline in my head, so I can translate it into written sentences more smoothly. The confidence that comes from knowing the material well makes me less worried about making mistakes.

In short, reading aloud deepens my comprehension, sharpens my oral skills, and eases the transition from reading to writing. By practicing this habit regularly, I keep the essence of every book alive in my mind and feel prepared to express it clearly on paper.

Albert Einstein once said, “Imagination is more important than knowledge.” I completely agree with this view. Imagination brings joy, helps others, and can even lead to a fulfilling career. I will explain how.

First, imagination can make us happier. When we use our imagination, we can picture anything we enjoy. For example, we might daydream about flying like a bird—even though we cannot actually do it. Visualising the wind in our hair and the sense of freedom can lift our mood. We also enjoy imagining what we will look like when we reach a future age, such as a hundred years old. These mental pictures offer comfort and excitement, which can bring happiness into our everyday life.

Second, imagination is a useful tool for helping people. Suppose you see a child crying in a busy mall because someone laughed at her “weird” dress. You could use imagination to soothe her. You might tell her, “Stop crying, sweetie. Imagine that everyone is admiring you like a princess. You are the one visiting them now, so think of yourself as graceful and confident.” By encouraging the child to picture a more positive scenario, you help her calm down and feel better.

Lastly, many parents say that imagination cannot lead to a good job. I disagree. If you dream of being a home designer, an inadequate imagination can result in uninspiring designs that might get you fired. On the other hand, a writer with a rich imagination can create dozens of engaging books, earning more than many other professions, even rivaling a doctor’s salary. Thus, imagination is an asset that can help you secure the career you desire.

In conclusion, I wholeheartedly support Einstein’s statement. Imagination not only brings happiness, it also assists others and can guide us toward rewarding work. For these reasons, I believe imagination is the most important force in our lives.

The Benefits of Working in Groups

Working in groups has many advantages. When students collaborate, they can help each other, produce better work, and acquire new skills. Group work also fosters friendships, increases communication, and encourages the sharing of ideas. Because some students may not know what to do, working together can be especially helpful, and teachers should encourage group work so that students assist one another and achieve better results. Learning to work in a group is valuable for life, benefiting future jobs, family relationships, and overall teamwork.

First, group work generates more ideas and provides support. With more people, students can brainstorm better solutions and help those who are unsure of how to proceed. Group collaboration allows students to understand concepts more deeply, communicate effectively, and produce quality work that leads to passing grades. It also offers the chance to meet classmates who otherwise might not interact.

Second, group work develops essential skills such as communication, written expression, and interpersonal interaction. These abilities are crucial in many situations; for instance, if a student doesn’t understand a topic, they can ask for help from a group member. Practicing communication daily strengthens these skills. Additionally, groups accommodate students who need extra support—more knowledgeable peers can guide those who struggle, especially when language barriers exist.

Third, group work provides a valuable learning experience that extends beyond the classroom. Students who start with little familiarity can build friendships and improve academically, earning better grades. Positive group relationships also translate to success at home and in future careers, where teamwork is vital. Just as a soccer team coordinates strategies and supports one another, students learn to collaborate to achieve common goals.

Effective communication is critical in a group. Clear exchanges help everyone understand tasks and contribute meaningfully. Generosity—helping others—creates a supportive environment. When students work alone, they may become stuck without assistance; in a group, peers can step in. While some teachers prefer independent work to prevent distraction or copying, collaboration often yields faster progress and a richer learning experience.

In conclusion, encouraging group work is highly beneficial. Groups generate better ideas, foster stronger relationships, and build communication skills that carry into future success. Students who learn to thrive in collaborative settings are more likely to excel academically and professionally. Teachers should continue promoting group activities, as students and educators alike will reap the advantages of teamwork. I personally value group work because it allows me to learn from others and complete tasks more effectively.

Working together also improves communication; students practice listening and speaking, which prepares them for future jobs and social situations.

One activity I consider truly enjoyable is science experiments. One reason I find these activities fun is that they differ from other types of projects. By this I mean that, for example, when one does a math project or a language arts project, it is nothing more than doing many math exercises or writing an essay. Unlike those, in the science projects—such as the time I got to observe a frog’s interior—it’s a different experience. It might sound disgusting to many readers, and to be honest it didn’t smell good either. But one of the things that fascinated me about the project was that frogs don’t have as many organs as we humans do. Perhaps some are removed, but there weren’t a lot of organs inside.

Another curious detail was the color variation. I remembered seeing blue and pink, unlike the typical red that dominates most human insides. Frogs actually had varied interior colors, but they looked a little dry because my teacher mentioned they had been frozen for some time. That certainly made it easier to cut tissue from the frog’s interior. Moreover, since my teacher said we could cut whatever we wanted, my group and I explored as thoroughly as possible. One part was startling—flies in the frog’s stomach. That scene definitely disgusted me, yet it didn’t stop me.

After we finished examining the frog’s interior, the teacher explained the name and function of each part. A friend of mine, however, thought it was silly to poke the frog’s eye. I still don’t know what crossed his mind at that moment. When he did, the frog’s eye wasn’t completely frozen, so liquid rushed out, soaking him. Fortunately, it didn’t reach me, but it did reach my friend. The teacher then sent him to the bathroom to wash up.

Following this, the teacher decided it was best to end the project. Still, it was undeniably a lot of fun.

After four seconds, faint waves appeared for a few moments, and I eventually enjoyed the experiment. It had drawbacks: it was brief, and the teacher took a long time to explain the concept. A small act of kindness is important because it can bring a smile to someone’s face when they need it most. That smile is beneficial for personal health. Even a modest gesture can brighten a day that might otherwise feel bleak. We often overlook how powerful such small acts can be in people’s lives, and yet they are the building blocks of compassion.

When people receive kindness, they often feel loved. They sense the tenderness that the giver has toward them, which can flood them with happiness both inside and out. It is perhaps one of the greatest feelings in the world. We don’t need to give grand gifts to make someone happy; a simple act of kindness can be enough to lift a person’s mood.

When you receive an act of kindness, it is valuable to return some light kindness to someone else. The act of kindness should be shared with others to show that love is mutual. Even being present for someone or helping them clean a house is a way of giving back. A friendly smile can also be a gesture that communicates kindness.

Consider who in your family routinely offers small acts of kindness. Notice how your family feels when they experience kindness in their lives. And when you receive a little act of kindness, think about how you can give a modest return.

Have you ever needed examples to learn something, or do you learn better through different methods instead of receiving examples? Albert Schweitzer once said, “Example is not the main thing to influence others.” He meant that there are other ways to influence people without using examples.

One way people may be influenced is when they receive help from others rather than examples. In my ceramic class, the teacher rarely helped me; she would give an example of how to shape clay once and then let us figure it out on our own. Many of us struggled because that single demonstration was forgotten. When the teacher does offer help, the students who receive it are usually the best in the class because of her guidance.

Some people say that examples can actually cause confusion. If an example forces you to change your perspective on what you’re doing, it can be distracting. For instance, a teacher might say, “Draw from your imagination,” meaning to draw whatever comes to mind. Yet if she then provides specific examples of what to draw, students may think she wants them to draw something other than their own ideas. In such cases, examples can create confusion rather than clarity.

Although others argue that using examples makes it easier to influence people—because they show real experience and demonstrate how to do something—many people learn better and feel more influenced when examples are minimized. I believe that there are stronger methods than relying on examples, and for these reasons, there are better ways to influence others without using them.

Have you ever wondered whether we learn better from examples or from alternative methods? Albert Schweitzer once said, “Examples are not the primary means of influencing others.” He meant that influence can come from many sources besides simple examples.

One convincing way to affect others is through personal assistance rather than showing them examples. In my ceramic class, the teacher rarely demonstrates how to shape clay. She only explains the process once, and many students, including myself, forget what was said. When she does give someone help, that student’s project usually turns out the best in the class. This shows that direct support can be more valuable than a one‑time example.

Some people feel that examples can actually confuse them. This happens when the examples change their own understanding of a task. For instance, a drawing teacher might tell students to depict something from their imagination. That instruction suggests creativity, but then the teacher provides specific example images to guide them. Students may think the teacher wants them to copy those images rather than express their own thoughts. In such cases, examples can blur the original goal and create confusion.

While others argue that examples are powerful because they show real experience and show how to do something, I believe there are stronger methods that make examples less effective. By offering direct help, encouraging independent thinking, or sharing personal stories, we can influence others more deeply without relying on simple examples.

For these reasons, I believe that alternative approaches to teaching and influencing others are generally more effective than using examples alone.

They rescued her, and the grateful husband sent them $2,000 a month to purchase new equipment, demonstrating how love and risk protection can create lasting influence.

Some argue that our behavior can affect others by building trust and generating a broad positive impact. Whether through helping, showing respect, or risk-taking, the same principles apply. We should examine how others’ behavior influences us and consider how our actions might change the world.

Teachers are another example: their supportive behavior inspires students to trust them, even if the students feel uncertain at times. They believe in their students’ potential and encourage them to volunteer for extra effort. Families, too, set a standard of trust; they model caring behaviors that we then replicate in our own relationships.

Helping others is a clear demonstration of how personal behavior can shape the attitudes of those we encounter. My family once organized a community drive in Generic City, where we built houses and distributed food to the impoverished. This act of service left a lasting impression on everyone involved. Friends regularly offer emotional support during stressful moments, bringing comfort when I feel upset. Teachers also invest time to ensure that students succeed, even if some struggle initially. Their persistent encouragement motivates us to persevere. When we help others, those people return the favor, creating a supportive network of friends, teachers, and family members.

The wider social effect of positive behavior is significant. When we show kindness and respect, others are more likely to do the same, fostering a culture of love and goodwill. A family that consistently radiates positivity can bring warmth to its members and strengthen bonds. Even public servants, like firefighters, exemplify this impact. One day, firefighters confronted a house fire despite their equipment being in disrepair. A man, grateful for their bravery, offered them a monthly stipend so they could purchase new gear. That gesture, fueled by love and gratitude, further reinforced the cycle of care and protection.

Some might argue that individual behavior alone cannot change the world, but by cultivating trust, offering help, and displaying compassion, each person can influence those around them. If we encourage others to act similarly, we may gradually transform society for the better.

Second, educational activities foster friendship. Working together on projects encourages mutual support and strengthens bonds. Spending time with friends creates lasting memories and reminds us how important companionship is, especially when we need encouragement or someone to talk to during tough times.

Third, educational activities teach us to learn from mistakes. The adage “failure is the key to success” holds true: each time we fail, we analyze what went wrong and improve. Facing setbacks in a project or task forces us to reflect and refine our approach.

Friends play a vital role in our lives: they help us when we’re stuck, listen when we’re upset, and celebrate our successes. The memories we create together in class or during group activities remind us of just how important friendship is.  

Third, making mistakes is a natural part of learning, and it can be surprisingly rewarding. As the saying goes, “failure is the key to success.” Each error we encounter forces us to examine what went wrong, to adjust our approach, and to improve. When we conquer a problem that once failed us, we feel a great sense of achievement.  

In conclusion, educational activities are enjoyable because they combine knowledge, companionship, and personal growth. They broaden our minds, sharpen our thinking, and keep our imagination alive. By embracing learning in these ways, we enrich our lives and become more capable and curious individuals.

When cellphones were first allowed in the classroom, there were many benefits. For example, it became easier for teachers and students to complete their work; students could more readily find information about a topic by using their cellphones instead of a computer, especially when there are not enough computers for every student. For teachers, allowing cellphones enabled them to explore better ways to conduct classwork using apps that might not be possible on a computer. However, nothing is perfect. For the past few years, students have been using cellphones more frequently than in the last 15 years, and the cellphone has become an essential part of daily life. During that time, cellphones were not allowed in the classroom, but times have changed and now students are allowed to use their cellphones in the classroom. In this essay I will answer the question, “What are the effects of allowing students to have and use cellphones in the classroom?”

When cellphones were first allowed in the classroom, many benefits emerged. For example, it became easier for teachers and students to complete their work. Students could find information about a topic more quickly on their phones than on a computer, especially when there are not enough computers available for everyone. Teachers could also use apps that might not be possible on a computer, allowing them to find better ways to conduct classwork. However, nothing is perfect. With cellphone use in the classroom, many students began using their phones irresponsibly—such as while the teacher is explaining a subject or using their phones to distract others.

These examples illustrate both the positive and negative effects of allowing students to use cellphones in the classroom.

In recent years, students have started to use cellphones much more than they did in the past fifteen years. When smartphones first emerged, they were not allowed in classrooms. Times have changed, and many schools now permit students to bring their phones into class. This essay will explore the consequences of allowing cellphones in the classroom.

Initially, enabling phone use in class brought many advantages. For both teachers and students, tasks became simpler. Students could quickly search for information with a search engine on their phone, which was useful when there were not enough computers available for everyone. Teachers, on the other hand, could integrate apps and digital tools that might have been difficult to use on a classroom computer. These apps could make lessons more interactive and engaging.

However, the freedom to use phones in class also created problems. Many students began misusing their devices during lessons, sending text messages while the teacher was speaking or calling classmates. This distracted not only the individual but also other students, disrupting the learning environment. The temptation to use phones for non‑academic purposes, such as social media or games, grew as well.

In short, there are clear benefits and disadvantages to allowing students to use cellphones in the classroom. The challenge for schools is to make the most of the advantages while minimizing the disruptions.

Whether Winston Churchill’s claim that “success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm” is true depends on what we learn from failure. I believe that failure is vital for those who are willing to change their lives. Three main reasons support this view.

First, every mistake is an opportunity to learn. Humans make errors all the time, and the people who take the time to reflect on those errors become the best guides for others who face similar problems. Because failures are inevitable, it is useful to absorb the lessons each one offers.

Second, failure reveals the people who truly matter. When you stumble, the friends you thought were unreliable may step forward. A genuine companion will not abandon you at your first setback, while those who claim friendship but act otherwise may disappear. This moment of hardship can expose the real support system in our lives.

Finally, it is crucial not to repeat the same mistake endlessly. Repeated failures drain enthusiasm and eventually make it harder to keep going. Each failure should be a turning point, so that future obstacles become easier to handle.

In conclusion, everyone faces failures, but the most important part of a setback is the chance to learn and commit to doing better. Life can change, yet this change can only happen if the individual is willing and ready to learn from past mistakes.

This prompt asks whether summer vacations should be shortened because it seems difficult for students to retain information after a long break.

Firstly, summer allows families to travel to different places, have fun, and relax without worrying about school. Secondly, students benefit from a break after months of school, relieving stress and enabling them to focus on life outside academics. Thirdly, traveling to see loved ones who may not have been seen for a long time becomes possible during this time. Fourthly, summer feels like a period for personal enjoyment, because you can do activities that are hard to fit into a school year, and the two‑month break provides ample time. Fifthly, students can use the summer to retake classes if they have failed, allowing them to recover credits. Sixthly, athletes can play sports more freely because they have fewer obligations, helping them stay in shape. Seventhly, avid readers have extra time for themselves and can spend long hours in the library, absorbing many books. Eighthly, those who enjoy travel can visit various places, later documenting their adventures in journals or photos to share with classmates. 

If summer break were reduced, the negative effects would be significant. Firstly, students would have less time to travel and would need to attend school continuously, causing increased worry. Secondly, the lack of a long break would raise stress levels, as many would feel pressured by continuous academic demands. Thirdly, the time when students gather and enjoy each other’s company would be lost, diminishing the fun aspect of their break. 

In conclusion, I believe school boards should not reduce summer break because a summer vacation allows families to travel, students to relieve stress, and offers opportunities for academic recovery, sports, reading, and travel. These benefits collectively support the idea that shortening summer breaks would have detrimental effects, potentially making everyone feel overwhelmed.

It gives them time to visit loved ones they haven’t seen in a while, explore new places, or simply relax. Because the break lasts about two months, students can engage in activities—such as reading, traveling, or sports—that they cannot fit into the school year’s tight schedule. Students who fail a course can take summer classes to recover a credit. Athletes enjoy more practice time without academic pressures, helping them stay in shape. Book lovers can spend hours in the library, and travelers can document their adventures with journals or photos to share with classmates.

If summer break were reduced, students would have less school time and fewer opportunities to travel or relax. The question asks whether summer vacations should be shortened because students find it difficult to keep information after a long break. I believe that schools should keep the long summer break.  

Long summer breaks give students a chance to relax after months of school work. They can spend quality time with family, travel to places they otherwise cannot visit during the school year, and enjoy activities that are impossible during term time. This rest period helps reduce stress and can actually improve learning when the new year begins.  

Students who fall behind can still take summer courses to recover credits, so a longer break does not hurt their academic progress. Athletes benefit as well; they can train without the pressure of school, keeping fit for the next season. Readers have plenty of free time to visit libraries or bookshops, which can deepen their love for books. Travelers use the break to explore new destinations, create journals, take photographs, and share their adventures with classmates when school resumes.  

If the summer break were cut, those opportunities would disappear. Students would have less time to visit relatives or travel, and schoolwork would feel more constant without a clear long pause. Stress could increase, and the overall enjoyment of students’ lives would drop. This would make the academic year more exhausting.  

Because a lengthy summer holiday allows students to rest, explore, and prepare physically and mentally for the next term, I strongly support keeping the current summer break. Reducing it would be detrimental to students’ wellbeing and academic success.

Do curfews keep teenagers out of trouble, or do they unfairly interfere with young people’s lives?

I believe that curfews are necessary to protect teens. Even though they are young, they are still vulnerable after dark, and a nighttime curfew can prevent them from getting into dangerous situations.

Teenagers who stay out late can encounter many risks. They may wander into places where crime is more likely, or they may choose to act recklessly when no one is watching. A curfew forces them to respect a rule that keeps them from being exposed to that danger.

When most people have closed their day and are at home, the streets become quieter and safer. The same logic should apply to teenagers: if the rest of society withdraws from the streets at night, young people should too, as it reduces the likelihood of accidents or violence.

Even simple thefts or violent incidents can happen in the quiet night, and the fear of being assaulted or having property stolen discourages outdoor activity. By restricting nighttime freedom, curfews can reduce the chances of such events.

Some argue that having fun at night is a healthy way for teens to socialize, and that restriction is overbearing. I disagree. For instance, night clubs can pose serious risks: they are often targets for crime, and situations can quickly turn violent, as happened in a Las Vegas club shooting a few years ago that claimed many lives.

In short, curfews are a practical means of safeguarding teenagers. They are a sensible measure to keep youth out of harm’s way and are ultimately beneficial for their safety and wellbeing.

I believe that the school menu should be balanced, offering both healthy options and a few favorite treats. The current approach has advantages and shortcomings that deserve attention.

Firstly, many students prefer high‑calorie foods like pizza or other popular snacks. When these items dominate the lunchroom, students often skip nutritious alternatives such as milk, leading to a lack of essential nutrients. Without proper diet, their stomachs and overall health can suffer.

Secondly, choosing healthier meals during the school week makes students feel more energetic and relaxed. A diet rich in protein and vitamins supports growth and helps prevent illness. When children nourish their bodies correctly, they are better prepared for future challenges and less likely to fall ill.

However, completely removing favorite foods can backfire. Students may refuse to eat the lunch altogether, as happened when fried chicken was taken away for a day. In such situations, teachers noticed a decline in attendance and cafeteria attendance, demonstrating that a few indulgent items can motivate students to eat.

For these reasons, I propose a hybrid schedule: some days feature regular healthy meals, while other days allow popular favorites in limited portions. This balance can increase student satisfaction, encourage healthier eating habits, and support overall well‑being.

Thank you for considering this suggestion. I hope the school continues to provide both nutritious and enjoyable choices for all students.

Do you think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home? Some argue that online learning is a good idea because it gives students more time for homework. Others say that studying from home is easier than going to school. I disagree with this view, because without a teacher’s guidance the learning process can become difficult and ineffective. In my opinion, remote learning is not a good solution, as students often need help from teachers, enjoy being in school, and experience distractions in the classroom.

One group of learners prefers to work on their own, but many others need teacher support. For example, my sister always stays after school to ask her teachers questions. She says that the teachers help her understand topics she doesn’t grasp while in class. When she fails a test, she spends time with the teacher to review the material and learns more that way. The teachers find a way to assist students after school. They have other duties, but they prioritize helping students succeed.

Some students like going to school because they can make friends and have fun. My brother, for instance, enjoys playing sports at school. He says that playtime allows him to chat with classmates, and that social interaction is important. School provides opportunities for daily learning, and after graduation, a diploma can bring personal satisfaction.

Others might argue that online classes are good for those who prefer solitude. The school environment can distract people at home, so the structured setting of a classroom helps. Some students need interaction with peers and mentors, so being in school feels safer and more supportive. For example, a friend of mine says she gets distracted at home, so she plays sports or engages in group activities at school. Talking with knowledgeable adults and doing assignments in a focused setting is also an advantage.

In conclusion, teachers play a vital role in helping students understand the material that they would otherwise struggle with online. Attending school remains the best way to learn what you want for your future. School offers distractions such as games and books, but these do not outweigh the benefits of face‑to‑face instruction. I believe students should attend school rather than rely solely on online classes. Teachers are the most effective guides, and a good education is essential for a successful future.

People should seek guidance from experts and authorities about life's important matters because those who choose to make their own decisions often lack sufficient knowledge; they simply follow instincts and ideas, believing their actions are correct when they are not, and even when they violate rules.

First, consider the laws: the consumption of drugs and alcohol, carrying guns, and driving all have specific legal requirements. For example, drug use is unlawful in many states and requires a prescription, whereas alcohol is legal but only for those 21 and older. Similarly, owning a gun is lawful, but like drugs and alcohol, it requires proper licensing and age restrictions. As for driving, a license can be obtained at 16 or older; however, if you decide to drive at 16, you must have a copilot who is older, because the law ensures you have enough experience to drive alone.

Second, work environments impose rules that must be followed, such as schedules and duties. Your employer will set a specific timetable for when you must arrive at work and when you can go home, which helps keep the organization running smoothly. If you, for instance, choose to ignore this schedule—say you are an accountant who decides to come in the afternoon instead of the required morning—your absence can disrupt the entire accounting process. Likewise, you have specific duties aligned with your skills, and making independent decisions about how to perform them can result in serious consequences, including losing your job.

Third, society itself places limits on what we can do. You cannot, for example, destroy a library because you have an idea you think is brilliant, or you cannot randomly assault people just to amuse friends. Nor can you trespass on private property to take a flower you like. These prohibitions exist because we, as a community, recognize that unchecked individual decisions can harm others.

In conclusion, while people have the right to pursue their own goals, they cannot act completely independently of established guidelines. Guidance from experts and authorities is essential, especially for those who lack the maturity or insight to discern right from wrong on their own.

People should seek guidance from experts and authorities about life's important matters because individuals who insist on making all of their own decisions often lack knowledge; they rely only on instincts and ideas, which can lead them to believe they are acting correctly when they are not and when they violate rules.

Laws govern the consumption of drugs and alcohol, the carrying of guns, and driving. The use of most drugs is illegal in many states and a permit is required to purchase them. Alcohol is legal for those 21 or older. Carrying a gun, like drugs and alcohol, requires a permit and age restrictions. To drive, one must obtain a license at age 16 or older. If you obtain your license at 16, you must drive with a copilot who is older than you, to ensure you have sufficient experience.

Work comes with rules such as schedules and duties. Your schedule tells you when to arrive at work and when to go home, keeping the employer organized. If you, say, are an accountant and the company needs you in the morning but you choose to arrive in the afternoon, you disrupt the accounting and are at fault for not following the schedule. Your duties, set by your skills, also must be followed; otherwise you risk being fired.

Society imposes limits on personal freedom as well. You cannot burn a library because you think it’s a brilliant idea, nor can you kick or hit people simply to amuse friends. You cannot intrude on private property to take a flower you like. These are examples of decisions you should not make without guidance.

In conclusion, people cannot be allowed to make every decision on their own. I am not denying that people have rights, but they cannot do everything they wish. They need guidance from experts and authorities, especially minors who may lack the conscience to discern right from wrong.

People should seek guidance from experts and authorities when making important life choices. Those who rely only on their own instincts often fail to understand the consequences of their actions, believing that they are always right, even when they break rules or harm themselves and others.

First, the law sets clear limits on many everyday activities. For example, the use of drugs is illegal in most states unless a prescription is provided. Alcohol is legal, yet you must be at least 21 to purchase it. Owning a gun is also regulated: you need a license and must meet an age requirement. Driving requires a license, which normally starts at 16, and new drivers must share the road with a supervised adult. These rules exist so that inexperienced people do not cause unnecessary harm. By following them, we protect both ourselves and society.

Employment also demonstrates how rules help keep things running smoothly. Jobs come with schedules and duties that must be respected. Imagine an accountant who keeps the company’s finances. If the manager needs the accountant in the morning but the worker decides to come in the afternoon, the company may suffer errors and lose money. Ignoring the agreed timetable can lead to penalties or even dismissal. In workplaces, the rules protect the employer’s interests and ensure that the employee’s role is performed correctly.

In society, certain actions are prohibited not because people disagree, but because they are dangerous or illegal. A person cannot decide to set fire to a library, strike others for amusement, or trespass into a private property to pick a flower. Even if these ideas seem harmless or clever to the individual, they carry risks and are often punishable by law. Respecting these limits preserves safety and order for everyone.

In conclusion, while everyone has the right to personal freedom, that freedom must be exercised within certain boundaries. Experts and authorities provide essential guidance that helps us recognize what is right and safe. By heeding their advice, especially for those who may not yet have fully developed judgment, society can protect itself from harmful decisions that undermine the well‑being of individuals and the community as a whole.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once said, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” He believed that true accomplishment comes from taking control of one’s own life rather than letting the world impose its expectations.

First, be yourself and never hand over your freedom to external forces. If you allow the world to make decisions for you, you risk losing direction and becoming discontent. Ralph Waldo Emerson once claimed that “to be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” I believe that this claim is misguided. True achievement comes not from allowing the world to mould us, but from asserting our own agency and making choices that reflect who we truly are. In a society that often pressures us to conform, the only way to realise our greatest potential is to take control of our own path.

First, it is essential to refuse the world’s permission slips. When we let external forces decide our future, we risk losing our sense of direction and becoming exhausted by lives that are not ours. Making independent decisions keeps us grounded in our own values; we know why we make a choice and can stand by it. Those who surrender control often find themselves dissatisfied, looking back and wishing they had chosen differently.

Second, real accomplishment is achieved by pursuing passions that resonate with us, rather than accepting others’ impositions. When we engage in activities that genuinely interest us, work no longer feels like a chore. We become motivated, persistent, and creative. The greatest successes are rarely the result of following the crowd; they come from the courage to pursue what feels right for us, even when it goes against popular expectations.

Choosing our own path also allows us to identify what is beneficial and what is detrimental to our growth. We can evaluate career options, set personal goals, and decide which opportunities align with our values. Only we possess the complete picture of our strengths, weaknesses, and aspirations. By relinquishing control to external judgments, we risk making choices that derail us and leave us questioning our future.

In short, surrendering life to the world’s whims is a recipe for regret. To find true satisfaction, we must keep our autonomy intact. By standing firm in our individuality, we can steer towards achievements that feel authentic and meaningful. When we invest in our own vision rather than chasing others’ expectations, we turn our dreams into realities, and the journey itself becomes a fulfillment rather than a mere obligation.

I agree with Albert Einstein’s statement that imagination is more important than knowledge. Knowledge flows into us through learning, but it is imagination that directs us to seek new information and to see possibilities that we had previously imagined. Sometimes imagination can overwhelm the mind, leading it to stretch beyond what is immediately graspable, yet this very stretch often produces creative breakthroughs that pure facts alone cannot offer.

At times, however, knowledge can feel more efficient than imagination. When we confront a problem that seems impossible—like a difficult math question or a complex text—we rely on the mature reasoning that knowledge provides. Reading expands our vocabulary, and a solid knowledge base equips us to handle challenging situations with confidence.

Often, imagination and knowledge work in tandem. For instance, if you want to build something but have no concrete idea, imagination supplies a range of possibilities. Then, once an idea takes shape, your knowledge tells you how to realize that idea, whether it is acquiring the necessary materials or understanding the underlying principles. In this way, the two complement each other, each reinforcing the other’s strengths.

Both can also have negative effects. When you feel down, a vivid imagination may convince you that nothing can improve your mood. Likewise, an overactive imagination, reminiscent of silly childhood games, can sometimes lead to cheating or unfairness, damaging friendships. In a classroom setting, a student might perform extremely well and then brag excessively, alienating classmates and jeopardizing social bonds. The same ethical pitfalls can occur when knowledge is misused or misrepresented.

Consider a 16‑year‑old who struggles academically and has not studied hard enough. Without sufficient knowledge, he might find it difficult to secure a decent job. His peers, equipped with stronger academic records, could gain employment instead. If he is unable to pay for basic necessities, he might depend on friends, eventually placing himself in a precarious, even homeless, situation. In such stories, imagination alone does not protect against the harsh realities of life, while a solid knowledge base is essential for survival.

Young children possess the greatest imagination because they have few expectations. At night, a child may imagine monsters lurking in the closet, demanding parental reassurance that none exist. Even though no real danger is present, the child’s imagination fuels fear and excitement. When the parents play along to calm the child, the imagination often finds new evidence for the supposed monsters, perpetuating the cycle. Eventually, the child learns the difference between reality and fantasy, but the experience demonstrates how powerful, yet potentially troublesome, imagination can be.

In summary, imagination and knowledge are both vital. Imagination sparks new ideas, while knowledge solidifies and implements them. Each has its own strengths and weaknesses, but together they provide a balanced approach that can help individuals navigate both creative endeavors and practical challenges.

Technology lets us finish many tasks without meeting anyone face‑to‑face. Shopping, checking out books, or playing games can all be done online, but these conveniences also pull us further away from each other. Because we rely on gadgets every second, our lives feel empty without them.

In schools, teachers now often deliver lessons through video or texts instead of standing in front of a class. This distance means students do not receive the hands‑on guidance that used to help them understand their assignments. When I was younger, my teachers would explain problems on the board, and if a student didn’t get it, they would pause and explain again. That personal interaction is what learning should be about. I remember now that when I was a child, my friends and I sat in the cafeteria and talked loudly about our day. Today, the same friends tap their phones during lunch, and almost nothing is spoken aloud. The lessening of personal contact because of technology has clearly hurt our social bonds.

Technology can even influence global conflict. Modern warfare can now involve nuclear weapons, a capability that would never have existed without advanced technology. Besides war, people stay indoors more, watching movies or playing games on their screens. They pay little attention to events outside their homes—even tragedies beyond the doorstep seem distant because of that virtual disconnect. This reliance can sap our empathy and make us feel weaker. I used to walk to a library to find a new book; today, I might simply order it online and sit on my couch. The repetition of such habits encourages laziness. In social situations, what used to be moments shared in restaurants now often become solitary dining experiences while people scroll through their phones, missing genuine human interaction.

At work, technology is helpful but also distracting. When a colleague’s favourite team scores or an online game is live, many will pick up their phone and leave their desk, forgetting their tasks. This distraction can result in measurable losses—poor performance, missed deadlines, or even job loss. If technology were not so omnipresent, many of these distractions would not exist, and productivity might improve.

Driving is another area where technology can be harmful. Texting while driving leads to missed turns and car accidents, causing injury or death to others. In such situations, the driver’s mistake holds them morally, and families lose loved ones—a direct consequence of distraction enabled by technology.

In sum, while technology brings many conveniences, it also steers us toward laziness, weakens our empathy, and erodes essential human connections. Too much reliance on it can leave us feeling less human and more detached. If we were to step back from this dependence, we might rediscover the basic relationships and vitality that technology has obscured.

Technology has largely had positive effects on our lives.  
For instance, it enables people to stay in touch with friends and family who live abroad or in distant cities. Even if they cannot meet face‑to‑face, they can communicate through video calls and instant messaging, which keeps relationships strong and helps people feel more social. Many businesses rely on technology to store customer data, manage orders, archive records, and coordinate staff. By keeping information in a digital system, companies save time and reduce errors. Managers can inform employees about upcoming tasks through emails or phone calls, ensuring everyone stays on the same page.  

Students benefit as well. Many schools now permit laptops or tablets, replacing bulky textbooks. With all their notes and resources stored online, pupils need only bring a device, making it easier to access materials. Submitting assignments is also simpler—students click a button, and teachers receive the work electronically, speeding up grading. Digital resources and videos can make lessons clearer and more engaging.  

Overall, technology improves daily life. Any negative opinions likely stem from people who are less familiar with digital tools, such as older generations. For most, technology offers convenience, connectivity, and efficiency.

When I think of wisdom, the first image that comes to mind is my grand‑pa. He would often share stories of his youth, back in his homeland. He would describe growing up in poverty, spending his days fighting for enough to eat and struggling to survive. Education seemed almost a luxury, and yet he emphasized how precious it was. He also told me of the devastating losses he suffered—his mother and brother fell ill, and his father died when he was only six or eight years old. He later moved to America, and the challenges he faced there were immense.

Grand‑pa was born into a very poor family. He had one older brother and a father who worked as a construction worker, while his mother did her best to keep the family fed and ready for school. In their village the nearest school was more than three miles away, so he had to walk a long distance each day. Despite the hardship, he was determined to attend school because learning brought him joy. For many people in that small community, going to school was rarely an option, which made his perseverance all the more special.

When he was five, his father died. His father had many troubles, and his brother and the wider family struggled to keep him close to the work. One day he went out to work and was met by four men. He tried to escape, but the first shot struck him, and in a matter of moments, he was bloodied and lying on the dirt, with no one to save him. That shock left a deep mark on the family.

Grand‑pa also talked about his brother’s illnesses. He described his brother’s weakness and the deep respect he held for him. The brother taught him how to read and write with such passion that he earned high grades in school. When the illness worsened, grand‑pa did everything he could to protect his brother, even though medicine was not very advanced outside the U.S., especially in 1976. Their only comfort was prayer each night to ask God for blessings. The final loss was a heavy blow; the family buried his brother, and for a month, everyone prayed for him. In time, they accepted his passing.

As grand‑pa grew older, he had two daughters, two sons, and a loving wife. He had to pass a test in order to move to the U.S. He explained how hard the test was: he had to learn a lot about the U.S. from a thin notebook and could be asked any of 50 questions drawn from 200. After he passed, he began packing and said goodbye to his family. His plan was to settle in Virginia, despite the fact that he could only speak a little English. When he arrived, one of his first jobs was at a restaurant, followed by other work. He saved diligently so that after eight months, he could bring his wife, daughters, and sons to the country. After they reunited, I was born, and we settled in a small town that I will always remember. Today grand‑pa also works at a school, and he seems content, knowing his hard work has paid off and that he has created the legacy of wisdom I cherish.

In my opinion, it is a prudent idea to revamp the cafeteria menu, because in my school, there are occasional moments when the offerings are satisfactory, yet most often the cuisine is subpar—essentially a repetitive assortment of bland fare—and many students disapprove. Because each week the same dishes are served, numerous students develop a distaste for the cafeteria options.

I believe it is wise to adjust the pricing of the menu, since some students lack the funds to purchase lunch, and others forgo meals entirely due to financial constraints, especially when the cafeteria offers quality selections.

In my view, it would be beneficial to disclose the daily menu in advance; every student would appreciate knowing what will be served each day.

I think the most critical change is to extend the lunch period by an additional hour, as many students wish to converse with friends, and some prefer to return to a classroom afterward to discuss coursework with teachers.

In my opinion, adopting a new menu is advantageous because most students dislike the current cafeteria food. For instance, at my school, the meals are frequently unsatisfying because the administration resists modifying the offerings. My friends and I often lament the poor quality; they express a widespread aversion to the cafeteria menu. An additional important issue concerns food prices: many students cannot afford meals due to high costs. It would be wise to lower all prices so that students with limited means can still purchase food. Furthermore, providing daily menu information—perhaps by placing a calendar on the cafeteria’s front door—would allow all students to see which day features appealing dishes. Changing the lunch schedule is also advisable; for example, my school offers a one‑hour lunch break, after which I can roam freely. However, most students then return to their classrooms to complete assignments or chat with friends, thereby enhancing learning through more extensive discussions about subjects, games, or social matters. Are you in agreement or disagreement with Emerson’s statement about individuality?

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s view. When you are yourself, some people feel comfortable, while others do not. Yet there is nothing more important than being yourself; you cannot know what you can achieve until you put yourself to the test. The world will try to bring you down, presenting challenges that might lead you astray or tempt you to become someone else. You must confront those challenges and refuse to give others the power to bring you down. People who witness your accomplishments may grow envious, but you do not need to listen to their negativity or change your mind because of their words. Sometimes others try to decide for you, especially when choosing a career. For instance, friends and parents may suggest a path you dislike; you need not heed them. A growing man chooses the path that genuinely interests him, and that is why you should always stay true to yourself, regardless of circumstances.

For example, my father recently left. He left my mother to earn a living so that I could be here. I witnessed her effort—and it was amazing—so I have always tried to be myself and work hard every day. In my country, gangs shoot without reason, and I grew up with my grandmother while the gangs roamed nearby. Despite that environment, I did not change; I could have become one of them, but I pursued a good education and did not waste a moment.

I did not pretend to be someone I was not, and as Emerson once said, “It is an accomplishment to be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else.” Always remain authentic; life is hard, and no one said it would be easy. You must work diligently for your own goals, become someone meaningful, and ignore the world’s discouragement. Trust in God and in yourself, and you will see the amazing things you can achieve. In conclusion, do not listen to anyone who opposes your decisions; such people only want to harm you.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s statement about individuality. The main reason is that when you stay true to yourself, some people will support you while others may not, but the most important thing is to remain authentic. You will discover skills and strengths you did not know you had when you challenge yourself. 

Life will bring obstacles that try to change who you are. It may tempt you to act in ways you never intended or push you into someone else’s expectations. It is essential to confront these pressures instead of giving them power over you. When others see what you achieve, they may become jealous or hostile, but you must not let their words dictate your path. 

Many times people around us want to decide for us. For example, if you dream of becoming a scientist but your family insists on a different career, listening to them is not necessary. A grown person should make choices that reflect their own interests and values. That is why it is crucial always to remain yourself regardless of the circumstances.

A personal example: after my father left, my mother worked tirelessly to support us. Seeing her dedication has always motivated me to work hard and stay genuine, just as Emerson says, “to be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else” is an accomplishment. Growing up in a neighborhood where violence was common, I could have joined the trouble, but I chose education instead and did not let my background define me.

I have never pretended to be someone else. Emerson’s words remind us that enduring authenticity is a triumph. Life is hard, and no one promises it will be easy. We must persist, trust in ourselves and in God, and let our own strengths guide us. In the end, do not heed those who oppose your choices; they merely seek to hurt you. By staying true to who you are, you will unlock amazing possibilities.

I believe that extending the school day is not a good idea.  
After school, students and teachers must take care of important family duties. Parents often have to drive their children to soccer practice, the doctor’s office, or extracurricular clubs. These are the only times many families have a chance, so adding more school time would cut into that essential period.

Many students live far from school. I know people from Generic City who struggle to commute. If the school day were lengthened, those families would arrive home at very late hours – sometimes around 8 or 9 p.m. – after a very long day of travel. Then they would still need to sit down and finish homework. Families would spend most nights dragging their children home, carrying a bag full of late‑night assignments, and then getting to bed by 11 p.m. The extra time at school would inevitably increase stress for everyone.

Parents also feel the strain. With a longer day, the schedule that allows them to pick up their children, watch their homework, and still have time for a family dinner becomes impossible. Some parents might miss their children’s soccer games or other events because they have to be at school or at work. The extra school hours would make the overall routine feel more exhausting.

Teachers are similarly affected, especially those who have to travel back home after a long day. If the school ends later, traffic congestion becomes a major issue, and teachers could return home very late, exhausted and with little time to prepare for the next day. I can understand how this could become a permanent cycle of fatigue for them, reducing the enthusiasm that is essential for quality teaching.

If we need to shift the schedule, a better solution would be to start the school day later. The current early‑morning start pushes parents to wake up at 7 a.m., leaving them little time to get ready. A later start, say 8 a.m., would give them more flexibility, lessen rush‑hour traffic, and help everyone keep a more balanced timetable.

Furthermore, 8th graders already have a packed schedule. Our lunch break at 1:40 p.m. is frequently pushed to 2:10 p.m. if extra classes are added, leaving us nearly starving before the afternoon session begins. This not only affects our concentration but also makes us hungrier and more irritable. Even the bus driver’s schedule is affected; if the school day extends, the bus has to wait at the stop much longer, disrupting families’ evening routines.

In short, adding an extra half hour or more to the school day would create a cascade of problems: late arrivals for those living far away, more homework for students, reduced family time, higher stress for teachers, and logistical challenges for transportation. Instead of extending hours, rethinking the schedule or improving efficiency would better serve students, teachers, and families alike.

Skydiving can also change the way you feel about other thrill rides. If you once avoided roller coasters because they seemed too high, trying a jump from an airplane might give you new confidence. Once you’ve experienced being at great heights, you may no longer fear flights and will be eager to travel to places you couldn’t reach by car, such as Bora Bora or other tropical destinations.

Teachers and some adults believe that students should already be able to identify a career by the time they enter high school, but only students themselves can decide whether they are ready to take on that responsibility. In my opinion, I disagree. I think young students are not yet equipped to handle a career decision.

First, many students are already independent; they might have jobs and must pay for rent, phone bills, and other expenses. Juggling work, school, and a career plan is difficult. They also have large amounts of homework and professional responsibilities that leave little time for career planning. Moreover, students who lack time often receive no help or support. Those who cannot afford tutoring or class materials may find no one willing to assist. Teachers sometimes dismiss them as unprepared, refusing to give them the chance to prove their capability. Other students give everything they can to their studies but feel overwhelmed by the many responsibilities they already carry. Despite hardships at home or within families, many are determined to move forward.

Some students are simply too young to understand the weight of adult responsibilities. They feel that deciding on a career while also taking all required courses will overload them. When high school begins, most focus on survival—managing their existing responsibilities—rather than contemplating a future career. Many make mistakes, such as neglecting academics in favor of social popularity. They need to mature their attitudes, prioritize education, and consider what grades and achievements would make their families proud.

People might argue that this path is easy for some students, or that few can manage it. I believe that guiding young people toward a specific career too early is ill-advised. It is difficult, stressful, and demands maturity that many do not yet possess.

Teachers and some adults believe that students should be able to choose a career by the time they reach high school, but I disagree. I think that young people are simply not ready to take on such a great responsibility.  

First, many high‑school students are already independent and must pay for rent, a phone, and other living expenses. Balancing a job, full‑time schooling, and a career decision is too demanding for most of them. They already have a heavy homework load and the pressure to perform well at both work and school.  

Second, not every student has access to the help they need to explore career options. Some lack financial resources to pay for guidance counselors or career‑testing materials. Others do not receive support from teachers or family because those adults assume the students are not yet mature enough to make such decisions. When guidance is offered, it may be conditional on the student’s perceived readiness, leaving many without the chance to prove themselves.  

Some students simply burn out. The combined weight of classes, extracurricular commitments, and personal responsibilities can be overwhelming. While a subset of students remains strong and continues to prepare for the future, many feel exhausted and give up on their studies.  

Additionally, high‑schoolers are still learning how to navigate life. They are still figuring out how difficult adult responsibilities can be, and adding a career choice to that list seems too much. Most new high‑school students are preoccupied with the immediate demands of school and personal life, not with thinking about a future profession.  

In short, early career guidance may seem helpful, but it also risks adding unnecessary stress. Young students should be given time to grow, learn, and establish a solid foundation before they are asked to decide on a lifelong path.

Whether it is sports, a book club, or community service, these activities can change a student’s life for the better, adding new experiences and reducing stress.

Physical activity is essential. Most students sit for long periods at school and often remain seated at home. Exercise gives the body movement and keeps us healthy. Even a short 20‑minute workout each day can improve heart health, increase energy, and help teenagers grow better. Regular sports also boost confidence and teach teamwork.

Reading clubs are another valuable option. When the mind needs rest, books offer an escape to imaginary worlds filled with adventure, drama, and romance. They let us experience feelings and situations we would never encounter in our everyday life. Discussing these stories with other members encourages conversation, lets us share ideas, and can help us find friends who enjoy the same books.

Volunteering in the community benefits both the community and the student. Helping others teaches cooperation, makes us feel proud and responsible, and often results in extra credit or scholarship opportunities for college. If you’ve never volunteered, it’s worth trying—doing good for others can bring you joy and strengthen your resume.

Overall, after school a student should dedicate time to an extracurricular pursuit. These activities give a productive break for both the mind and body. Pick something you enjoy, and make the most of your free time.

Overall, learning Vietnamese is a rewarding challenge. It opens doors for travel, helps you connect with others, and prepares you for a visit to Vietnam one day.

The British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once said that success means “going from failure to failure without losing enthusiasm.” I agree with him because experiencing setbacks is essential on the path to achievement. Success usually comes from hard work and determination, and most people hope to achieve it in school and through a dream job.

Graduating from school is a major milestone, especially for those who find exams difficult. Students work hard to pass difficult subjects so they can move on to the next stage of their lives. Consider someone who has come from another country and does not speak English. They might fail many classes—English, history, science—but with persistence they keep trying, and eventually they succeed. When a student learns from a failed test, they discover what needs improvement and can prepare better for the next attempt.

Many people search for a job that they enjoy, but not everyone gets their dream position. Some never give up. For example, a young man wanted to become a dancer, but his father disapproved. Despite this, he did not give up: he left home, had nothing, and could not pay for dance school. Nevertheless, he began hosting dance workshops, earning enough to fund his education. Today he is one of India’s top choreographers, Remo Dsoza. In job interviews, some people get hired on the first try, while others must keep practicing. They reflect on past interviews, learn from their mistakes, and continually strive to do better.

In conclusion, success is something everyone desires, but it is not guaranteed unless one works hard. To become successful, people must learn from their mistakes. Failure acts as a key to success because without losing progress, one cannot improve. Even those who are successful now have faced failures during their journeys. Thus, the path to success is paved with persistence and the ability to learn from failure.

People everywhere can be hard to reverse once their first impressions have set in. Those initial judgments shape ideas, feelings, or opinions. If someone speaks thoughtlessly, they can hurt another’s feelings, and by the time they try to fix the mistake, it may be too late. Because first impressions are so powerful, changing them is almost impossible.

I tried to illustrate this with a recent example. Yesterday, my sister and I were preparing for her wedding next April. We were browsing wedding dresses online when she found one she loved. My first thought was that the dress was ugly, and I blurted out that she would look like a “real skull” in it because she was skinny. I had no intention of hurting her, but the words did. She was upset, pulled away, and we weren’t talking for a while. I later apologized, and she forgave me. We’re happy now, but the incident shows how quickly words can damage feelings.

A similar situation occurred at a friend’s birthday party. I was told in front of several others that I looked ugly. The comment was cruel and unexpected. I left the party feeling sad, but the girl later apologized. Although her apology helped, the hurt lingered, underscoring how first impressions can be hard to erase.

First impressions can also change relationships. I once told a close friend that her boyfriend didn’t love her after seeing him kiss another girl at school. She called me crazy, and our friendship cooled. It turned out I’d mistaken his twin brother for the boyfriend. My unfounded judgment damaged our connection, and even after apologizing, the hurt was deep. Today we barely speak, and I can’t fully recover the friendship I had before. This demonstrates that first impressions can alter the course of relationships.

Some argue that first impressions are easily corrected, claiming people don’t mind them. In reality, negative first impressions can hurt deeply, provoke self‑reflection, and cause lasting change. Even a minor misstep can be difficult to undo.

In conclusion, first impressions are difficult to retract or correct. Unthoughtful words often leave lasting damage, and the effort to repair the hurt can be exhausting. Though apologies may help, the impact of a misjudged initial impression can persist, shaping how others see and treat us.

People all over the world cannot always control how they are perceived based on their words or actions, especially when first impressions are involved. These initial judgments can shape how others feel and what opinions they form, sometimes causing lasting damage. It is often hard to reverse a negative first impression because it may hurt someone’s feelings, leading to changes in relationships.

I agree with William E. Emerson’s prompt. He wrote that “to be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.”

“Never give up.” These words convey the intensity of our thoughts and make us courageous. Life is not a bed of roses; life is struggle. Every single person faces a struggle. Nobody is perfect in appearance. A perfect man is someone who wins his struggle. A successful man does not achieve success in a second; he endures many struggles but does not stop striving toward his goal. After a long time of perseverance he becomes successful because he adjusts to the struggle, keeps going, and ultimately wins.

For example, a soccer player’s goal is to score so his team can win. To score, he must cross the opposition, and only then can he succeed.

You failed! You think your life has ended. We cannot expect this from you. You are a fool, a loser. Go home and sleep; that is all you can do. Should I listen to them, do what they want, or give up my life? NO! I am a failure, a loser, but that does not mean I cannot win. Don’t lose hope. You have a hand, a brain, and legs—use them. When the day comes that you win, you will show them that you did. You made it.

For example, you may not be good at math, but that does not mean you are bad at social science. Use your talent. One can struggle with math equations but have the talent to formulate social science theories.

Time is more valuable than everything. Good people use their time wisely. If you use time and fail, do not lose hope, do not stop, and do not blame yourself or time. Time can give you more opportunity to succeed. Keep trying. If you are lazy, you waste time and receive a loser’s reward. Remember that time never comes back.

For example, if you do not do your homework, the teacher will not give you a grade. You will fail the subject and waste your time. But if you do the homework incorrectly, the teacher can give you another chance to correct it, even though it is wrong.

Inspiration can help you set goals. If you read about successful people and how they achieved success, you can be inspired to do what they did. Inspiration encourages you and helps you understand what you want to do and what you must do for your future. Different people have different choices, and you can learn from successful people to organize your life.

For example, there is a story about Robert Bruce and a spider. One day Bruce lay in a cave and saw a spider try to climb a wall, failing seven times before it reached the top. The spider’s persistence made it successful. Bruce was inspired by this event.

Everything has opposition. If you want to be a good man, you must know what is bad. Likewise, if you want to win, you must know what losing is. Failure is common in human life. If you never fail, you have never tried. Failure is part of life, but do not become depressed. When you fail, you have many options to start again. Before you stop trying, think: should I try one more time? Maybe this time I can become a winner. Just one more thought can lead to success.

For example, imagine you are digging for gold. You are almost there but give up. If you dig one more time, you will see the gold you want. So always think one more time before you give up.

An aim guides your decisions. A man without an aim cannot succeed. The right decisions depend on your future. First create a routine for your work. If you want to succeed in your goal, follow your routine. In student life, it is hard to follow the rules, but if you try, you can do it. Students should give full attention to their lessons. Homework should be done before school or college. If you continuously follow the rules, it will be easier for you to succeed.

Do not be lazy. Laziness is a weakness in our lives. From laziness your life will never be successful. Therefore always work hard until you finish. Some people in society have dreams but do not want to work. If you do not work, you cannot fulfill your life. Always keep trying to achieve your dream. We have time and life, so try as much as you can.

Sometimes people in society damage your dream or your work. They do not want you to do your work. These people are harmful to our lives. They always bother you and prevent you from working. At that time we should ignore them and say nothing. One day they will leave you automatically.

For example, if a person bothers you every day and you ignore them, one day he will no longer be interested and will leave.

The success of life brings you happiness. You will feel proud of yourself. If you show them that you did it, they will feel ashamed because they thought wrong about you. So never be lazy. Always work hard, keep trying, and think about what you should or should not do. The end of the moment will lead to a happy ending for you because you erased the wrong thoughts that people had about you.

I agree with the idea that it is one of the greatest achievements to stay true to yourself in a world that constantly tries to shape you into someone else.

The motto “never give up” captures the spirit that fuels our determination. Life is not a garden of roses; it is a series of challenges. Everyone faces struggles, and no one arrives at success on their first try. A truly successful person is not the one who succeeds immediately but the one who persists through hardships until victory is reached. By facing difficulties, adapting, and continuing forward, they transform struggle into accomplishment.

Take, for example, a soccer player whose aim is to score a goal. To achieve that, he must get past defenders, face opposition, and keep striving. When the moment arrives, skill and perseverance combine to turn effort into victory.

When people discourage us, telling us we’re failures, we might feel like we’ve lost. But failure does not mean we cannot win again. It only reminds us that we still have our hands, brain, and legs to use. When the right opportunity presents itself, we can prove that the doubts were unfounded. Even if we are weak in one area, such as math, we may excel in another, like social science. Showing talent in any field can lead to success.

Time is a precious resource. Those who use time wisely never lose hope. Even if we fail at first, patience and perseverance give us more chances to improve. A good person values every moment and learns from mistakes rather than blaming time or themselves. Since time never comes back, we must make the most of each instant.

For instance, a student who skips homework will receive a poor grade. A student who submits incorrect work can ask for a chance to correct it. Both situations illustrate that effort and commitment ultimately determine the outcome.

Being inspired by successful people can spark our own goals. Their stories provide a roadmap for how to work toward our future. Learning about figures like Robert Bruce—who fashioned a metaphorical spider that overcame failure after seven attempts—reminds us that persistence leads to triumph.

Every victory has its counterpart, and to be good, we must also understand what constitutes failure. Experiencing failure is a normal part of life; it simply means we did not try hard enough. It is not a reason to depress ourselves but an invitation to start again. One more attempt can translate into a win.

Consider digging for gold. If we stop after the first failure, we miss the reward; but digging once more may unlock the treasure. This illustrates the importance of persistence.

Having a clear goal helps us make good decisions. A well‑defined objective, supported by a solid routine, creates the path to success. Students find it challenging to follow rules, yet with consistent effort, the tasks become manageable. Paying attention in class and completing homework beforehand can make the journey smoother.

Avoiding laziness is crucial. Laziness erodes the possibility of achieving our dreams. Hard work, dedication, and continual effort are the only ways to turn aspiration into reality.

Negative influences may try to derail our progress. When we face constant criticism, we should ignore those voices. In time, their effect will diminish, allowing us to focus on our path.

Ultimately, achieving success brings satisfaction and confidence. When we prove to ourselves—and to the doubters—that we can succeed, we cast aside false beliefs and replace them with self‑belief.

The moment we choose persistence over resignation, we open the door to a hopeful future, free from the constraints of others’ opinions.
