Many students and teachers believe that online classes are detrimental to both learning and schooling. The main problems are that students are less likely to take notes and more likely to become distracted during lectures. Because of this, they do not gain as much benefit from an online course.

In a traditional classroom, teachers can monitor students and encourage note-taking. Online, however, instructors can’t see whether a learner is writing down information, so many students simply do not. Taking notes helps retain new topics and fosters deeper comprehension; without them, students forget key points and struggle to understand the material. Teachers, too, are unaware when students neglect to write, which hampers their ability to assess progress.

Similarly, distraction is a frequent issue in virtual settings. If a learner looks around the screen instead of focusing on the teacher, they miss crucial information. Missing essential details can lead to confusion about assignments, lost deadlines, and poor performance. Paying attention allows students to catch important cues and prepare effectively for tasks. When attention lapses, learners often find themselves unsure of how to solve problems on their own.

In short, the combination of no note-taking and constant distraction makes online classes less productive. Without observable note-taking, teachers cannot gauge student engagement, and without focus, students cannot retain or apply the material. As a result, both educators and learners suffer when these habits are not addressed in a virtual classroom.

One of the main concerns is that students rarely write down notes in a remote setting. On campus, pupils tend to jot down points because a teacher is watching them, so they feel compelled to keep up. In a video‑conference, however, the teacher cannot see whether a student is scribbling. As a result, many learners let the class pass without recording anything, assuming that there’s no risk of being checked. When students do not create written reminders, they miss the opportunity to consolidate what they hear and to review the material later, which hampers understanding.

Another problem is the lack of concentration during online lectures. In a physical classroom, a student who looks away from the teacher usually misses out on important details. The same applies to virtual classes: staring at a phone or browsing the internet means missing evidence, explanations, and instructions that are essential for the assignment. When pupils are distracted, they also risk losing the steps needed to solve problems posed by the teacher. Missing key points can create gaps in knowledge, leading to confusion and anxiety when they try to complete coursework.

Therefore, the argument that students cannot gain from online courses rests on two main points: the absence of note‑taking and the loss of attention. Because teachers are unable to monitor scribble‑making and because learners are prone to be sidetracked by the broader internet, critical information may be omitted. This combination jeopardizes the learning experience, which is why many stakeholders advocate for in‑person instruction over distant virtual lessons.

Do we choose our own character traits?

As the British naturalist and politician John Lubbock wrote, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it.” I certainly agree that everyone is capable of choosing their own character traits; they are independent enough to have control over themselves, capable of choosing the type of environment they want to be in, and deciding how to react to both good and bad circumstances. At the end of the day, we all have the freedom to choose who, and what, we want to be.

Lubbock’s remark reminds us that, no matter how bad the circumstances may be or how tough a problem seems, everyone will always be allowed to choose whether to smile or cry, to remain positive or negative, for example.

My grandma—a 78‑year‑old woman who worked her entire life—is a very independent woman who always says, “If I don’t do it, no one can do it as well as I can.” With a positive attitude, she never sits down, claiming that sitting is a waste of time. She has always been energetic; however, one day she suffered a severe stroke that left her with paralysis on one side of her body and impaired speech. Her doctor told us she would likely remain in a wheelchair for the rest of her life. Seeing someone so positive and energetic suddenly confined was shocking and depressing for everyone, including my mom. Yet, even as my grandma faced this reality, her positive attitude never changed; she took control of the circumstances and never gave up on herself. She decided to stay positive, even through this rough time. This example helped me see that everyone has the power to choose how they respond, whether in hard or easy times.

Everyone can also choose the environment around them, decide how they want to live, and choose whom they spend time with. People have the ability to recognize toxic influences, understand how much an environment can shape their behavior, and change a negative setting into a positive one. Although the environment affects our daily actions, at the end of the day it always depends on us—on who we want to be, how we want others to feel about us, and whether we pursue positivity or negativity.

Reactions to others can reveal our character; they expose our weakest points and show us how calm or volatile we can be. Reactions are an essential part of our character, whether we control them or not. For many people, shaping their own character is challenging because moods fluctuate. Sometimes we want to emulate people we see at school, which can feel like “stealing” their traits. Still, everyone has the freedom to choose the character traits they want.

In conclusion, everyone is free to choose what their character should be, no matter if they are going through a rough time or feel the whole world is against them. They will always have the chance to try becoming someone else—or to build their own—because ultimately it is what they choose that defines their character.

Responsibility is another crucial attribute that employers value. Being responsible shows that an employee can complete tasks reliably, which is attractive to employers. Companies grow when employees are dependable and finish the work asked of them. In my former country, many small stores failed because the staff failed to arrive on time or complete their duties, causing the business to close. Failure is a feared element of everyday life, something that most people try to keep at bay. Many avoid situations that could lead to failure, while a smaller group embraces it, seeing it as a learning opportunity that can lead to great achievements.

Fear dominates many aspects of our existence. We question whether we made the right decision and whether a positive outcome is possible. This fear splits us into two camps: the cautious risk‑averse and the bold risk‑takers. Each approach has its strengths and weaknesses.

Risk‑averse individuals rely on their accumulated knowledge to avoid failure. They are reluctant to step into the unknown, and for them the word “shy” may be fitting when new challenges arise. They may avoid answering a question in class, trying a new sport, going to the gym, or wearing unfamiliar clothes. Fear is the barrier that stops them from attempting anything. Because they never try, they never know the outcome. If they fail, they interpret it as a loss, while the benefit is the absence of risk and the preservation of their current situation. Their caution may be practical, but it also limits their success. Many have made mistakes before—being laughed at for a careless remark in class, failing at a sport, or feeling weak in the gym—yet fear keeps them from trying again.

In contrast, risk‑takers embrace new experiences, and they are often the ones who leave a lasting mark. A prime example is Winston Churchill. His journey to becoming Prime Minister was riddled with setbacks, yet he persisted. Churchill viewed failure as a teaching moment—an opportunity to refine an idea, improve an action, and choose the right path. He took pride not in his failures but in the corrections and knowledge gained, which propelled him forward. Such enthusiasm turns setbacks into stepping stones, and it is this drive that helped him lead Britain through World War II.

Enthusiasm fuels the pursuit of goals. For some, it manifests as duty, like a president; for others, as joy, like a musician; or as happiness, like a parent. Maintaining enthusiasm depends on the individual, more than on the size of the goal. Anyone can aspire to become president if they truly desire it, but they might struggle to attend the gym if they lack motivation. Whether short‑ or long‑term, goals demand persistent enthusiasm; failure can either dampen it or strengthen it.

A personal example comes from learning to dual‑wield the nunchaku. Using my left hand to spin them caused my forearm to burn from repeated impact. My skin turned red after an hour of practice, yet I pressed on because of my enthusiasm for mastering this martial art. After months of practice, I could perform basic techniques, and even though I am not yet a master, I no longer injure myself.

Some setbacks are so severe that they halt future attempts—death or crippling injury, for instance. However, there are stories of people who recover and thrive after such trials. One boy adored bicycle tricks; a car crash left him with a missing leg. Though he spent months in a wheelchair, he later received a prosthetic limb and, after many failed attempts, returned to riding his bike with confidence. His perseverance is inspirational.

I agree with Churchill’s view that failing is essential for learning and enjoyment. We must keep trying, training until we succeed, and not give up after each failure. By setting goals that spark enthusiasm, we can keep that passion alive, turning every setback into a chance for growth. We can either retreat into comfort zones to avoid failure or confront it head‑on, gaining experience and resilience in the process.

When we stay upbeat, we attract more friends, become memorable to others, and experience greater joy.

Being optimistic encourages conversation; when we reach out to people, they respond positively, which in turn boosts our happiness and friendliness. With a larger social circle, we feel less isolated and are more likely to stay busy, leaving less room for stress.

First impressions matter, and a positive demeanor helps us make a lasting impact. Whether at school or work, a cheerful attitude not only endears us to others but also opens doors to new opportunities.

Research shows that stress negatively affects health, so cultivating positivity is vital. A hopeful mindset helps us cope better, strengthens neighborhood ties, and expands our support network, ultimately contributing to a healthier, happier life.

In conclusion, a positive attitude is indeed essential for success, as it helps us build relationships, stay healthy, and remain joyful.

I told him that you never know, no matter how many times you fail. I know I am going to be a lawyer because you have to fight back for your dreams. That means I am not a failure, even when others say I will never succeed.

Failing once or more does not mean you will never succeed. In my 18 years of life, I have failed many times, but I always kept my goal in mind. Each failure is a new lesson that helps me prepare for the real world.

Someone may think it is wrong to think this way, but they are wrong because no one is perfect in life. Everyone makes mistakes or fails at something.

To be a successful person, you have to take steps one by one and keep going, no matter how many times you fail. You will succeed, so do not let others tell you what you must do.

In the future, I hope people never give up on their dreams just because they have failed once or more, and I hope people who tell you “You will never make it” will see that you did it all by yourself.

It is important to believe that failure is an essential step toward success. If you fail at least once, you become more resilient, gain confidence, and learn how to prepare for the challenges that life will bring.

My mother always tells me, “Be confident; I believe in you.” When I was in first grade in Honduras, a teacher warned my mother that I would fail math and, consequently, the grade. I did fail that year. My mother reassured me that the failure did not reflect my intelligence; it simply meant that the material was difficult for me at that time. She encouraged me to keep trying, and the next year I repeated first grade. That time, the teacher praised my progress in math and other classes. The experience taught me that one failure does not mean you should give up—you must fight back, just as I did.

I have always believed that we must never abandon our dreams, no matter how difficult they seem. As a child, I dreamed of becoming a lawyer. During a school presentation where we shared future aspirations, a classmate challenged my choice, saying that I would never finish that career. I told him that one could never be certain; every time I fail, I learn and grow. That conversation reinforced my conviction that if you do not fight for your goals, you become a failure in the eyes of others, not in reality.

Failing one or more times does not prevent you from succeeding. Throughout my life, at eighteen years old, I have experienced many setbacks. Each failure, however, has offered a lesson that helps me prepare for the real world. Those moments have shaped my resilience.

Some people might disagree with this view, but they misunderstand the nature of success. No one is perfect; everyone makes mistakes or encounters failures. To become successful, you must take incremental steps and keep moving forward, regardless of how many times you stumble. Do not let others dictate your potential.

In the future, I hope people will not let a single failure deter them from their dreams. Let those who say, “You’ll never make it,” witness your perseverance and success.  

By embracing failure as a learning opportunity, you build the confidence and determination needed to achieve your goals.

Second, staying home by 10 p.m. on weekdays would reduce the likelihood of encountering violent crime, as many offenses happen late in the evening. Finally, an earlier curfew would cut down on opportunities for teens to get involved with drug dealers, since they would be home before illegal activities begin.

A sensible schedule would be Monday‑Friday until 10 p.m., and on Saturday and Sunday until midnight. This gives adolescents a reasonable amount of time to enjoy themselves while still protecting them from the risks of staying out too late. The law would not prevent socializing; it would simply require that gatherings finish by the specified times unless there is an extraordinary reason for staying out longer. Teenagers who violate the curfew could receive a warning first, followed by progressively stricter consequences if the behavior continues.

The purpose of this regulation is not to punish but to safeguard the community. It would keep young people away from the streets where they are most vulnerable to crime. While some may argue that teens should have more freedom, they are still capable of knowing right from wrong and can make responsible choices. A curfew would provide a structure that encourages safer habits without unduly restricting their lives.

Implementing a statewide curfew would address a wider range of dangers beyond driving. The overall advantages, including reduced crime exposure and drug influence, suggest that a curfew would be a worthwhile addition to existing safety measures.

In sum, an age‑based curfew would help protect youth from theft, assault, and other nighttime threats. By ensuring that teenagers return home earlier, we can lower the chances of dangerous encounters and keep our communities safer. This policy would only bring more security to young people while allowing them reasonable freedom during the day.

Confidence is better seen as a result of achievement than as its source. Many people believe that a student’s self‑esteem must grow after they succeed, and I think this view is correct. When a person accomplishes a goal, the joy and sense of worth that come from that success naturally boost confidence. Without that feeling of progress, a student is likely to stay stuck in doubt.

First, achieving something gives a clear indication that a person can reach goals. For instance, taking a driving test and passing it after hours of study demonstrates that you can apply knowledge to real situations. The satisfaction of proving yourself can turn fear into a steady belief in your own abilities. Even if you fail the first attempt, the effort you put in still teaches you resilience—learning from mistakes makes future attempts easier and reinforces confidence.

Second, accomplishment is linked to the practical demands of learning itself. Schools test students repeatedly through exams and continual assignments. When a student works hard to prepare for a SOL test or a midterm and then passes, the reality that they have mastered the material solidifies self‑confidence. The feeling of “I did it” turns the unknown into something concrete: a proof that you can understand the content, solve problems, and succeed under pressure. That proof is often missing when a student merely “does” the class the way their teacher expects without seeing real results.

Third, the social feedback that follows success contributes to confidence. When teachers and peers celebrate a student’s achievement, the acknowledgment reinforces the belief that the student is valuable and capable. This social validation encourages the student to take on even larger tasks, therefore creating a positive cycle of achievement and confidence.

Some argue that confidence must come first to achieve anything, but the evidence suggests the opposite. Confidence alone can inspire effort, but effort alone without a positive outcome never develops into true confidence. A person who practices maths every day but never sees the correct answer on a test will likely doubt their ability, even though they have the potential to succeed.

Consider learning a new language. You might read textbooks, practice speaking, and listen to native speakers daily, but without understanding or feeling successful—such as holding a conversation without help—you may feel stuck and grow unsure of your skills. Only when you pass a fluency test or can hold a conversation can the confidence to keep learning grow naturally.

In the workplace, confidence is often seen in those who achieve projects or receive promotions. They gain confidence because the achievement means they met expectations and were rewarded. This confidence then allows them to take on even more responsibilities. If confidence had simply started before any achievements, it would be merely wishful thinking, not a reliable basis for success.

The conclusion is that achievement fuels confidence, not the reverse. Confidence is a response to evidence of skill and result, not a mysterious, innate quality that appears before any effort. Students who aim to build real confidence should focus on setting realistic goals and working steadily toward them. When they reach these goals, confidence will naturally appear as a reward. Cultivating confidence is therefore a process that benefits from measurable achievements, with each success building the foundation for the next one.

It is nice to say “thank you” or “you’re welcome” to someone. When you speak kindly, show good manners, and express gratitude for what others do—whether they help you or give you something—you build reciprocity. If you say thank you, they are more likely to thank you back. Showing kindness and love while being grateful makes everyone happier and fosters good manners everywhere you go.

If you are kind to others and polite, they will reciprocate. The habit of saying “yes sir,” “thank you,” or “you’re welcome” ensures you receive the same courtesy in return. The key is to treat people well in the first place, and the exchange of politeness will follow naturally.

Being positive and courteous helps you make new friends. Saying thanks after someone helps you or does a favor leaves them with a good impression of you, and the gesture may improve their entire day. Good manners, when practiced consistently, invite others to respond in kind. We all appreciate being treated kindly, so we should practice courtesy ourselves.

If you never said thank you or “you’re welcome,” you may miss a chance to create goodwill, but adopting polite habits invites others to reciprocate. If you hurt someone, apologize; be kind and say something encouraging, and you’ll recover. To gain respect and kindness, you must give it first. Saying “thanks” or “you’re welcome” when appropriate is essential, because no one likes rude behavior. Offer help or a kind word, and the other person is likely to respond similarly. For example, if you see someone drop their belongings and help them pick up, they will thank you, and you can reply with “you’re welcome.”

Good manners and kindness reflect well on you and demonstrate your character. When you’re about to pay for something, ask the cashier how their day is going and show appreciation. Making a small gesture—be it a thank you, a question about their well‑being, or a simple “I hope today’s good for you”—can brighten a stranger’s day. Never say something that could hurt a person; this undermines the mutual respect you seek.

When you dine out, say thank you, tip, and show gratitude. If you notice a waiter or employee struggling, offer to share a meal or give a small favor; such kindness is easily reciprocated.

In short, saying something nice and being courteous invites the same from others. The more manners you practice, the more respect and kindness you receive in return.

It is really pleasant to say “thank you” or “you’re welcome” to someone. When you speak kindly and show good manners, you express gratitude for what others do for you. Saying thanks is a simple way to acknowledge their effort, and most people will respond with the same courtesy. By being polite and respectful, you spread kindness and make everyone feel happy.

If you treat others kindly and say polite phrases, they are likely to return the behavior. For example, saying “please” or “thank you” encourages others to say those same words back. Manners create a cycle of positive interaction. When you want someone to thank you, it’s essential that you say thank you yourself. Respectful communication is all about being nice and considerate.

Always look for moments to offer compliments or friendly words, especially when you’re making new friends. Good manners help you build friendships because people appreciate helpful, polite people. Expressing gratitude after someone gives you a favor not only shows respect, but it may also brighten their day. A small thank you can have a big impact, and you’ll likely receive the same kindness in return. We all desire courteous treatment, so it is important to practice good manners yourself.

Missing a thank‑you might seem harmless, but showing courtesy can encourage others to behave politely toward you. If you ever make a mistake, saying “I’m sorry” and behaving kindly will usually restore goodwill. People are more inclined to show kindness when you show them respect first. A simple apology or a friendly comment can smooth over any tension.

Manners and kindness reflect well on yourself. When you’re shopping, you can ask the cashier how their day is going, which adds a personal touch. A kind question or a small compliment can make others feel appreciated. Even if you’re not familiar with the person, extending politeness can create a pleasant atmosphere. Also, giving a tip or asking a waiter to have a good day shows generosity and consideration.

When you eat out, it’s polite to say thank you and tip the staff. If you notice someone struggling, you might invite them to join you or bring them a small gift. Acts of kindness are always appreciated, and they encourage reciprocity.

In short, saying something nice and practicing manners is a powerful way to receive kindness in return. The more polite you are, the more you’ll get back a friendly response. Be cheerful, speak politely, and you’ll see that courteous behavior brings more good to everyone around you.

First, a curfew would help teenagers sleep better and absorb knowledge more effectively. When teens are prohibited from roaming after midnight, they are likely to get a full night’s rest, which in turn makes them more alert in class. Staying home longer also gives them extra time to complete homework, leading to higher grades. In short, overnight restrictions can boost study habits and academic performance.

Second, curfews can improve teenagers’ social lives. Late‑night street activity often creates a perception that teens are rebellious or involved in gangs, which can make others wary of interacting with them. By staying home, teens avoid such stigmas and can focus on building friendships in safer, more positive environments. When they are not seen out after dark, they are less likely to be shunned and more likely to engage in healthy socialization.

Third, there are clear medical advantages to enforcing curfews. Teenagers hanging out on the streets at night face a higher risk of getting into fights, which can result in injuries requiring medical care. By restricting nighttime outings, authorities can reduce the likelihood of violence and the associated hospital visits, keeping teens physically safer.

Finally, curfews can provide economic benefits. Teens who are expected to stay home are more likely to seek evening employment that fits the schedule, allowing them to earn money rather than waste time in potentially harmful activities. Earning an income helps them learn responsibility, save for the future, and prepare for unexpected expenses.

Overall, adopting curfews for teenagers is advantageous. They enhance academic achievement, foster better social interactions, protect health, and encourage financial independence. Keeping teens off the streets after dark is a simple yet effective tool for improving their safety and overall well‑being.

An issue that is often debated is whether schools should regulate students’ involvement in extracurricular activities. Some argue that schools ought to direct students’ free time so they can engage in more educational pursuits. I contend that students should decide how to spend their after‑school hours, because many have work obligations, family responsibilities, or personal interests that differ from a school‑imposed schedule.

First, many students work part‑time to support their families. Balancing a job and studies is exhausting, and the priority for many is simply to get home and rest. This makes it hard to study for quizzes, complete homework, or participate in after‑school clubs. A study hall could help, but often the reality is that working students sacrifice extracurriculars to save for college or simply to meet day‑to‑day needs. Therefore, forcing them to join club activities would add an unnecessary burden.

Second, some students must take care of siblings while their parents are at work. They usually cannot afford a babysitter, so they use the time when a parent has a day off to run errands, cook, or clean. These responsibilities clash with school work and the desire to join a club. Allowing them the freedom to choose how to allocate that time respects their situation and lets them manage both family duties and studies at their own pace.

Third, many students are naturally drawn to activities like sports, art, or language learning. They enjoy daily practice of basketball, baseball, tennis, gymnastics, painting, environmental projects, or foreign languages. These students thrive when they can choose the clubs that match their passions. Imposing school control would stifle their enthusiasm and limit the development of skills that matter most to them.

In short, I believe schools should not dictate students’ after‑school activities. By understanding each individual’s dreams and challenges, society can better support those who work, those who care for family, and those who pursue personal interests. Respecting personal choice is key to fostering both academic success and happiness.

A Career at a Young Age  

In some societies, students are expected to have chosen a career by the time they enter high school, but the real question is whether it is a good idea for students to commit to a career at such a young age.  

Choosing a career early can be beneficial for students who are interested in long‑term professions such as doctors, pediatricians, lawyers, or teachers. If students begin studying these careers early, they can contribute positively to the country’s future.  

Early study also provides more opportunities for career advancement. For example, a teacher who brings new energy at a young age may successfully transition into a different teaching specialty.  

However, starting a career too early has disadvantages. Students may become tired of school, or they may later regret a choice they made and realize that they do not truly enjoy it.  

In conclusion, committing to a career at a young age can be a good idea for motivated students. Therefore, teachers and counselors should motivate and support them in finding the right career for their lives.

Choosing a career early

In some communities students are urged to decide what they will do once they reach high school. The real question is whether it is wise for young people to settle on a career at such a young age.

For some students it can be a good idea to pick a long‑term profession early, especially those who are already drawn to jobs that require many years of study, such as doctors, teachers, lawyers, or nurses. If they start preparing for these careers while they are still teenagers, they will have a strong advantage in the future. They can begin relevant classes, take exams early, and finish their university studies sooner. This not only benefits the students but also the country, as it brings skilled professionals into the workforce more quickly.

Another benefit is that starting young gives students lots of time to explore different paths. A teacher, for example, might discover a passion for a special‑needs classroom or a new subject area while still in training. Because they are younger, they can change direction more easily during their early career, without having invested too much time in a single path.

However, there are disadvantages as well. Students may become exhausted by school demands and lose enthusiasm for the subject. They could also experience regret later in life if they realize the career they chose does not truly suit them. Choosing a major too early might mean missing other interests that develop during adolescence.

In conclusion, deciding on a career early can be very useful, but it must be handled with care. Teachers, parents, and advisors should encourage students to investigate their interests and support them in making informed choices. A balanced approach will give young people the best chance to find a fulfilling and successful career.

Summer projects can be fun, but only when students choose them. If students pick their own projects based on subject, they will be more interested, more likely to complete them, and enjoy the process.

Teachers often spend an entire summer—or a whole school year—developing topics for students to work on. Yet students frequently give little effort to the assignments they receive. This wastes teachers’ time and energy. If instead students propose their own topics and ideas, they will likely complete the projects.

When students choose their own projects, they work on topics that spark their curiosity. Curious students tend to explore deeply, becoming more engaged and eager to learn. They can generate innovative ideas for their projects. Choosing a topic that interests them allows students to explore their minds and pursue activities they might never have considered.

Summer projects can also improve class grades. For example, a student who struggles to keep pace in class may benefit from working at their own speed on a summer project. This independent study is ideal for students who thrive outside a crowded classroom. With the whole summer to complete the project, they can work at a pace that suits them and avoid the stress of a looming deadline. If they still fail to finish, it reflects laziness rather than the project’s difficulty, and this can affect their grade.

Subjects have a strong impact on motivation. When given an assignment on a topic the student dislikes, they may procrastinate or ignore it altogether. Thus they lose interest in the summer assignment. For instance, if I had to choose between a history project and a science research paper on gene mutation, I would ignore the science paper because science does not fascinate me as much as history.

Being able to choose a project makes the experience enjoyable and gives students something to look forward to. Students should design their own summer projects, which reduces the teacher’s workload. This opportunity lets students think outside the box and make their teachers proud, setting the stage for a better school year.

Creativity thrives when students have control over their learning.

Summer projects can be enjoyable, but only when the students themselves decide what to work on. When a teacher chooses a topic, many students find it difficult to find interest in it. They may give it little effort, turning what could be a valuable learning experience into a waste of teachers’ time and students’ energy. If, instead, pupils pick a subject that sparks their curiosity, they are more likely to complete the assignment with enthusiasm.

Choosing their own project allows students to work at a pace that suits them. A child who struggles to keep up during regular lessons can focus on the summer project at their own rhythm. In a quieter setting, they may concentrate better and achieve higher grades. Moreover, having an entire summer to finish the work means that procrastination can be managed more easily. Students can finish at a comfortable pace, and only those who simply avoid the task are left with its consequences.

The subject matter also matters. When a student is handed a project in a topic they are not passionate about, they often procrastinate or abandon it. For example, a history teacher might assign a research paper on gene mutation. Even if the topic is interesting, a student who loves history more than science will likely ignore it. Giving them the choice fosters genuine interest and commitment.

Allowing students to design their own summer projects has many benefits. It reduces the workload for teachers, who no longer need to devise every assignment. It also encourages students to think creatively and take ownership of their learning. As they complete a project they care about, they can take pride in their work and come into the next school year more motivated and ready to excel.

Is it hard to be yourself in a world that is trying to make you something else? Think about it: we live in a society that constantly urges us to mimic everyone else, rather than embrace our own identity and live happily. In this paper, I will argue how the world attempts to change us every day, how we are influenced by it and ultimately alter ourselves, and how each year seems to make our generation worse.

First, the world continuously seeks ways to reshape us; therefore, as humans we must pause and ask, what do we truly want for our future? Why would I want to be like everyone else? Do I want to be wealthy in this society? Do I want to accomplish all my goals? These are the types of questions we should ask ourselves and think deeply about because, unless we follow our own path, we risk simply copying the rest of the world. Moreover, because the world rarely offers us success on its own terms, we must do it ourselves.

Furthermore, the world has a profound influence on our activities, the way we speak, how we dress, our choice of clothing, even our spiritual beliefs. If we do not conform—for example, by not wearing the latest trends—we may feel “not cool” in society. This pressure can lead to bullying or depression for those who cannot afford these fashions, and it is disheartening to see how pervasive this dynamic is.

In addition, each passing year seems to worsen our generation’s trajectory, largely due to the world’s influence. The spread of destructive drugs, ongoing wars, and new artists who glorify substance abuse, violence, and sex all contribute to a negative environment. Consequently, if we do not begin to embrace our authentic selves and pursue healthier paths, we are likely to end up in a deteriorated state.

However, some people argue that the world is merely bad and that it provides us with negative influence. This is not entirely accurate: often we are the ones who become involved in harmful situations and then blame the world, while in reality we are accountable for our choices. Going forward, I hope that this world changes, because we still have time to do so. It is not impossible; if this generation can muster the courage to shift the narrative, then we can create a kinder, more welcoming world.

In online school, sometimes there is no teacher available at the time when you need them. Consequently, students may not have the time, and they might not turn in their work on time; they might simply put it aside, thinking they will do it later, and never finish it. Thus, online classes may leave you isolated from peers your age.

The school’s online‑class program can have both positive and negative outcomes. Schools vary in how they implement such programs; some offer them, others do not. People’s opinions about online learning also differ: some find it convenient, while others believe it is disadvantageous.  

With online classes you are not required to wait for classmates to finish each step, allowing you to work at your own pace. However, this flexibility can also be a drawback. Your Wi‑Fi may become slow or fail entirely, making it difficult to complete assignments. You may also miss the benefit of a shared environment with peers of the same age, which can make it harder to stay motivated and to complete the work assigned to you.  

When a student attends a class online, they may find it challenging to finish the assigned work. You cannot immediately ask a teacher or classmates about a problem; you must figure it out on your own. Some online resources may provide incorrect answers, leading to misunderstandings. Even if helpful videos exist, there may be few that cover the specific topic you need. In a physical classroom, a teacher can demonstrate a solution in real time, which often leads to better comprehension. Online, a teacher may not be available when you need assistance, causing students to postpone their work and, in some cases, never complete it.  

Being surrounded by peers of the same age offers advantages: you can share study strategies and seek help from classmates. In an online setting, you are essentially alone with your computer, even if friends are nearby but taking different courses. You may miss opportunities to socialize or collaborate, especially if you also have work or other commitments. A shared learning environment can enhance motivation and accountability, preventing you from feeling isolated at home.  

Online coursework sometimes requires a large amount of work to be completed and submitted within a single day. This can be challenging if the material is unclear or confusing. Rushing to submit assignments without fully understanding the content often leads to poor grades or failure to pass the class. Additionally, students may become distracted by other aspects of their lives, leave tasks unfinished, and miss deadlines.  

The school offers multiple ways for students to attend class, either online or in a traditional classroom. This flexibility can provide more free time and convenience, but some students may misuse the program by staying home without engaging in coursework. Life’s unpredictability may also prevent a student from keeping up with the material, especially if no teacher is available to help. Students ultimately choose what best suits them. While online classes can be convenient, they may also hinder learning if the student is not adequately supported or motivated.

The possibility of schools offering fully online programs can lead to both benefits and drawbacks. Every institution approaches it differently—some have no online option at all, while others actively promote it and have mixed results.

On the positive side, online learning lets students avoid waiting for classmates to finish. They can work at their own pace and fit lessons around their schedule. They also enjoy a quieter environment, free from the distractions of a typical classroom. The flexibility of online classes can help people who have other commitments, like part‑time jobs or family responsibilities, to keep up with coursework.

However, there are serious disadvantages that many students may face. Technical problems—slow or unreliable Wi‑Fi, power outages, or software glitches—can disrupt lessons and prevent students from completing assignments on time. They may find it difficult to obtain a “real” classroom environment, where peers and teachers are physically present to support learning.

When studying online, students often have to solve problems alone. They cannot ask a teacher or classmate the instant they get stuck. Many resources on the internet are not reliable; an incorrect video or tutorial can lead to misunderstandings and bad work. Without the teacher’s immediate help, students might blame everything on their own lack of effort rather than the system’s limitations. As a result, homework can get deferred or never submitted, making timely completion even more difficult.

Social interaction is another major issue. In a physical classroom pupils share study habits, ask each other for help, and build friendships. Online learning isolates them to the single screen and the silence at home. Friends may not be enrolled in the same courses, reducing the chance to collaborate on project work. Regular in‑person contact with classmates of the same age is missing, which can reduce motivation and the sense of belonging that fuels academic persistence.

The pace of an online course can also overload students. Assignments frequently arrive with tight deadlines. If a student does not comprehend the material quickly, they may jeopardise their grades. Being at home means they are surrounded by easily distracting things—phones, games, household chores. Some learners may procrastinate, submitting work at the last minute or not at all, leading to poor results.

Schools often try to provide a variety of options—online or face‑to‑face. While online classes offer flexibility, they can also allow students to simply stay home and do nothing if they lack discipline. Life’s unforeseen difficulties sometimes make home learning harder than it sounds. The question is not whether online learning is bad, but whether it is suitable for each student’s circumstances.

In conclusion, attending classes online can bring many advantages, but there are also important challenges. Students need to choose the modality that best fits their learning style, discipline, and personal circumstances. Without adequate support and motivation, online classes may not serve all learners well.

I believe Ralph Waldo Emerson was right when he wrote that passage. Most people think that once you finish college and earn a degree you should move out and begin your own life—get a job, start saving money, and eventually buy a house. Yet many still stay with their parents, and that can prevent them from gaining true independence. Parents will keep seeing their adult children like they did when they were kids, expecting them to buy groceries and run errands forever. Emerson was pointing out this reality.

When you grow up and build your own family—getting a car, owning a home, and caring for your children—you will begin to see the cycle from a new perspective. You will do for your kids what your parents did for you, and the pattern continues. I’ve observed this myself. I saw my older sister take care of her daughter and it opened my eyes to how families continue to support each other across generations. Even though I moved out of my parents’ house at 15, I still felt a responsibility to keep up with my own life while caring for my family.

I think the most important part of growing up is taking responsibility for yourself first. You don’t have to leave your family to become mature; you just need to adopt a new view of the world. True growth is not measured by age but by how well you can focus on what matters—your family and close friends—and leave other people’s expectations behind. As someone who has lived this experience from a young age, I can say that learning to care for others while caring for yourself is what really makes you an adult.

People have been debating for a long time whether it is better to work alone or to work in a group.

Most experts believe that teamwork offers greater advantages.

One reason for this view is the variety of perspectives you find in a group. Different members have different thoughts, ideas, and ways of looking at a problem, which can be especially helpful when you hit a roadblock. For instance, when planning anything from a large school event to a simple classroom presentation, you might run out of ideas. In a group, members can fire off a range of solutions, whereas working alone you could feel stuck like being on a road with no exit.

Working with others can also lighten the mood. Group interaction often brings laughter and positivity, even during stressful times. You never have to deal with tedious moments alone, because there is always something to talk about. The experiences you share with your teammates become memories that you look back on with a smile.

Another advantage of teamwork is speed. With multiple people tackling different parts of a task simultaneously, the work is finished more quickly than it would be by one person. This also frees up space for creativity, allowing you to practice more, add details, or even invent new ideas.

Because you are part of a team, you learn to think beyond “I” and adopt a “we” mindset. This lesson becomes invaluable in the real world, where you must collaborate with people who have varied personalities and thoughts. The teamwork skills you acquire stay with you throughout life.

When a team completes a project, the sense of euphoria and pride everyone feels is powerful. It motivates each member to keep working hard and never give up.

Although teamwork can sometimes seem challenging, it actually teaches new experiences and abilities. It becomes a useful tool for developing character and personal growth. You learn how to communicate ideas clearly and listen to others. That is why many people conclude that working in a team brings more benefits than working alone.

My grandmother used to say, “It’s alright to fail; what matters most is that you get back up and keep trying.” In life, a decision is simply the act of choosing one option over another, a conclusion arrived at after weighing a question or controversy. When people make their own choices, they stand to gain in several important ways. Deciding independently is a fundamental right, it allows individuals to learn from the consequences of their actions, and it empowers them to use their own judgment.

Some people argue that we should seek counsel before making decisions, believing that guidance counselors or mentors possess more experience in problem-solving. Yet this view misses a crucial point: throughout history, people have fought and even died for the right to speak for themselves. Today, everyone has that privilege, and a society that tolerates unjust interference would lose that liberty. Therefore, encouragement to await external advice should not be a prerequisite for making sound personal decisions.

Consider, for example, John, an American citizen who discovers his spouse’s infidelity and decides to file for divorce. The legal system grants him the right to pursue this action; it is a matter of personal dignity and freedom. He does not require an outside aide to take this step because it is deeply personal. This illustrates that the authority to decide is inherent in each individual.

Mistakes are also part of the learning process. Suppose Emily, under peer pressure, tries an illegal drug, only to later realize the grave risks it poses to her health. Once she recognizes her error, she can take concrete steps to recover and correct her path. Society may pressure people, but ultimately, each person must refuse to be contained by that pressure and correct their own missteps.

Furthermore, everyone views the world through a unique lens shaped by background, values, and experience. This diversity means that what feels right for one might be wrong for another. If Linda’s parents taught her to distinguish right from wrong, she can use that foundation to make morally sound choices without external input. Contradictory opinions do not make one correct and the other incorrect; we must acknowledge that each individual is entitled to respect for their own decision.

In conclusion, the ability to decide has been entrusted to us by our ancestors. Mistakes will occur, but they enable progress, and each individual is fit to speak for themselves. Therefore, seeking an external guide is not essential for making a decision. Respect for diverse viewpoints is essential, and we must remember that no matter what others say, each of us has the power to decide.

Online learning can spare us from many of these problems and also saves time.

Some people argue that students won’t benefit from home‑based classes because they might not grasp the material or complete assignments properly. They claim that a project could be confusing or a lecture’s key points could be missed online, leading to poorer grades.

However, students do gain from being able to attend classes online. When illness or other circumstances prevent a student from being physically present, they can still participate from home. If I am sick, I can stay in bed and take my lessons without turning in a sick note. Even when I’m staying with relatives or friends, I am still able to attend. Moreover, online schooling allows high school students to save considerable time. Without the commute, I can structure my schedule more flexibly, work extra hours, or engage in additional courses that benefit my future career.

In summary, the ability to attend online classes from home gives students many advantages. They can avoid missing school due to sickness or being away, they can work or study more efficiently, and they have extra time for other activities. Online learning can therefore improve both academic performance and overall life balance.

Farmer and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once said, “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” I agree with Churchill’s statement because everyone fails at some point in life, yet many never give up. By keeping the fight alive and working hard—even after a setback—you’ll eventually reach the place you want to be. Never say “I’m done” after one failure; instead, keep trying, and someday you’ll discover what’s possible.

For example, if you aspire to become a future prime minister but hear that it is unattainable, you might think the only thing you can do is work hard and trust yourself. This mindset can help you achieve anything you set your mind to.

Others believe that success works better when failure is accompanied by loss. In this view, people deliberately repeat the same effort, believing they will improve even if they do not succeed at first. They keep trying because they believe repeated attempts can yield success.

In contrast, those who embrace repeated attempts view failure as a stepping stone; the loss they incur encourages them to adjust their strategy and try again.

In conclusion, success can be defined both ways. On one hand, moving through failures without losing enthusiasm maintains resilience in life. On the other hand, moving through failures while accepting some loss of enthusiasm can also bring growth and insight. Both approaches can prove valuable depending on the situation.

It reminds us that in every aspect of life, staying motivated through obstacles can lead to triumph. While some may prefer to avoid repeated failures, those who persevere are often the ones who ultimately achieve their aspirations.

I have multiple talents and skills, but my favorite one is skateboarding. Skateboarding is a very difficult skill; it takes several hours, days, maybe even years to accomplish and learn a trick on a skateboard, but that’s why it’s such a unique sport and skill. Skateboarding has become a daily activity for me; it takes all my stress and problems away, and that’s why I enjoy it so much. I skate everywhere—to the store, a friend’s house, and maybe even to school. Although I get lots of injuries like scrapes, bruises, and many more, I still love this sport because skateboarding has taught me a lot: being able to be confident when I try new things, getting right back up when I fall, and being able to learn from my mistakes. Skateboarding isn’t just a sport, skill, activity, or hobby; it’s a way of life, and even though it may not be the safest sport ever, it’s still one of my favorite skills that I think I won’t get bored of any time soon. When I was nine I had lots of friends that would skateboard, and I didn’t know anything about it at the time, so it was really cool observing such a unique sport. I would always see them practicing and skating everywhere, and that encouraged me one day to try it. A couple days later I went up to my parents and told them that I wanted to try something new, and that was skateboarding. My mom said she would think about it because she didn’t want me to hurt herself, but my dad, on the other hand, told me to just go for it, and that’s exactly what I did. The next day after school I asked my mom if we could go to the nearest skate shop, and she said yes. Once we got to the skate shop I was looking around and I was so confused—I saw decks, wheels, and so much more that I didn’t even know about. As I walked in, the guy that was working there asked me, “Is there something specific you are looking for?” I told him I was new to skateboarding and that I’d never been on top of one, so he taught me what I needed to know about a skateboard, like about the deck, grip tape, trucks, wheels, and hardware. After that we got into assembling my first ever skateboard. Once I was done picking out all the stuff that was going to be on my skateboard, we paid and he started assembling it. Once he finished we left the skate shop, and it was too dark, so I didn’t get to skate that day, sadly. The next day I get back home from school, I put down my backpack, and I immediately went outside to try my new skateboard. The only thing I knew was to ride, but I immediately fell in love with skating. Since that day I’ve been skating every day, and if it’s not every day, it’s every other day.

When I was nine, I had many friends who skateboarded, but I knew nothing about it. Watching them practice and skate everywhere was fascinating, and that curiosity encouraged me to try it. A couple of days later, I approached my parents and said I wanted to try skateboarding. My mother said she would think about it because she didn’t want me to get hurt, but my father told me to just go for it, and that’s exactly what I did. The next day after school, I asked my mother if we could go to the nearest skate shop, and she said yes.

When we arrived, I was overwhelmed by the various decks, wheels, and other parts I had never seen before. As I looked around, the shop employee asked if I was looking for something specific. I explained that I was new and had never ridden a skateboard. He taught me the basics: the deck, grip tape, trucks, wheels, and hardware. After we selected all the components, we paid, and the employee assembled my first skateboard. By the time he finished, it was dark, so I didn’t get to skate that evening.

The next day, after school, I took my backpack down, went straight outside, and tried my new skateboard. The only thing I knew initially was to ride, but I immediately fell in love with skating. Since then, I have been skating every day, or at least every other day.

I have many passions, yet my favorite has always been skateboarding. It is a skill that demands countless hours, sometimes months or years, to master a single trick. That very difficulty makes it so special. For me, skateboarding has become part of my everyday routine—it lifts my stress and troubles right off. I ride to the store, a friend’s place, or even to school. I often fall, scrape, or bruise, but the joy I feel keeps me coming back. This sport has taught me confidence when I face new challenges, resilience when I get up after a fall, and the ability to learn from mistakes. Skateboarding is more than a hobby; it’s a way of life. Even though it isn’t the safest activity, it is one of the few skills I can’t imagine getting bored with.

When I was nine, most of my friends skateboarded and I watched in amazement, not knowing the basics. Watching them hone their balance inspired me one day to give it a try. I approached my parents with my idea. My mother hesitated, worried about injuries, while my father encouraged me to go for it. The next day I insisted on visiting a local skate shop. Inside, I was overwhelmed by decks, wheels, and barrels I didn’t recognize. The shop clerk asked what I was looking for. I explained I was a beginner, and he guided me through the essential parts: deck, grip tape, trucks, wheels, and hardware. Together we assembled my first board. Though it was too late to test it that night, I returned home the next day, helped myself into the shoes, and immediately fell in love with the motion of riding. Since then I’ve skateboarded daily, or at least every other day, and I know this passion will stay with me for years to come.

Can failure lead to success?

Winston Churchill once remarked that “success is achieved by going from failure to failure without losing enthusiasm.” Many people who pursue dreams and goals resonate with this idea.

When failure is part of the journey, it can serve as motivation, encourage reflection, and provide valuable experience. Failure need not always be a negative outcome. It can spark the drive that many people need to keep trying. If a student fails once, does that mean they will simply give up? Certainly not. Those who set ambitious goals must anticipate setbacks as a natural part of a long reach. When failure arrives, the motivation should rise in tandem; otherwise the desired success may seem forever out of reach. For instance, a student may spend the night preparing for a test, submit it believing she performed well, only to discover she did poorly. Often there is an option to retake the exam, and the student must decide to seize that chance. Expectations do not always match reality, but that does not negate future attainment—it simply means persistence is required.

Another reason failure can steer one toward success is that it prompts evaluation and improvement. The familiar adage “you learn from your mistakes” holds true. When a problem arises, people analyse whether it was caused by an inadequate approach. If they see that a particular mistake has already occurred, they will adjust their methods to avoid repeating it. This process of learning and refinement leads directly toward success. By identifying exactly where things went wrong, individuals can plan the steps needed to fix them.

Success stories often include at least one major failure—without it, many achievers wonder how they would have progressed. In addition, failure provides experience that is otherwise unavailable. If one never failed, there would be no opportunity to gain firsthand knowledge that informs future actions. When the goal is finally achieved, the journey—including the hurdles faced and how they were overcome—becomes an inspiring tale that can motivate others. People who have failed but not given up become powerful examples of resilience.

In conclusion, failure can be a critical step toward success when approached properly. Instead of surrendering, view failure as a closer approach to the goal. Use it to fuel motivation, prompt self‑improvement, and accumulate experiential learning. In this light, failure is not a setback but a valuable ally.

People and teachers often argue that we should move to a year‑round school schedule. I agree that this is a worthwhile idea. When students return after a long break, they usually forget a lot of what they studied in the previous year. By spreading the same amount of instruction across the whole year, we give students more opportunities to revisit and deepen their understanding, which makes the knowledge more durable.

If learners keep the material in their minds, teachers will not need to spend as much time re‑teaching basic concepts. This means more time for exploring new ideas, especially in subjects like mathematics, history, and English. The extra instructional days also allow for varied teaching methods, such as projects, group work, and hands‑on activities, which can capture students’ interest and help them retain information better.

I often notice that after a summer break I struggle to remember the problems we solved in math or the themes we discussed in English. The reason is usually a lack of continuous practice and engagement. In a year‑round schedule, the longer time in school would give us the chance to repeat lessons, ask questions, and apply what we learned right away. This reinforcement would make it easier to recall concepts when faced with new challenges or tests.

There are potential downsides, such as shorter summer holidays. However, the schedule could still incorporate periodic breaks to give students time to rest and recharge. Overall, the benefits of improved retention and smoother academic progression outweigh the inconvenience of a shorter summer.

I believe that implementing a year‑round school could work well. It would help many students remember what they studied previously, making classes less repetitive and more engaging. For me personally, having the material fresh in my mind would allow me to complete assignments more efficiently and confidently. I am optimistic that this approach could lead to greater success in learning and would welcome the opportunity to see it put into practice.

It is true that there are many ways to influence others.  What defines your actions is not just your behavior, but how you show people what you stand for through your actions, your goals, and your motivation.  Sometimes you don’t have to be outwardly positive to influence others.  For example, in the movie *The Princess and the Frog* the protagonist wanted to open a restaurant because it was her dad’s dream.  She kept working to save enough money for a building; she did not succeed at first, but by the end she did.  What this illustrates is that a clear goal—opening a restaurant—paired with motivation can lead to success.

The first reason you can influence others is through your actions.  The most effective way to inspire people is to act in a way that demonstrates your values.  For instance, if you donate food to a local food bank once in a while, the impact is minimal.  However, if you donate regularly, word will spread about your consistent generosity.  If the media pick up the story, even more people may be encouraged to volunteer, amplifying the ripple effect.

The second reason you can influence people is by having clear goals.  People with goals tend to achieve more than those without.  Suppose you want to buy an $80 video game but have no savings.  You might do chores like cleaning, washing your parents’ car, or cutting the grass; still, you fall short.  You then offer to help your neighbors with errands or small tasks.  Gradually, you earn enough to purchase the game.  The lesson is simple: set specific goals and work toward them to attain what you want.

The third way to influence others is by remaining motivated.  If you are feeling down, it’s difficult to inspire confidence in others.  When you exhibit enthusiasm and energy, people are more likely to respond in kind.  Motivation signals purpose and demonstrates the effort you’re willing to put into achieving a goal.

Some argue that one’s behavior is the best way to influence others because it sets the right mood.  Yet behavior alone does not reveal how a person can be influenced to act.  Therefore, the most effective method to influence people is by demonstrating your actions, clearly stating your goals, and maintaining motivation.

There are many ways to influence others, and it isn’t just what you do that matters. What stands out are the actions you take, the goals you set, and the motivation you display. Sometimes even a negative attitude can have an impact, but usually, positive determination is the most powerful tool.

For instance, in the film *The Princess and the Frog* the main character, Tiana, is driven to open a restaurant out of respect for her father’s dream. From the beginning she works hard, saving money and searching for a suitable location. Although she faces setbacks, her unwavering goal keeps her motivated, and by the end of the story she finally opens the restaurant. Her example shows that a clear aim, backed by persistent effort, can persuade others around her to support her vision.

The first reason we can influence people is through our behavior. When you act consistently, people notice. Imagine you regularly donate food to a local food bank. Even if one act seems small, the repetition builds a reputation for generosity. The news coverage that follows can inspire others to contribute, creating a ripple effect. Thus, everyday conduct becomes a persuasive signal to those nearby.

The second way to sway others is by setting goals. Many people achieve more when they picture a specific target. Suppose you want to buy an $80 video game but have no savings. You might take on odd jobs: cleaning, washing cars, mowing lawns, even helping neighbors with chores. Each task earns a few dollars, and eventually enough that you can buy the game. By demonstrating how a clear goal leads to specific actions, you encourage others to set and pursue their own objectives.

Lastly, motivation is essential. If you’re feeling low, it is hard to inspire those around you. An energetic and determined attitude shows that you’re devoted to a purpose, which can prompt others to adopt a similar mindset. Motivation signals that you’re willing to make the effort needed to see a goal through, and this appeal can influence people to join you or at least believe in the possibility of success.

Some might argue that a person’s behavior is the most effective influencer because it sets a mood that motivates others. Yet behavior alone doesn’t demonstrate the process of achieving something. The strongest influence comes from exhibiting your actions, clearly articulating your goals, and maintaining motivation. This blend shows how to act, what to aim for, and why to keep moving forward, which is truly compelling to those around us.

Dear diary, today in English class my friends claimed that first impressions hardly ever change. I asked the rest of the class what they thought, and I told them they were wrong. A person can be having a rough time, and that can affect how they act toward others. One of my classmates suggested that people might behave differently in different situations, and I thanked him for that point of view.  

My first point is that someone might be going through a bad period. Maybe they have just moved to a new city far from the friends and family they left behind. Perhaps a family member has died or they are feeling lonely. I have lived that life many times because my parents’ jobs keep moving us every year. I used to be upset and stopped wanting to go to school, hoping instead to just have fun. This year we haven’t moved yet, but my parents are looking at houses an hour away; we might move in January, and I don’t feel good thinking about it. In my current school, however, I feel like home. The teachers always help me when I need them, both inside and outside of class. I have made many friends here and I really don’t want to leave them; the people are great.  

Another reason is that not everyone treats everyone the same way. Sometimes a person may act differently toward different people. I remember once at a party I was excited to join a group of friends, but when I arrived they seemed uninterested in talking to me. I asked why, and a girl explained that they had seen me staring at them. I told the group I didn’t intend to do anything; I mentioned that I have a twin sister whom I hadn’t told them about and that she is the opposite of me. Once I clarified, the misunderstanding went away and we ended up having a great night together.  

The student who shared his experience said that some kids can act differently in various parts of their life. They might be aggressive or friendly, unable to control their emotions. For instance, he knew a boy who was usually kind and helpful, yet sometimes he would become very angry and say harsh things to the people he knew. The teachers explained what was happening, and he could become better by not saying hurtful things.  

Looking at everything, I believe I am right: people are not always perfect, and everyone makes mistakes or causes trouble. Thanks for listening to me today!  

Have a great day!

If I were to explain to my teacher whether I prefer to work in groups or alone, I would choose to work alone. Working alone is beneficial because it allows you to generate ideas that some group members might overlook. For instance, solo work often leads to higher class scores than group work. When working in a group, the task can be left unfinished because members either talk excessively or lose focus on their assigned portion. Some students also prefer working alone because they can submit their work on time and avoid failing the class. Additionally, quiet or shy students may choose solo work to avoid waiting for others who are not contributing.

Students rarely receive much help from peers in group settings. Many join groups but then only two members do the work while the others stay idle. Some participants merely chat with friends about unrelated topics, using phones or playing games instead of addressing the task. Consequently, those who appreciate working alone are often more effective than those who insist on group participation. In some cases, parents discourage their children from associating with peers who might influence them negatively. For example, when a teacher calls a parent to report that their child is failing because they are not completing assignments as before, the parent feels guilty and worries that the child’s friendships are harming academic performance.

In my view, students should work alone rather than in groups. Life often demands that we earn everything by ourselves, relying on our own effort rather than someone else’s help.

I would explain to my teacher that I prefer to work alone. Working by myself allows me to come up with ideas that might not arise in a group. For instance, doing a project individually often leads to a higher grade than when I collaborate with others. In group work, we can get distracted by talking or become unfocused on the task. Some students like to work solo because it guarantees they will submit their work on time and avoid failing the class.

Quiet or shy students also find it easier to stay on track when they are alone because they do not have to keep up with the conversation of others or take turns speaking. In many teams, the workload is uneven; only a couple of members finish the work while the others do little or nothing. Some students sit around chatting about unrelated topics, playing games, or using their phones instead of contributing. Consequently, the group’s progress stalls.

Besides, parents sometimes worry that a child’s friends might negatively influence him or her. If a teacher reports that a student is failing because he or she is not completing assignments, parents may blame the peer group for causing the problem. Under such pressure, working alone feels safer and more reliable.

Overall, I believe that learning best happens when students work independently. While collaboration has its benefits, it can also introduce delays and distractions. At times we desire everything at once, but we often have to earn our success through our own effort rather than relying on others.

Most students enjoy summer vacation, but some educators argue that the long break leads to laziness and hampers students’ ability to retain information when they return in the fall.

The summer break is the only extended pause that schools offer, giving students a chance to rest and do things they cannot during the school year. I do not agree with the critics for several reasons:

First, many students wish to work or pursue other activities during the school year, but they are prevented from doing so by heavy homework loads and frequent tests. During the three months of summer, they can work, gain experience, and acquire skills that will help them secure better future employment.

Second, students need a break after a hectic academic year. Constant work and testing can cause significant stress and fatigue. Summer break provides a period for relaxation and mental recovery. Students can visit the beach, spend time with family, hang out with friends, explore new places, and enjoy the pleasant weather—all things that would be impossible during the school term.

Finally, during summer students are free from classroom assignments and exams. In contrast, shorter breaks in winter, spring, and fall are often filled with assignments that must be completed immediately after the break. Thus, students have almost no uninterrupted rest during those periods. In summer, they can truly unwind and enjoy the time they have.

Some may argue that more frequent breaks would be better, yet those shorter breaks still come with assignments and post‑break tests, leaving little time for genuine relaxation. 

In conclusion, summer break remains the sole long period available for students to rest and pursue activities that are impossible during the school year due to workload and testing. It should therefore remain this way, providing students with the best opportunity to recharge and have fun.

Most students look forward to the summer holidays, but some teachers worry that the long break leads to laziness and a loss of information when classes resume. I disagree with that concern and believe that the summer vacation is a valuable time for students. The reason is simple: a long break gives students time to work, rest, and stay free from the pressure that shorter breaks impose.

First of all, many students are keen to work or take on longer‑term projects during the regular school year, but they find themselves stuck with a heavy workload. Homework, tests, and constant studying leave little extra time for these activities. A three‑month summer break allows students to pursue paid work, enrol in summer courses, or simply gain hands‑on experience that will help them future job applications or personal growth. In this way, the summer interval turns into a period of practical learning that the school schedule otherwise cannot provide.

Second, after a year of continuous study, students inevitably accumulate stress. The constant cycle of assignments and exams can be exhausting for both mind and body. A substantial break offers a chance for mental recovery. Students can visit family, travel, or enjoy outdoor activities such as beach trips, all of which help recharge their energy. The warm weather of summer also makes outdoor recreation more pleasant, giving students an enjoyable way to unwind.

Finally, shorter breaks, like the one‑week recesses during the school year, often bring new academic demands. Teachers commonly assign projects or tests that must be completed the following week, which blurs the distinction between rest and work. In contrast, the summer holiday is almost entirely detached from academic obligations, enabling students to truly disconnect from school stress and simply enjoy the extra days.

Some critics claim that more frequent short breaks would benefit students. However, these brief intervals frequently come with their own set of homework and test deadlines, leaving little real downtime for relaxation. In comparison, the lengthy summer vacation offers a unique, uninterrupted pause that cannot be matched by shorter intermissions.

In conclusion, the summer break should remain a long, restorative period for students. It offers them the chance to work, rest, and avoid the academic fatigue that shorter breaks sometimes bring. By preserving this extended holiday, schools give students the opportunity to recharge and return to the classroom refreshed and ready to succeed.
