Distance learning offers many advantages for students. Through the Internet, pupils can attend online classes and communicate with teachers from anywhere, whether at home or in school. They receive the same knowledge as their classmates, but with greater convenience. Bullying, a major issue in traditional schools, can be reduced because students are not physically present in the same environment. Teenagers who might otherwise influence each other toward harmful habits such as drinking, smoking, or drug use have less opportunity to do so when they learn remotely. Many students already juggle after‑school responsibilities, extra courses, caring for siblings, or working part‑time, and distance learning provides a flexible schedule that fits these demands.

Teachers can do more to prevent bullying, yet ensuring every student behaves properly is difficult. Some learners become indifferent or lazy, while others face difficult home situations, lack of parental support, or overwhelming academic pressure. These factors sometimes lead to extreme outcomes like depression or suicide. Schools alone cannot guarantee safety, and students often feel that adults are not fully aware of the problems they face. They may not realize that their actions—such as teasing, bullying, or violent acts—could have serious legal consequences and ruin lives.

Peer pressure is another problem. It is not uncommon for students to threaten friends with exclusion or blackmail if they do not part with drugs or alcohol. Such tactics create fear and force unhealthy choices. In a traditional classroom environment, disruptive students can distract and negatively influence others. Rather than relying solely on disciplinary actions, offering an alternative such as home schooling can help keep everyone focused on their studies.

Distance learning also supports financial planning. Students can work part‑time jobs while studying online, allowing them to save for college. Balancing schoolwork and employment is stressful; online classes let students complete assignments at home at their own pace, reducing the time wasted on commuting and in-school activities. This flexibility gives them time to rest, reducing fatigue and improving concentration. Poor sleep severely affects grades and attendance, undermining future prospects.

In summary, online education can make a significant positive impact on students and schools. It provides the same educational content in a more flexible, engaging way, helping students avoid negative influences. With internet resources and interactive tools, learning becomes enjoyable and less stressful. Distance learning is a practical option for many teenagers who may otherwise neglect their education in a conventional school setting.

Honesty has always been regarded as the best policy, but its value depends on how it is applied. I strongly agree with the idea that honesty is essential, yet misuse of honesty can damage trust. When people act honestly, they strengthen relationships, resolve disputes, and help others feel secure.  

I have seen the power of honesty firsthand. A dangerous road accident taught me that a driver who was not truthful about his fault won the legal case. In contrast, a different driver’s sincere confession led to a quick settlement. My father has also told me stories about friends who solved thefts because witnesses gave honest statements to the police. Even small acts of truthfulness can prevent misunderstandings and build confidence. Nonetheless, it is important not to use honesty in a way that unnecessarily hurts another’s feelings.  

Once I played a sport in which the opponents were not entirely truthful about the rules. Their lies upset several of my teammates, causing tension throughout the game. That experience reinforced how honesty can maintain goodwill. I also had a friend who rarely spoke honestly. Over time he saw how dishonest remarks caused conflicts and, gradually, he began to value integrity. Honest communication can also bring new friendships; I have met people who appreciated my openness and have turned those encounters into lasting connections.  

People who consistently display honesty earn respect. I have witnessed situations where a sincere apology or confession earned people’s trust and admiration. Creating a trustworthy environment encourages cooperation and strengthens bonds. Conversely, when others use honesty as a weapon—saying things they know are untrue to hurt you—it feels like a betrayal. I remember once walking past a street where police cars surrounded a neighbor’s house after a robbery. She had been honest with the police and her cooperation led to the thief’s arrest. That incident made me realize how genuine candour can protect and serve a community.  

In conclusion, honesty remains the best policy across all circumstances. Even in the future, your integrity will shape how others perceive you and influence the outcomes of your actions. By remaining honest, you demonstrate confidence in yourself and promote a healthier, more respectful environment for everyone around you.

The first impressions are almost impossible to change because when people meet someone new, all they have to go on is that person’s appearance.  Because of this, first impressions persist and are rarely altered.  

Firstly, we form a first impression and make guesses about someone’s character based solely on what we see.  For example, a student sees a new classmate whose body does not look healthy and assumes he cannot play sports.  Even if the student later watches him play and sees that he is the best player on the team, it is difficult to shift the initial judgment because the student still remembers the unhealthy appearance.  

Secondly, people often keep their initial impressions because they are personal opinions to hold onto.  For instance, a shy man may appear uninterested in conversation, so others decide not to talk to him.  One day, he shows friends that he enjoys talking; nevertheless, most people continue to treat him as shy and avoid conversation because they have not changed their first impression.  

However, first impressions can be altered when a good relationship develops.  Consider a man with a big, angry face who frightens everyone.  A student takes the time to talk to him and discovers he is friendly.  Over time, people may adjust their first impression, which improves the relationship.  

It is also possible to change first impressions by demonstrating a contrast between past and present behavior.  A student who was once mean to friends may later show kindness and help.  Observing this change can shift friends’ initial judgments, leading to happier, stronger friendships.  

Despite these possibilities, changing first impressions remains difficult.  Therefore, we should not focus too heavily on them.

It is very hard to change the first impression people make of us. When someone meets a new person, the only information they have is what the person looks like, so they form an opinion quickly and it is difficult to change that opinion later. Most people leave that first impression unchanged.

First, people automatically judge a stranger by his appearance. For instance, a student sees a new boy who looks thin and weak. The student assumes the boy cannot be a good athlete, even though the boy turns out to be the best player on the team. After watching the game, the student still remembers the boy’s weak look, so the initial judgement stays.

Second, first impressions are often personal opinions that people hold onto. Imagine a shy man who looks like he does not want to talk to anyone. Everyone assumes he is uninterested in conversation. One day he finally talks to a group of friends and reveals he loves socialising. But the group still thinks he is shy because their original impression has taken root.

However, first impressions can change if a person actively builds a relationship. For example, there is a man with a large, grumpy face who scares people away. A student decides to talk to him and discovers that he is actually friendly. As they get to know one another, the student’s initial negative view fades and others become more willing to approach him.

In addition, people can alter their impressions by showing them how they have changed. Suppose a student used to treat friends poorly. Later he starts being helpful and kind to others, and he may explain this change to his classmates. Their perception of him can improve, leading to stronger friendships.

Despite these possibilities, it is overall very difficult to shift first impressions. Therefore, we should not over‑emphasize them and should give ourselves room to learn more about the person as we interact.

Kindness—you may know it, and everyone might know it—yet what exactly is kindness, and why does it have such a huge impact on others?

First of all, what is kindness? Well, kindness is when you give back to others—whether it’s doing big things like donating to charity or something small like holding the door for someone. But what really is kindness? Those are just simple actions we perform, yet we do them because we want to help others, to create a chain of reciprocity, and to show the world that it can be better. Thus, kindness is the key to making someone happy or inspiring them to give back, thereby perpetuating a cycle of generosity.

Secondly, why does kindness have such a huge impact on others? Well, we all enjoy giving back; some people may disagree, while others agree. Nevertheless, we all want the world to be a better place—not just for ourselves but also for our children. By acting kindly, we set an example for our kids to follow. One day they will look back and be grateful that someone held the door or offered a compliment, and just by that small act they feel a profound sense of happiness. Consequently, a single gesture can have a huge impact on someone.

In conclusion, kindness has a huge impact on others, and what it really means to you and to me is that by just doing the smallest things you can change someone, and they, in turn, can change someone else because of you.

Kindness—whether you know it, I know it, or everyone does—refers to actions that help others, from large gestures like donating to small acts such as holding a door. It is simple in practice but deeply intentional, because when we help someone we often inspire them to help others, creating a ripple effect that improves the world for everyone.

Why does kindness have such a profound impact? Because it satisfies a fundamental human desire to give back. Even if opinions differ, we all share a common hope that the world will be better—not only for ourselves but for future generations. Small acts of kindness, like a polite gesture or a compliment, can trigger a powerful emotional response in someone. That single moment of appreciation can inspire the recipient to carry that generosity forward.

In conclusion, kindness has a tremendous impact. By performing even the smallest helpful acts, we can change a life—and that change may, in turn, transform someone else’s future as well.

Kindness is a word we all know, but what does it really mean, and why does it leave such a strong impression on people?

First, let’s define kindness. It can be a grand gesture like giving to charity, or a small act such as holding a door open. These actions show generosity and concern for others. We choose to help because it creates a cycle of goodwill—we encourage others to help in turn and demonstrate that the world can be a better place.

Second, why does kindness feel so powerful? Many argue that we all want to contribute to a kinder society. Even if some disagree, the idea of improving the world for ourselves and the next generation is compelling. When someone offers a simple kindness—a compliment or a friendly gesture—it can lift the receiver's spirits and inspire them to repay the kindness. That ripple effect can magnify the initial act into a much larger positive impact.

In short, kindness—whether grand or modest—has a profound effect on others. By taking a few small steps, you can change someone’s day and, through their response, help shape a kinder world for everyone.

Technology lets people finish many tasks without meeting anyone else.  
Now it is easy to check out a book, shop for groceries or download a game, all from the comfort of one’s home.  
The question is: does this lack of face‑to‑face contact harm or help society?

I believe it is harmful. In the coming years mobile phones will become even more powerful, and it is likely that human interaction will shrink further. A story illustrates this danger. Two students first talked online on a social‑media platform. They were nervous when they finally met at a café, but after a few awkward moments they became close friends, later going to movies, shopping malls and restaurants together. While this gentle romance seems charming, the background is that the two people have spent most of their time talking through screens. They have not practised the deeper conversations that happen in real life, and the confidence to say “I love you” or “I want to break up” in person is missing. Instead, they prefer phone messages that feel safe but feel hollow. When the trouble becomes serious, they feel like they lack the courage to speak face‑to‑face, which weakens real relationships.

If society continues this trend, eventually many people will abandon their phones altogether because they feel paralyzed by the fear of real communication. We would then lose the ability to support each other, which is essential when we encounter difficulties. The positive energy that comes from seeing a smile, feeling a hug, or being there for someone cannot be replaced by a screen.

It is therefore crucial that people remember the importance of direct human contact. We should encourage ourselves to meet face to face, to speak honestly, and to build relationships that rely on genuine interaction. Only by doing so can we avoid becoming a society that lives brokenly and in isolation.

Some schools are considering offering distance learning so students can attend classes from home. While many students could benefit from this idea—by accessing lessons through online platforms or videos—others would disagree.

I do not support students attending classes from home. First, the home environment can be highly distracting. Students may be tempted by food, television, and particularly by their cell phones, which are rarely checked or restricted when no teacher is present. Second, the lack of formal structure can lead to a casual attitude toward learning; students may attend only sporadically because they are not held accountable by classroom rules. In a physical classroom, teachers can give immediate attention, provide examples, and enforce rules that promote success. Third, remote learning limits opportunities for spontaneous questions and personalized feedback, which are often more readily available in person.

Nevertheless, many students favor home‑based learning. It eliminates commuting time and eliminates cancellations caused by inclement weather, which can disrupt on‑site schedules. Students without reliable transportation—those who must walk or pay for rides—stand to gain significantly by staying home. An online program can serve as important support in such circumstances.

In conclusion, distance learning can be both an advantage and a disadvantage depending on the student. I believe that in‑class instruction remains the most effective way for students to receive comprehensive education, support, and guidance.

Some educational institutions are thinking about letting students learn from home through online classes or recorded lessons. While a number of students see potential benefits in this approach, others are not convinced.

I personally do not support the idea of students attending classes from home. First, the home environment is full of distractions. Food, television programs, and especially cell phones can easily pull a student’s focus away from their studies. In a classroom, a teacher can intervene and remind students to stay on task, but at home no one is there to enforce this discipline. As a result, many students may not attend their lessons regularly, treating the schedule as optional rather than mandatory. In a school setting, teachers enforce rules and provide structure that helps students succeed.

Second, learning from home often means missing out on immediate help. In a classroom, students can ask questions right away and receive instant clarification. They also benefit from the teacher’s attention and from peer discussion. When lessons are delivered via video or online, that spontaneous interaction is largely absent, and students may feel isolated or confused.

However, it is worth noting that some students appreciate the convenience of home‑based learning. It eliminates travel time and saves money, especially for those who must walk or take costly transport to school. During bad weather, schools sometimes cancel classes, causing students to lose valuable instructional time. Online learning would allow lessons to continue without interruption from rain or snow.

In conclusion, while distance learning might be convenient for some, I believe that attending classes in person remains the most effective way for students to learn. The structure, immediate support, and reduced distractions of a classroom environment help students stay focused and achieve better outcomes. Therefore, I maintain that students should continue to attend school in person whenever possible.

Are you a student who is homeschooled? If not, read on to learn why some students prefer to attend classes from home, whether online or through video conferencing.

Many people believe that attending classes from home benefits students. Homeschooling allows students to focus on their studies, feel safer, and avoid negative influences from peers.

Online or video-conferenced classes offer several advantages. They enable students to concentrate on learning, which can be difficult in traditional schools where classmates may be disruptive or rude. Such distractions can lead to students withdrawing, refusing to listen, or even walking out of class because they do not want to confront disobedient peers. Homeschooling also provides a safer environment. In today’s society, incidents such as school shootings have claimed innocent lives, as recently occurred in Florida, and such risks are reduced when students study at home. Moreover, homeschooling helps students steer clear of inappropriate influences. Some schools host a mix of ethnic and cultural backgrounds, and students may be exposed to various harmful behaviors, such as bullying, fighting, or wandering off to unfamiliar places after school.

While attending school in person does offer some benefits, homeschooling can offer even greater advantages. Online or video-conferenced instruction allows students to study safely, concentrate better, and avoid negative influences that might otherwise affect their learning.

Many students still go to school, but a growing number prefer to learn from home, either through online lessons or video conferencing. Those who choose this option often say that it helps them concentrate, keeps them safer, and protects them from negative influences.

One of the main advantages of home schooling is the ability to focus. In a traditional classroom, students can be easily distracted by noisy classmates or disruptive peers. When studying at home, they can create a quiet environment that allows them to dedicate more time and energy to their coursework. This level of concentration can lead to better academic results.

Safety is another important concern. Today, schools face numerous threats ranging from bullying to more serious events such as school shootings. A recent incident in Florida highlighted how vulnerable schoolchildren can feel in crowded campuses. By staying at home, students are shielded from such dangers and can learn in a peaceable setting. They also avoid the stress that can come from a hectic school day.

Furthermore, home schooling removes the chance of encountering harmful peer pressure. In many schools there are students who enjoy risky behaviors—going to malls late, hanging out at strangers’ houses, or simply picking fights. These activities can influence younger classmates negatively. Parents and students who teach themselves at home can steer clear of such temptations and maintain a healthier lifestyle.

In conclusion, while regular schools have their benefits, learning from home provides greater focus, safety, and protection from unwanted peer influences. These factors make home schooling an appealing choice for many families today.

When I lived in my country, many rural families had no devices to talk to anyone else, and they suffered greatly. Some schools offer distance learning as an option that allows students to attend classes from home through online or video conferencing. This arrangement would benefit students who struggle to socialize and have difficulty communicating with classmates or teachers, as well as those who have had negative experiences in traditional school settings. By studying in a familiar environment, students can focus better and avoid many distractions.

Opponents argue that home-based learning can be distracting and that students may fail to complete their agenda. They also worry that students may find self‑instruction challenging and that absence from a physical classroom deprives them of the social and experiential benefits of school life.

However, many students grow up under different circumstances; some have endured traumatic childhoods that affect their present behavior. Providing a comfortable learning environment gives them the chance to demonstrate their true potential—an opportunity that many lack in a conventional school setting where social pressures can be overwhelming.

Bullying remains a significant issue, often discouraging students from attending school altogether. By allowing them to learn online, schools can remove them from traumatic environments and help them concentrate on their studies.

Students who remain in their comfort zone can maintain focus and reach their full potential. A supportive home setting, combined with family encouragement, can motivate those serious about their success to persevere through challenges.

Therefore, I firmly believe that students should have the option to take online classes or participate in video conferencing. This flexibility would benefit those who struggle socially, who have had negative school experiences, and those who thrive when studying in a comfortable, distraction‑free environment.

Some schools now provide distance education as a way for students to attend classes from home using online platforms or video‑conferencing. This option can be especially helpful for learners who feel uncomfortable socializing and who have difficulty interacting with classmates or teachers in a traditional setting. By studying in a familiar, supportive environment, they may be able to concentrate better and avoid many of the distractions that occur in a crowded classroom.

Critics argue that learning from home can lead to procrastination and a lack of motivation. They believe that the absence of a structured school day might make it harder for some students to keep up with their coursework. Additionally, those who rely heavily on teacher guidance might struggle to stay on track without face‑to‑face instruction. It is also true that remote learning does not provide the same campus experience that some students value, such as extracurricular activities and spontaneous interactions with peers.

However, those who have faced negative school experiences—such as bullying or other traumatic events—often find the traditional school environment frightening. For these students, being able to study from a safe, familiar space can reduce anxiety, giving them a chance to focus on their academics without fear. The freedom to learn at their own pace can allow them to regain confidence and re‑engage with their studies.

Moreover, many students thrive when they are in their personal comfort zone. When they are surrounded by familiar surroundings and supportive family members, they can channel their energies toward academic success. This sense of control over their learning environment can lead to higher motivation and stronger results. Families can play a vital role as well, encouraging diligence and celebrating progress, which is harder to achieve in a strictly regulated school setting.

In conclusion, providing the option of online or video‑conferencing classes offers significant benefits. It can help students who struggle with social interaction, those who have suffered negative school experiences, and those who excel when working in a familiar setting. While there are valid concerns about potential distractions, the flexibility and support afforded by distance learning often outweigh these challenges, making it a worthwhile alternative for many students.

First, students who take online classes at the end of the semester often do not learn anything. Second, they are easily distracted and fail to focus on what they are supposed to be focusing on. In my experience, when I learn something on a computer, the light of the screen seems to block my mind. It is very easy for students to be distracted by electronic devices at home, such as cell phones, the same computer, or a TV. For example, a family member might ask a student to help with their siblings, causing them to be unable to focus on classwork. If friends are also at home, they may be playing video games, which only increases the temptation to get distracted.

Finally, learning in a classroom where the teacher is physically present is more efficient. I enjoy interacting with the teacher and classmates about the topics we are studying, which helps me understand better and see different viewpoints. When learning on a computer, students often forget what they have seen right away.

In conclusion, being in a classroom and interacting with teachers and classmates is the best way to learn and obtain the information needed to succeed. Attending online classes at home can lead to a wasted semester and the inability to score enough to pass. Electronic distractions are more readily available at home and capture students’ attention easily. Classroom learning, on the other hand, is the most convenient and effective way to become educated, not just academically but also socially, which is essential for success in life.

In today’s world, teachers often ask whether students would benefit from attending lectures from the home. I firmly think that learning online offers no advantages. I will explain three main reasons: lack of effective learning, easy distractions, and the superiority of in‑person instruction.

First, students tend to learn very little when they attend classes from a computer. When the bell rings no one can “just sit and absorb knowledge.” Experiencing the lecture from home, many students rush through the material to finish it quickly and move on. Because they do not engage deeply, they easily forget what they have seen. When it comes time to assess their understanding, they have nothing to show.

An example is my own experience. I try to study a topic on a laptop, but the light and the constant notifications jolt my mind away from the material. It is hard to focus when the screen is all I have to look at. The result is that my learning is superficial and short‑lived.

Second, it is very easy to get distracted at home. When the whole classroom is online, the same device that the teacher is using can also be used for every other purpose: phone calls, social media, games, or watching television. Even the family around can become a source of interruption. For instance, a sibling might need help with homework or a parent might ask for assistance with daily chores, pulling the student away from the lesson. In a traditional classroom, teachers can keep students’ attention, which online classes simply cannot guarantee.

Third, there is no doubt that learning in a classroom is far more convenient and productive. The presence of a teacher is essential. After a lecture, I like to ask questions and discuss topics with classmates and enjoy alternative viewpoints. This interaction helps me grasp the content better and prevents the forgetting that often follows solitary screen‑time. Moreover, teachers can instantly read body language and tone to adjust their explanations, something that would be difficult when the medium is just a screen.

In conclusion, the best way to learn is to attend classes in person. The interaction that happened in a real classroom provides information, understanding, and the experience necessary to pass examinations. By choosing online learning, students lose the opportunity to focus, become distracted, and ultimately fail to retain what is crucial for their future success in life. Only through direct contact with teachers and classmates can students gain the full range of skills and knowledge required to become well‑educated and able to navigate the real world effectively.

Removing the foods students love could be a bad decision because it would make lunch less enjoyable, leave some children hungry, and hurt their focus in class.

Alex has never tried a salad before and feels reluctant to eat it. If the meal is not appealing, the child may choose not to eat at all, risking poor nutrition. When a child is not eating enough, the benefit of “healthy” foods becomes irrelevant.

Second, the lack of satisfying choices can affect students during lessons. Suppose Alex returns from lunch without eating because the menu he was offered does not satisfy him. As the day goes on, his stomach growls, his energy dips, and he cannot concentrate on the teacher’s instructions. The absence of a tasty, filling lunch leads to distraction, poorer performance, and a need for extra snacks that may be unhealthy. Keeping the existing lunch system would provide familiar and satisfying meals that give kids the energy they need to stay attentive.

Some will argue that replacing junk food with healthier options is rewarding because it promotes growth and lasting wellbeing. They expect students to be stronger and more energetic. While this seems logical, the reality is that kids are comfortable with the foods they already enjoy. Forcing a new diet that they find unappetizing risks reducing their overall intake. The key is to provide options that are both healthy and appealing, rather than eliminating favorite junk foods outright. Forcing a drastic change without consideration for taste and appetite could undermine the very health goals it was meant to support.

The more people practice kindness, the larger the circle of influence grows. I have seen this in my own life. A third powerful impact of kindness is that it can boost people’s self‑esteem. As Aesop reminds us, “No act of kindness—no matter how small—ever goes wasted.” A simple compliment can lift a person’s spirit, and the ripple of this positivity spreads to anyone who witnesses or hears about it. All of these examples show that even the smallest gestures of kindness can profoundly influence someone’s life. By choosing to be kind, we create personal reputations, inspire community change, and lift others up—making the world a brighter place, one act at a time.

I believe that taking classes from home can be beneficial, not just for students with health problems, but also for those who simply need a different learning environment.

First, remote learning can help students with health issues—such as those who have mobility problems or chronic diseases—who might otherwise be unable to attend school. For example, a student with arthritis may find it difficult to walk to school, but online or video‑conferencing tutors can provide the instruction they need. This allows the student to pursue a diploma that will be useful for their future. Remote learning can also benefit students who experience conflict at school, such as those who get into fights. By studying from home with a tutor’s help, they can learn without the stress of the school environment.

However, remote learning is not a benefit for students who simply don’t want to attend school. If a student dislikes the school setting, they may show up to online sessions doing whatever they choose because there is no teacher to guide them. They may also struggle to learn effectively because there is no one present to explain concepts. Some students who do not speak English fluently prefer the immersive environment of a classroom where they are surrounded by native speakers. For instance, as someone who does not speak English well, I find that learning at home slows me down compared with attending school, where I encounter English speakers every day. In school, I can practice with teachers and friends, which accelerates my progress.

In conclusion, taking classes from home is not inherently a hundred percent benefit. It offers advantages to some students but can be challenging for others who do not learn as effectively at home. Whether a student chooses home or school learning, both environments provide opportunities to learn. Each day, whether in class or online, I gain new knowledge, and the support I receive from classmates and teachers strengthens me. Ultimately, attending school each day helps me improve my life and language skills, and I feel more confident because I am actively learning.

I believe that studying from home can be useful, but only for certain learners. It is not a universal solution, because many pupils do not learn as effectively outside a classroom environment.

Firstly, remote learning can be a clear advantage for students with health problems. If a child suffers from a chronic illness, has difficulty walking, or is physically disabled, going to school every day can be impossible or exhausting. In that case, attending lessons online lets them keep up with the curriculum, earn a diploma, and pursue future opportunities. Some families also keep their children at home for safety reasons, such as to avoid bullying or violence at school. For those students, learning online offers a safe and supportive alternative.

On the other hand, teaching from home is not beneficial for students who simply dislike the school setting or who are unwilling to put in the effort. Without a teacher present to guide them, these students may become careless or unmotivated. They might also miss out on explanations and interactions that help them understand difficult topics. Moreover, for learners who need an immersive environment—such as non‑native speakers of English—studying at home can slow progress. In a classroom they hear the language constantly from teachers and peers, which speeds up acquisition. I disagree with this idea because it would harm my high school rather than help it. The most immediate effect would be on after‑school programs and activities. Adding two hours to the daily schedule would extend the school day to ten hours, making students more tired and less inclined to participate in extracurriculars, which could lead to cancellations. This would be especially problematic for juniors and seniors who already work after school; many would be forced to quit their jobs.

The proposal also has potential benefits and drawbacks. One advantage is that longer classes could give students more time to complete assignments during school. Another benefit is that a shorter week might help conserve the school’s energy and resources. However, the disadvantages are significant. After‑school programs could close due to reduced participation, and some students would need to adjust or abandon their part‑time jobs, which is not easy for many.

Before any school implements this change, several actions should be taken. First, the school staff should hold a meeting to discuss the idea internally. Next, a separate meeting should include parents, during which the proposal should be explained in detail. Then a letter should be sent home for parents to read and sign, indicating whether they support or oppose the proposal. Only after gathering this input should the school decide whether to proceed.

In conclusion, I oppose implementing the four‑day work week in my school. It would bring more disadvantages—such as canceled after‑school activities, loss of part‑time jobs for students, and greater fatigue—than advantages. The current schedule already allows students to play sports, participate in extracurriculars, and maintain jobs. Therefore, my school should maintain its existing schedule rather than adding two hours to each day.

This essay discusses whether a school should adopt a four‑day week that lengthens the remaining days by two hours. I will explain my position on this proposal, outline its pros and cons, and suggest steps a school should take before deciding.

Imagine receiving a notice from your high school announcing a plan to move to a four‑day schedule, with each day extended to ten hours. I oppose this change because it would harm rather than help our school community. The most obvious impact would be on after‑school programs. Extending the school day would leave students more exhausted, reducing interest in extracurriculars and possibly leading the school to cancel them. For junior and senior students who already work part‑time jobs, an extra two hours each day could force many to quit their employment.

There are, however, arguments in favour of the new schedule. Longer days would give teachers more time to cover material, potentially improving the depth of learning. Additionally, a shorter overall week might lower the school’s energy consumption and maintenance costs. Yet these benefits come with drawbacks. The likely decline in participation could see after‑school clubs shut down, limiting social and athletic opportunities. Furthermore, students who rely on part‑time work would need to adjust their schedules, which is not always feasible, and some might lose their jobs altogether.

Before a school implements such a change, it should take careful steps. First, the administration should convene a meeting with teachers and staff to discuss the proposal in detail. Next, they should involve parents by holding a separate forum where the benefits and risks are explained. The school could then circulate a letter to families that clearly outlines the plan and requests written consent or objection. After collecting parental responses, the school can make an informed decision.

In conclusion, I believe adopting a four‑day, ten‑hour schedule would do more harm than good for my high school. The potential loss of after‑school activities, disruption of student jobs, and increased fatigue outweigh the modest benefits of extended class time and lower operating costs. Our current schedule allows students to balance academics, sports, extracurriculars, and work, and I would prefer to maintain it rather than implement a more burdensome system.

As a student, I agree with the potential benefit, but I do not support extending the school day by two hours. Most people find eight hours in school sufficient because sitting in a classroom most of the day can be exhausting. In every classroom, there are students who fall asleep because of the heavy workload, after‑school jobs, or sports commitments. These factors make it difficult to stay alert for an extra two hours when a three‑day weekend is the goal, and the drawback outweighs the perceived benefit.

Adding two extra hours each day for four days does not actually save energy. The extra hours on Monday through Thursday add up to eight hours, which simply replaces the hours lost on the fifth day. Thus, the total energy use remains the same.

Teachers’ opinions matter too. They will find ten straight hours exhausting, as they are not robots programmed by the government. Consequently, they may not support a longer school day for students and teachers alike.

They must focus on their studies before their activities, and as I mentioned earlier, playing sports can lead to failing grades. If no one pushes for a change in the grading requirement, the rule could stay, but we should keep a B average as the minimum for sports participation. This will motivate students to strive for better grades.

Keeping a high average is useful for several reasons. It shows up on report cards and progress reports, and students can see whether they are falling behind because they are spending too much time on sports or other activities. The principal should observe how students respond to the new rule, and if it works, keep it; if not, it can be revised later. It does not matter if a student is a high C; they still need to reach a B to play.

Most students will argue that studying is hard, but it is in their best interest. Schools that allow a C average to play sports may lose reputation, whereas a school that demands a B average can be recognized for higher academic standards. Students who truly care about sports will try harder to meet the new requirement. Those who already study, attend tutoring, and submit their work can show their teachers; then the school can allow them to participate. Everyone can achieve at least a B, even if not an A. Those who complain, slack off, or sleep in class will not see improvement, and that is their loss. We want our school to be known for its players who maintain a B average.

In conclusion, I support the new policy. Even if a student thought they couldn’t pass, they can prove otherwise by working hard in school, regardless of what others say. It is not so hard to try; doing so for sports, or for personal success, makes a real difference.

Technology plays a vital role in our lives today, and its importance will only grow in the future. Humanity constantly seeks ways to improve our existence and to make everything simpler. While some people praise this progress, others argue that it negatively affects our lives: face‑to‑face interaction in public is declining, people prefer to stay within the confines of technology, and some become aggressive when told that technology is harmful.

In the past, people met in the streets without the aid of technology; we could only view each other on tiny screens and talk to friends remotely. This shift has become problematic: people no longer go outside to meet friends or simply enjoy the city; instead, they stay at home and chat with strangers online. Some argue there is no difference because strangers previously met in public, but online interactions carry risks—such as fake accounts that can harvest personal information. When we met strangers face‑to‑face, we could observe their behavior and trust them, but the internet makes it difficult to verify authenticity.

As children, we enjoyed playing outside—exploring the streets, visiting friends’ houses, or spending time in parks. Those days have changed dramatically. Modern technology introduced video games, which are now popular among kids and teenagers. Connecting a device to a TV and playing is effortless, yet some spend entire days indoors, refusing to play sports or visit friends. At school, discussion often revolves around video games, and excessive play interferes with studying and completing homework. When the first consoles appeared, many kids could not afford them and would instead save for treats or amusement parks. Today, however, many youths stay indoors where technology dominates.

The proliferation of technology has led to a new behavior: when technology access is restricted, some children become aggressive. Families experience conflicts when kids react angrily to such prohibitions, a trend seen worldwide. Doctors attribute this aggression to a reliance on an imaginary world where they can do anything until parents intervene to ground them in reality. With technology everywhere, it is difficult to compel a child to stop using it, and even teenagers have been observed breaking devices while playing.

Some people view technology as a positive force that creates artifacts simplifying our lives. Others believe it is harmful because it erodes normal human interaction and encourages overreliance on convenience. Whether we embrace or regulate technology, its impact on future society cannot be ignored.

In earlier times, people met on the streets; they could see and speak to each other without any screen between them. Today, many choose not to step outside to meet friends or simply to appreciate urban life. Instead, they remain indoors, talking to strangers on the internet. Some claim that online conversations are no different from meeting a stranger on the street, but the danger lies in the fact that many online identities are fake, which can lead to identity theft or other dangers. In the past, meeting a stranger meant observing their behavior directly, which helped build trust; online, we often have no way of verifying authenticity.

As children, it was exciting to play outside: visiting friends’ houses or spending time in parks. That experience has changed dramatically with the rise of digital entertainment. Video games have become a staple among kids and teenagers. All one needs is a device connected to a TV, and hours can pass in front of the screen. Some children now spend entire days gaming instead of engaging in sports or visiting friends. When they go to school, the most common topic among classmates centers on video games, which can distract them from studying and completing homework. In the past, a new gaming console was considered a major milestone; many families saved money to purchase one. They also spent that money on treats or theme park tickets. Today, many youngsters prioritize gadgets over experiences that involve real‑world interaction.

The abundance of technology has given rise to a new pattern of behavior. When technology use is restricted, some children become irritable or even aggressive. Families worldwide report similar difficulties when trying to limit screen time. Professionals explain that teenagers are often immersed in a virtual world where they feel they have unlimited freedom. When parents step in and remove that “world,” the teens can react strongly. In extreme cases, they might damage the very devices their parents bought for them.

Some argue that technology is a positive force because it creates useful tools that simplify life. However, the negative side—loss of normal social interaction, overreliance on digital convenience—cannot be ignored. If we do not manage our relationship with technology, it may undermine the social fabric of future society.

Music, drama, and art are regarded as elective subjects. Since such courses are seldom required in everyday life, they are not mandatory for graduation; there are many alternatives available. They should not be compulsory, as each student’s aspirations differ.

We learn practical skills like basic math for taxes and bills, but when will you ever employ music, drama, or art in your daily routine? They are more recreational than essential for sustaining a stable life. Knowing how to compose, perform melodramatically, or replicate the Mona Lisa rarely enhances employability; a portfolio featuring these talents rarely secures a job in most fields. Only exceptionally gifted individuals in these disciplines can achieve lasting success. Electives serve a purpose: providing a starting point for future ambitions; making them mandatory would stifle individual growth.

Graduation is independent of such courses. Colleges prioritize prerequisites related to diplomas or majors more than artistry. Skills in painting or sculpting are not evaluated on the SAT, but rather on how they align with your academic eligibility. As students mature, their goals evolve; a student may shift from medicine to science, and though both streams require foundational science courses, music, drama, and art do not share transferable content. They remain highly specialized.

Mastering music, drama, or art can be rewarding—writing songs for renowned artists, starring in plays or films, or earning acclaim and income. Yet success hinges on innate talent or relentless dedication; only a minority can sustain a livelihood from these endeavors, making them unreliable career paths to mandate.

Focusing exclusively on such subjects narrows future options. They are not indispensable in reality; therefore, music, drama, and art should remain electives. Students ought not be required to take these classes, preserving the breadth of choices for their lives.

Music, drama, and art classes are considered electives because, **firstly**, such classes are unlikely to be used on a daily basis in most people’s lives. **Moreover**, they are not required for graduation; therefore, **additionally**, there are many more options available to replace them with other subjects. **Consequently**, compulsory enrollment would be unnecessary since each student has a different vision for their future.

**For instance**, basic math is something we learn at school because it helps with everyday tasks such as filing taxes and paying bills. **In contrast**, music, drama, and art are more akin to hobbies than essential skills needed to maintain a stable life. **Therefore**, having the ability to write a song, perform melodramatically, or draw a portrait of the Mona Lisa does not typically guarantee employment, and **hence** such abilities are rarely sought after by most employers. **Only** those who are exceptionally talented and skilled in these arts can succeed professionally; **otherwise**, the benefits of these electives remain limited. **Thus**, electives exist precisely to provide a starting point for future aspirations; **otherwise**, making them compulsory might have caused the world to miss a second renaissance.

**Similarly**, college admissions focus on prerequisites relevant to a student’s diploma or major, **not** on whether a student can paint or sculpt. **Hence**, a student’s goals often evolve during college—perhaps shifting from a desire to become a doctor to pursuing a career as a scientist. **Both** science majors share overlapping coursework, **but** music, drama, and art do not share such common ground, **making** them unique subjects with no broad overlap.

Learning to create music, act, or draw art can indeed be useful: **for example**, one might write songs for famous artists, perform on stage or in films, and earn recognition and income from their work. **However**, success in these fields largely depends on innate talent or relentless passion and a clear goal from the start. **Consequently**, only a small number of individuals can make a living from the arts **and** it is not a reliable career path, **which explains** why it should not be required in school.

**In summary**, focusing excessively on such subjects reduces the breadth of options a student can pursue. **Thus**, music, drama, and art should remain elective courses, allowing students the freedom to choose paths that best align with their interests and career aspirations.

As people mature, their academic interests can shift—for example, a student may begin the year aspiring to be a doctor and later pivot to science. While both goals share many core courses, the elective arts classes remain specialized and do not connect broadly to other subjects.

Learning music, drama, or art can be beneficial: it may lead to writing songs for famous artists, acting in films, or earning a substantial income from creative work. However, such success depends on innate talent, intense dedication, and a singular focus from the outset, and only a small fraction of students can achieve it. Consequently, the arts are not a reliable career path for most.

Requiring students to concentrate solely on these subjects limits their options and fails to match the demands of the real world. Therefore, music, drama, and art should remain elective courses, allowing students to pursue the fields that best align with their individual aspirations.

Music, drama, and art are usually offered as elective subjects. They are not essential to everyday life, and many students find that other courses give them more useful skills. Because everyone has different aspirations, these classes should not be compulsory.

Basic mathematics is taught because it is needed for paying taxes and managing bills. In contrast, the ability to compose a song, act dramatically, or paint a portrait is often more of a pastime than a necessity. Employers rarely request such talents on a résumé, and anyone who pursues a career in these fields must have exceptional skill. Electives exist to help students discover their interests, not to force everyone into the same artistic track. If schools made them required, we might see a “second renaissance” that would simply replace one form of training with another.

Moreover, electives are not part of the graduation requirement. College admissions focus on core subjects and prerequisites relevant to the intended degree. Skills like painting or sculpting are not evaluated in the SAT, and the ability to create art does not guarantee admission. As people mature, their goals can shift dramatically. A student studying pre‑medicine might later decide to become a scientist; their biology courses overlap somewhat, but art or drama have little relevance to either path. These artistic subjects are too specialized to support such flexibility.

It is true that excelling in music, drama, or art can lead to a successful career for a few lucky individuals. However, the odds are slim, and most students would be better served by learning skills with broader applicability. Fixating on these subjects limits the range of future opportunities.

In short, music, drama, and art are valuable for personal enrichment, but they do not meet the practical needs of most students. Therefore, they should remain electives, allowing learners to choose them voluntarily while preserving the freedom to pursue other, more universal skills.

Some people prefer to study from home or online because they can focus without distractions. For example, if they are in a group, they might talk and lose concentration; but with no one else around, they can work better. This may explain why more people enroll in such classes. Those who study online or at home often appear more intelligent and acquire more knowledge because they can concentrate on their lessons. In traditional schools, students may lose focus by playing or talking with friends, which can be distracting. Taking classes at home can benefit students in many ways, and they often know more by the time school ends. Regular school students face an SOL test at the end of the year, and some fail because they learned nothing but sat around, doing nothing. Those who study at home, however, can pass the SOL because they were interested in what they were learning and had no distractions all year.

I believe learning online or at home is a good option for many people because it allows them to focus more closely on their studies. When students are free from the usual classroom distractions—talking friends, hurried hallways, or noisy lunch periods—they can direct all their attention to the lesson. In an online or home setting, there is no one to interrupt them, so they can absorb the material more deeply and retain it longer.

One advantage of studying at home is that it can help students prepare for all kinds of situations. Since they are already practicing in a quiet environment, they learn to be more self‑disciplinary and ready to tackle real‑world challenges. They also tend to be more organized; without the structure of a school day, they must manage their own time, which builds strong planning skills that are useful beyond academics.

However, it is not true that studying at home means missing out on everything. Some people value the chance to make friends at school, and that interaction can be emotionally supportive. If you live alone or spend a lot of time online, you might still see your classmates regularly through video calls, message groups or discussion forums. Friendship is important, and one can develop it even from a distance, but the traditional classroom offers an environment where introductions happen naturally and relationships can grow more quickly than in a virtual setting.

A second benefit of online learning is the opportunity for students to compete against their peers in a controlled way. In a standard classroom, some students may not be fully attentive, sleeping or chatting during the lesson, and they risk falling behind. On the other hand, a student who studies online may show greater focus and preparedness. In a fair comparison, that student could out‑perform their classmates because they had fewer distractions and a stronger study routine. This shows that if a student dedicates themselves to online learning, they can gain a real advantage over those who are only present but not fully engaged in a schoolroom.

Studying from home also promotes responsibility. Students who take responsibility for their own learning tend to do better in exams and quizzes, whereas students who rely on the teacher’s guidance and seem to be half‑awake during the lesson may perform poorly. The ability to self‑manage time, set goals and review content is far stronger when students trust themselves to keep on track.

At the end of the school year, there is often a mixed picture of results. Some students have mastered the material because they studied intensively, while others flounder because they spent more time playing or simply ignored the lessons. Students who made a conscious choice to study online or at home are more likely to be prepared for the final tests, whether those are state level exams or other assessments. Their focused learning style means that they fully understand the concepts they are tested on, so they are typically better positioned to succeed.

In conclusion, although traditional schools offer opportunities for social interaction and routine, studying online or at home grants many students a chance to learn more effectively. With fewer distractions, higher focus, and greater self‑discipline, they are better able to master the curriculum and to succeed in important exams. Whether a student prefers the school environment or the home setting, the key is choosing the way that best supports their own learning style and goals.

Some schools offer students the option to attend classes from home via online or video conferencing. I think this is a great idea because it benefits many students who cannot attend regular school schedules. Students often lack the resources, time, or have personal reasons that prevent them from attending in person, and this option helps them finish their studies.

Online classes are one such option for those who want to complete school. Students can take courses from home without going to campus, fitting the schedule around their availability. Time is often a major obstacle; many students leave school because they must work after class and have insufficient time for homework or other activities. This leads to falling grades and eventually dropping out to support their families. Some students, even without family support, must balance studying and working to earn money. With online classes, they can continue their education while meeting these obligations.

Another option is video conferencing. Like online classes, it allows students to attend live sessions from home whenever the teacher’s schedule permits. Since these classes happen in real time with teachers visible on camera, students can ask questions, clarify confusion, and engage as they would in a traditional classroom.

What makes these options effective is that students can work and manage personal activities simultaneously. The programs are not limited to young people; adults can also enroll and complete high school, overcoming the barrier of age. 

We know that many teenagers are dropping out—some out of necessity, others due to lack of motivation. By providing these distance learning options, schools give former and current students an easier path to finish their studies and secure a better future. If more schools adopt distance learning, more people will benefit and gain better opportunities, and the opportunity to abandon school will no longer be an excuse.

The possibility of learning from home through online or video‑conference classes is becoming a reality in many schools. I believe this alternative is a valuable choice for students because it offers opportunities that traditional schooling cannot always provide.

For many learners, attending a physical classroom every day is difficult. Economic constraints, work commitments and family responsibilities often force them to miss school or make the life of a punctual student impossible. Online classes allow these students to study from their own homes at times that suit their schedules. Those who must work after school can still complete their homework, keep up with lessons, and avoid falling behind, which is a common reason pupils abandon their education.

Video‑conference learning is another promising option. It works much like an online class but is conducted in real time, so students can see and hear their teachers and classmates through a webcam. This live interaction lets them ask questions immediately and engage in discussions, making the experience as close to the classroom as possible.

Both formats let students balance schooling with other responsibilities, such as part‑time jobs or family care. They also open the door for adults who wish to finish their secondary education but cannot attend a traditional school because of age or other commitments. Distance learning removes that barrier and makes education inclusive for all ages.

The rising number of teenagers dropping out—whether due to lack of alternatives or indifference—could be mitigated if more schools adopted distance learning. When schools provide a flexible option, students who were previously unable or unwilling to attend can now complete their studies, ultimately gaining better prospects for the future.

In conclusion, by offering online and video‑conference classes, schools can attract a broader range of students and help them succeed. The more institutions that adopt this approach, the more learners will benefit from the opportunity to finish their education and improve their lives.

Most students enjoy summer vacation, but some educators feel that students do not retain information as well when they return in the fall. Educators should also consider the students’ point of view, which includes the need for family time and personal responsibilities. Therefore, they should not convert vacations into year‑round school, as a 3–4 week summer break and short breaks in spring and fall are essential.

The first reason is that students miss time with their families. When school resumes, students return home each day to do homework and prepare for the next day, and many have projects to finish. In doing so, they often forget to spend quality time with their parents, which can negatively affect family relationships. Because of this, teachers believe that breaks are too short to allow students to recharge and maintain healthy home lives.

The second reason is that most students have additional responsibilities. During the long summer, spring, and winter breaks, many help their parents and use their free time as they wish, without the stress of homework and projects. Many students also feel that the material they learn is not useful and therefore forget it quickly when they come back to school. This loss of motivation further underscores the importance of adequate breaks.

Although some people think that summer break is too long and that students do not retain information, the reality is that their rest is essential. Educators should maintain the 3–4 week summer break and short spring and winter breaks to give students time to spend with family and attend to personal responsibilities. That is why summer, spring, and winter breaks should not be removed.

Most students enjoy summer vacation, yet some teachers worry that the long break causes learners to lose information when they return in the fall. Even so, it is important to consider the students’ perspective. Ignoring how they feel is unfair; their experience matters. Teachers should not transform the schedule into a year‑round calendar with only a three‑ to four‑week break in summer and a one‑week pause each spring and fall.

The first point is that students miss family time. When the school year ends, many students rush back home to catch up on homework, prepare for the next day, and finish projects. They can become absorbed in their own tasks, forgetting about their parents for a while. This imbalance hurts the family bond and reduces the support children need. Consequently, the argument that breaks are too short is not convincing. A substantial summer break allows families to reconnect and provides students with a reset before the next academic cycle.

The second reason concerns students’ responsibilities outside school. During the vacation, many youngsters help out at home or pursue their personal interests, freeing their minds from academic pressure. They use the time to relax and recharge. They also feel that what they learned in class is often forgotten, reinforcing the belief that the long break is useful for regaining focus. Removing these pauses would give them more pressure, less rest, and consequently poorer academic performance.

In summary, although some argue that a lengthy summer break hampers learning, the evidence shows that students need ample time with their families and to attend to personal duties. Therefore, keeping the traditional summer, spring, and winter breaks is essential.

Students often lose focus during online classes because the teacher’s explanations are harder to follow remotely. They may find online instruction more challenging to understand, especially compared to the clarity of in‑person discussions. Consequently, learning at home can be less effective.

Some schools believe that offering classes from home is beneficial for students, who can relax, finish homework earlier, and feel comfortable and safe with family. They also report that students sleep better, which can boost their energy for online classes. Nevertheless, the proximity to family can also lead to more distractions, making it harder for students to stay focused.

In conclusion, students who learn from home via online classes often struggle to stay attentive because distractions are easy to find. They may not enjoy learning online, may fall into passive environments, and tend to use phones or play instead of studying. This reduces their learning effectiveness and can lead to frustration when they fail to understand the material, both in school and online.

Many schools in the United States offer remote classes because it seems like a convenient option for students. However, the idea that learning from home is beneficial turns out to be problematic for many learners. 

A major issue is distraction. When students are in their bedrooms, phones, social media, video games, and other gadgets are always within reach. This constant pull makes it hard for them to concentrate on the lesson. Even if the class is delivered over video, the students might start listening to music or chatting with friends instead of following along. The online environment also lacks the structure of a classroom, which can lead to a decline in motivation.

Another problem is the learning environment itself. In a classroom, teachers can explain concepts face‑to‑face, read the students’ body language, and address misunderstandings immediately. Over a screen, it is often harder to convey nuance and ask questions. Some students find it challenging to grasp difficult material through a webcam, so their confidence and understanding suffer. Without the direct support of a teacher present, students may feel lost and begin to fall behind.

Safety and comfort can feel appealing, but they hide other disadvantages. The comfort of staying at home does not automatically translate into better study habits. Being surrounded by family members can create a noisy or otherwise stimulating setting that is unsuitable for focused learning. Additionally, students who have part‑time jobs or other responsibilities are often exhausted by the time they sit down for an online lesson, which reduces their ability to engage fully.

While remote learning offers flexibility and can reduce issues like bullying, the downsides have a profound impact. The increased risk of distraction, the challenge of maintaining a conducive learning environment, and the lack of immediate teacher feedback all combine to make online classes an unreliable substitute for in‑person instruction.

In conclusion, although distance learning might seem like a comfortable alternative, it often leads to lower attention, decreased academic performance, and overall frustration. For many students, the best path to learning still involves being physically present in a classroom where structured guidance and a focused environment can truly support their education.

A city council is debating the adoption of a curfew for teenagers: 10 p.m. on weekdays and midnight on weekends. Some people think this is a good idea, while others—especially young people—disagree. There are conflicting opinions on this topic. In my view, setting a limit for teenagers who stay out late is a good idea because it can improve their sleeping habits, prevent unhealthy eating, and give them more time with their families.

Curfews that keep teenagers home at night can help them improve their sleep. When they are home, they go to bed earlier than if they stayed out until midnight. Young people need at least seven to eight hours of sleep because their bodies are growing. Adequate sleep makes them more energetic. Staying out late disrupts their bedtime, making them lazy, tired, and less active in everyday activities. Poor sleep also increases the risk of driving under the influence of fatigue. When you cannot sleep well, dizziness while driving can be dangerous. Many teenage deaths in road crashes result from inattentiveness caused by inadequate sleep. Additionally, staying out late can lead to drinking and driving. Curfews could protect teens from these dangers. For instance, when I cannot sleep well, I struggle to concentrate in class, which affects my grades. Staying awake late also isolates me from what is happening in the real world because my peers are alert while I am not.

Curfews also affect teenagers’ eating habits. Staying out often means eating unhealthy junk food, which is detrimental to their health. Adequate sleep is essential, but so is a healthy diet. Young people need nutritious food to support their active lives; otherwise, they may develop illnesses early. When teens go out with friends, they may also drink alcohol or beer, which is inappropriate for their age. Unhealthy food weakens the immune system and can lead to disease and excess weight. This, in turn, affects teens socially, mentally, and physically. Staying home allows them to eat meals prepared by their parents, which are typically healthier and less oily. Whenever I eat unhealthy food, I feel sick, and being in a place where no one knows me makes me uncomfortable. I have seen a family member who gained weight from junk food, now struggling to move and often teased for his size. To avoid such negative comments and poor health, teens should eat wholesome, homemade meals.

Beyond food and sleep, curfews keep teenagers home with their families. This encourages interaction with family instead of going out with friends. Often, a generation gap appears in families when members spend less time together. Having dinner together allows discussions about daily events. For example, when our family puts together at dinner, we talk about new experiences, like my sister and I making new friends after moving here this year. We also discuss health issues and problems we face, sharing joys and concerns. This strengthens family bonds.

There are many other reasons for this adoption that steer teens toward positive habits. Proper sleep, healthy food, and family interaction can all be achieved with curfews. To produce a future generation that is healthy and focused on the country’s development, such laws are necessary. Healthy teens will be fresh and present-minded citizens. If they sleep well, they will work hard to achieve their dreams. Moreover, interacting with family creates a more harmonious world. Teens should view a curfew as a benefit rather than a restriction on their freedom. It is not a limitation; rather, it is a key to a healthy, fresh, and active lifestyle. Give teens life by guiding their habits rather than exposing them to improper lifestyles.

The city council is debating the introduction of a curfew for teenagers: 10 p.m. on weekdays and midnight on weekends. Some people consider this measure sensible, while many young people feel it is unnecessary. I believe that imposing such a curfew is a good idea because it can improve teenagers’ sleeping patterns, reduce unhealthy eating, and encourage more family time.

A curfew would help teens get enough sleep. When they stay out until midnight, their bedtime is disrupted, leading to fatigue, sluggishness, and poor performance at school or work. Adequate sleep—seven to eight hours—is essential for growing bodies. Lack of rest can even endanger young drivers: a drowsy driver is more likely to suffer dizziness and lost concentration, increasing the risk of accidents. Too many teen deaths on the road are caused by fatigue and impaired judgment after staying out late. Personally, when I cannot sleep well, I struggle to focus in class and my grades suffer. Late nights keep me out of sync with the world around me.

Teenagers who stay out late also tend to eat quickly and choose junk food. Such habits weaken their immune system and raise the risk of early health problems. Excessive consumption of sugary drinks, alcohol, and greasy snacks can lead to weight gain, chronic illnesses, and social stigma. Knowing this, I see family dinners as a chance for healthier meals. When I eat at home, the food is balanced and made by my parents, which helps me stay energetic and alert. I have watched a family member who, after years of junk food, became overweight and dependent on others for simple tasks; he is now embarrassed by his body and struggles to keep up.

Beyond nutrition, a curfew encourages more interaction with family members. When teens are at home, they are more likely to have dinner with their parents and siblings, enabling meaningful conversations about daily life, new experiences, or health matters. These shared moments help bridge generational gaps, allowing everyone to discuss problems and joys alike. When my sister and I moved to a new city, our family gatherings made it easier for us to make friends and exchange life lessons. Such interactions can strengthen emotional bonds and foster a supportive environment.

In short, a teenage curfew can have several positive effects: improved sleep, healthier eating, and stronger family ties. For a healthy future generation, these policies are necessary. If teens remain well-rested, they will be more motivated to pursue their goals. Healthy habits cultivated early will lead to a society of engaged, productive citizens. Rather than being seen as a restriction on freedom, the curfew should be viewed as a protective measure that enables teens to lead healthy, lively lives and help build a better world together.

Without that guidance, the nation might still struggle with the racism that once existed. Many of us receive valuable advice from people we admire—parents, teachers, mentors. Even simple encouragement, such as “never give up on difficult tasks,” can leave a lasting impact, fostering resilience and a growth mindset that supports success and hard work.
