The problem is not that everyone is doing what they should, but that many people are content with doing what they already know. When individuals never seek new challenges, they never grow, and their lives remain stagnant.

I disagree with this tendency. First, it helps to try different things to secure a better future. Second, do not be shy about changing your routine. Third, do not stay the same all the time; if you never try new experiences, you will never truly understand the world you live in or even yourself.

For example, if you want to pursue something in life, you must start by thinking about it. In my family, my sister once wasted much time because she did the same things she was used to. One day my mother spoke with her about her future; she stopped repeating old habits and is now a doctor.

Another example is my father, who was afraid to start his own company because he thought the work would be too different. I encouraged him to try. He eventually launched the business, and it has become successful, partly because he worked hard.

My mother always told me to “be yourself.” I replied that being yourself all the time can keep you from achieving what you truly want. If you only focus on easy tasks you may remain stuck and fail to reach your potential.

In conclusion, I believe that people should not simply repeat what they have already done but should explore new possibilities. By thinking ahead and experimenting, we can grow and achieve more in life.

I don’t agree with the idea that most people stay stuck doing exactly what they have always done. There are three reasons for this.

First, experimenting with new activities can actually help shape a better future. For instance, my sister once spent a lot of time on the same routines and didn’t see any progress. When my mother pointed out that she needed to change her focus, my sister stopped repeating the same patterns and eventually became a doctor. The point is that stepping outside of familiar habits opens up new possibilities.

Second, don’t be afraid to try things that feel unfamiliar. My dad was hesitant to start his own business because he thought the work would be entirely different from what he was used to. I encouraged him to take the risk, and now the company is thriving. This shows that growth often comes from embracing the unknown rather than staying in your comfort zone.

Third, staying rigidly “yourself” can limit both personal and societal growth. My mom sometimes tells me to always be true to myself, but I believe that being too fixed in one way of thinking can prevent us from reaching our goals. If you never explore new ideas or challenge yourself, it’s hard to understand the world around you and truly grow as an individual.

In conclusion, I believe that most people would benefit from breaking out of repetitive patterns, challenging themselves, and being open to change. By doing so, they can create a brighter future for themselves and others.

When people ask you for advice, they sometimes talk to more than one person because they want good guidance; without good advice, they cannot think through a good decision. Sometimes a person who has trouble in life, or who feels depression or lack of happiness, cannot control the situation, which can panic them and make them unsure of what to do. That’s why they seek multiple opinions: they think it helps, but it can also confuse them, as they cannot choose the best one. It is okay to ask for opinions, but we also need to use our own minds; otherwise we cannot act. We should consider what each person says, evaluate whether it is good for us, and think about potential trouble that might arise if we follow it. If a close friend or someone we trust says yes, we can decide to proceed.

Properly, the process of getting a single good opinion involves asking two or three people. If none of those opinions feel right, we should rely on our own judgment and make a decision. Everyone makes their own decision. If you want advice, find a trustworthy adult who truly wants to help and will give you a better choice. Then consider that advice: if you believe it is right, follow it. For example, if I have a birthday party to plan, need to choose dresses, and feel worried and confused, I would seek help from friends, cousins, family, and teachers, but I might feel overwhelmed by too many opinions.

So what I did was ask my older cousin. We discussed it in detail, and she helped me manage my time, choose the dresses, and arrange the party within a week. Everything turned out well. That’s how we make better choices for ourselves. If you can’t do that, at least think on your own or ask a good person, not just anyone, because people can mislead you. We must be careful. Asking an adult is better than asking a lot of people because the adult can help you more. In my first experience, I asked many people and became confused; I didn't use my mind and felt it was a waste of time. I learned that I should never do anything that my parents or adults disapprove of. Another way to make a better choice is to always listen to your parents and adults. Sometimes the decisions we think are good turn out to be harmful later, causing trouble. Therefore, follow what your parents advise rather than your own desires. It is fine to listen to your heart, but sometimes the best way to make a good choice is to heed your parents and adults.

The second way is to use your mind to judge what is good or bad. The third way is to ask an adult who is kind, truthful, and supportive. Believe in yourself and in God; these are the best ways to make better choices. We should always trust ourselves and our parents, because they will always tell us something good for us. Just believe in what they say and in yourself, and everything will be fine. God is with you, so these are the best ways to make good choices.

When people ask for advice, they often talk to more than one person. If they do not receive good advice, they cannot make a sound decision. A person struggling with depression or any difficulty may feel out of control, leading to panic and an inability to think clearly. Seeking multiple opinions can then cause confusion, and selecting the best one becomes difficult. 

It is acceptable to ask others for their opinions, but we must also use our own judgment. Consider what someone says, whether it benefits you, and whether following it could cause trouble. If a close friend or trusted adult agrees, you may decide to follow their advice.

A better approach is to ask two or three people for input. If none of their advice feels right, rely on your own judgment to make a decision. Everyone makes their own choices. When you seek opinions, choose a trustworthy adult who genuinely cares for you and will give you a good choice. Then ponder it; if you believe they are right, follow their direction.

For example, when I had a birthday party to organize and needed to choose dresses and arrange everything in a short time, I felt worried and confused. I asked my friends, cousins, family, and teachers for help, but the many opinions made it hard to choose. I then spoke with my older cousin, who gave me detailed instructions. I managed my time, chose the dresses, and arranged the party in a week. Everything turned out well. 

If you cannot rely on others, at least think on your own or ask a good person, not just anyone. People can manipulate you, so be careful. Asking a single trusted adult is usually better than consulting many people. In my first experience, I consulted many people, became confused, and wasted time. I learned to consider what my parents or adult guardians advise, because they often know what is best.

The best ways to make a good choice are:
1. Use your own mind to evaluate whether something is good or bad.
2. Seek guidance from a trustworthy, honest adult.
3. Believe in yourself and in God’s help.

Trust your parents and adults, as they often know what will benefit you. Listen to their advice, yet also trust your own judgment. This balance will lead to better decisions.

When someone needs a decision, they often turn to many friends or relatives for advice. This is because a poor opinion can lead to a bad choice and life can feel overwhelming. If a person feels lost or depressed, he or she may let others’ ideas take control, causing panic and confusion.

It is natural to ask several people for their thoughts, but too many opinions can make it hard to choose the best one. That’s why it is important to listen to the advice, then use your own judgment to decide what is right for you. Ask a trusted adult who really cares for you. Think carefully about the advice: does it suit your situation? Will it cause problems? If the adult says yes, you can feel confident in following that suggestion.

In practice, I learned this lesson when I had to organize a birthday party. I asked friends, cousins, family, and teachers and received a flood of suggestions. I became confused and had almost no idea what to do. Then I spoke with my older cousin. She gave me a clear plan, helping me to choose dresses, set a schedule, and finish everything in one week. The party went smoothly because I had a focused, reliable opinion rather than a thousand vague ones.

The lesson is simple: ask for opinions, but don’t let them dominate your brain. Take advice from a reliable adult, evaluate it yourself, and then make your own decision. If you trust a parent or another responsible adult, their guidance often points to safer and wiser choices. Listening to your heart is useful, yet sometimes our emotions lead us astray. Combining parental wisdom, honest reflection, and thoughtful analysis gives the best path forward.

Another useful rule is to trust your own judgment after listening to trusted adults. Believe in yourself and in the support of those who care for you. When doubts arise, ask a thoughtful adult, weigh the advice, and then act with confidence. By doing so, you build better decision-making skills and avoid the pitfalls of endless, contradictory suggestions.

Additionally, many people do not believe in failure, saying it is something that happens in life to make a better person. If they fail a class or do not pass a class, they keep trying and never give up. Surely, with failures they learn from the experience and will not lose enthusiasm.

Ask yourself—you can see failure is not always a good way to major success. One needs to turn failure into attention and become a better person by trying hard. If these people keep trying, the things they do will improve. Although many people are successful with failure.

Truly, failure is part of life, and we need to understand our failures so that we can succeed. By understanding our failures, we learn how to do better and not worry about them. Since we are worried about the failures, one can have more enthusiasm for success.

Some people support the statement that “success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm” because they believe failure teaches new skills and prepares them better for future challenges. Others disagree with Churchill; they think failure is a bad thing, because when you fail you are forced to try again, and that process makes you stronger. Since no one is perfect and everyone experiences both good and bad moments, noticing failure should not make life fundamentally different for anyone.

Many argue that failure is not something to be avoided but something to be understood. By confronting failure, we can grow into better versions of ourselves. Those who see failure as worthwhile learn new things and put effort into becoming better people. In clarity, they accept that failure is a necessary step in life.

Additionally, some people dismiss failure because they see it as a sign that something went wrong. If they fail a class, they keep trying until they pass. When people learn from failure, they do not lose their enthusiasm, but instead gain a deeper understanding of the experience.

You can see that failure is not always a direct road to success. Success requires attention to, and learning from, failure and the willingness to try harder. If people keep trying, the things they work on will improve. Although everyone experiences failure, many achieve success by learning from it.

Truly, failure is a part of life, and we need to understand our failures so we can succeed. By learning from our failures, we can do better next time and not worry so much about the setbacks. Understanding that success often follows perseverance motivates us to keep an enthusiastic view toward our goals.

Many people believe that “success is going from failure to failure without losing enthusiasm,” as Winston Churchill suggested. They say that failing teaches us lessons, makes us better prepared, and deepens our understanding. Others, however, disagree, arguing that failure is simply a sign that the plan didn’t work and that we should change our approach instead of repeating the same mistakes. Neither view dismisses the fact that nobody is perfect; we all experience both successes and setbacks, and these experiences shape who we become.

Those who see value in failure think it is a necessary part of growth. When we fail, we take time to analyze what went wrong, ask for feedback, and adjust our strategies. This reflective process helps us develop new skills and improves our problem‑solving abilities. In this sense, failure becomes a stepping stone rather than a stumbling block. People who accept failure as a learning experience tend to remain motivated, because they understand that each setback brings them closer to their goal.

On the other hand, some people view failure as a discouraging event that diminishes motivation. They think that if something does not work on the first try, it might never work at all. These individuals prefer to avoid failure by choosing safer, more predictable paths or by giving up after a failure. While this attitude can preserve short‑term enthusiasm, it may also limit personal growth and innovation.

Ultimately, success depends on how we respond to failure. Those who embrace failure, learn from it, and use those lessons to improve are more likely to achieve long‑term success. In contrast, those who fear failure and avoid risks may miss opportunities that could lead to significant achievements. Understanding and accepting failure as a normal part of life is key to maintaining enthusiasm and progressing toward our goals.

The quotation by Ralph Waldo Emerson—“To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment”—serves as a guiding light for anyone who is contemplating how to live a meaningful life. Emerson encourages us to recognize the importance of individuality, especially in a society that often pressures us to conform.

I share Emerson’s view and believe that embracing our own identity is crucial for making thoughtful choices. When we understand our own purpose and the kind of life we want, we are better prepared to achieve our goals and to succeed in whatever organization or workplace we join.

Hard work is the foundation of credibility. By putting effort into what we do, we demonstrate to those around us that we are reliable and competent. This, in turn, will impress not only our colleagues but also our families. Maintaining a positive mindset, respecting others, and making sound decisions are essential on the path to self‑fulfillment.

Working independently can be a powerful catalyst for personal growth. When we listen to our own insights, we are more likely to make choices that align with our true selves, as Emerson suggests. I agree with his sentiment because staying true to one’s values fosters resilience and helps us become who we genuinely aspire to be.

Realistic teamwork requires everyone to contribute wholeheartedly. Without genuine effort, a team can become a mere survival mechanism rather than a source of innovation. Consistent dedication and perseverance pave the way for a brighter future and reflect personally on how we shape our surroundings.

Success manifests when we persistently work toward our goals. Consistency in effort will elevate us, both personally and professionally, as others observe the results of our work. This visibility reaffirms the significance of hard work and the value of staying true to oneself.

In essence, the message is clear: choose to be authentic in a society that often expects conformity. By doing so, we set the stage for a promising future and inspire those around us. Through continuous effort, responsible decision‑making, and positive self‑view, we will find that our perseverance pays off and that our achievements bring great satisfaction.

Believe in yourself, keep working hard, and remain optimistic about the path ahead.

In my experience, I agree that the Emerson idea that mastery will never allow one to grow is mistaken.

First reason: All people become mastered in a skill, and that blocks them from thriving in what they attempt. For example, if you are working in your own company and you are the manager, you will notice that the products you are selling are declining; your performance is suffering. Naturally, you will be tempted to quit and try selling a different product. This experience will make you feel terrible, and you will doubt your worth in your job because you are almost convinced that your career is falling rather than advancing.

Second reason: Mastery can make you overly comfortable with a particular stance, and even a friend’s critique may feel like an attack on everything you’re trying to do. After your friend accuses you of being rigid, you may try to correct yourself, yet you become entrenched, leaving no room for change. Everyone falls into the trap of repeating what they already master instead of experimenting. For instance, a teenager who scores poorly on a test may feel so defeated that they refuse to retake it, simply because they have become mastered in feeling like a failure.

Third reason: Fear of failure can stop someone from pursuing what they love, and they may think that re‑attempting will be exactly the same as the first time. Yet when you try again, you bring more experience and aim to avoid the mistakes you made previously. You learn to be more meticulous, and you will eventually succeed. All of us can repeat an action many times; the key is to believe in ourselves.

You will see that you can grow regardless of how hard or how many setbacks you face; you must remain positive and refrain from becoming overconfident if you have already mastered something.

Conclusion: Never give up on what you’re pursuing, no matter how many attempts or changes you make. Even when you feel mastered, you will always find opportunities to start anew, and trust that you can achieve it because that is all you need to begin again.

In my experience, I don't disagree that the Emerson idea about mastery is something that will never allow one to grow.

First, mastery can trap everyone and stop them from developing further. For example, if you are in your own job and you are the manager, you will notice that all the products you sell are declining. Your job is not going well, and therefore you feel the need to try selling other products. Yet what you end up doing is feeling terrible and doubting your value at work because you see your job as in decline rather than improving.

Second, mastery is like being too comfortable with something, and when a friend points out how you'll get stuck in your ways, you try to correct yourself, but you fall back into mastery. This stops you from making further changes, because everyone tends to avoid trying new things once they have mastered the old ones. For instance, a teenager who is in school and scores poorly on a test may feel so bad that they refuse to retake the test, assuming they have mastered failure.

Third, being scared to try something you love again makes you think that you will repeat the same mistakes you made the first time. But when you try again, you gain more experience, which helps you avoid previous errors. By learning from those mistakes, you can be more careful and grow. We can all repeat the same activity many times, but the key is to believe in ourselves and keep trying.

You will see that you grow regardless of how hard the situation or how many setbacks you face; you just have to stay positive and avoid becoming stuck in mastery.

Conclusion, never give up on what you try, no matter how many attempts or changes you make. If you feel trapped in mastery, remember that you always have another chance to start fresh and trust in yourself, because that is all you need to begin again.

In my experience, I do not agree that the Emerson notion that “one who is mastered will never grow” is true.

Firstly, everyone can become mastered, and mastery often stops further growth in whatever they are trying. For example, if you are a manager overseeing a product line that is declining, you will see your sales falling. You may feel compelled to switch to another product line, but this new venture can leave you feeling terrible, as if you are no longer valuable in your job because the original line is going down instead of up.

Secondly, being mastered means you have become comfortable with one approach, and a friend may point out that you are stuck in that pattern. Even after recognizing this, you may still try to do things the same way, trapped by mastery, and you will have no chance to try different methods. Consider a teenager who receives a poor test score; feeling inadequate, they may avoid retaking the test because they think they are already mastered at failure.

Thirdly, it is understandable to be scared of trying something you love again, fearing that the outcome will mirror the first attempt. However, each subsequent attempt gives you more experience, allowing you to avoid previous mistakes and approach the task more carefully. Believing in yourself and persisting ultimately leads to growth, no matter how hard or how many setbacks you face.

In conclusion, never give up on what you are trying. Even if you feel mastered, you can always find a fresh opportunity to start again, and believing in yourself is all you need to begin!

I have never really found the idea that “once you master something, you stop growing” to be true. I think the opposite is correct: mastering a skill can keep a person moving forward even more.

The first point is that even when someone has become an expert, they can still be held back by fear. If you’re a manager watching sales drop, it’s easy to feel useless and think there’s no point in trying new strategies. That feeling can stop you from learning even better methods, so mastery can feel like a trap instead of a source of confidence. I have seen colleagues who hit a plateau and then lost the motivation to keep improving.

The second reason is that people often hold on to a single way of doing things and ignore feedback. When a friend tells you that you’re stuck in a routine, it’s tempting to deny it. If you keep doing the same thing, you’re stuck in old habits and you can’t develop new strengths. It happened to me once in school: I scored badly on a test, and instead of retaking it, I decided I was “not cut out” for the subject. That choice made me miss a chance to improve.

The third argument is that trying again after failure actually deepens mastery. Each attempt gives you more experience, and you start to recognise what to avoid next time. If you keep believing in yourself and try again, you’ll learn from earlier mistakes and grow stronger. It’s all about staying positive and being open to learning, even when the result seems familiar.

In conclusion, I believe that continuing to push yourself after you feel you’ve mastered a skill is what really leads to growth. You may feel stagnant at times, but each new effort gives you a fresh chance to expand your abilities. Trust yourself, keep experimenting, and you will always find another way to progress.

I agree with Emerson's statement about individuality, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment,” because success, being yourself, and being the owner of your life are all vital.

First, success is the most important thing for society because we all need great people—such as philanthropists who help reduce poverty and inventors who create things that today we cannot live without, like cars, the internet, and computers. Secondly, being yourself is a great accomplishment because you become the person you truly want to be, remain genuine to those around you, and live a meaningful life by showing others who you really are instead of playing a role the world demands.

I agree with Emerson’s statement that “to be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment” because individuality leads to success, self‑authenticity, and ownership of one’s life.

First, success is essential to society. We need great people, such as philanthropists who reduce poverty, inventors who create indispensable tools like the car, the internet, and computers, and innovators who build safe environments that allow all of us to live longer, healthier lives.

Second, being yourself is a great achievement. When you pursue the person you truly want to be, you remain authentic to those around you and live a meaningful life instead of conforming to external expectations.

Third, owning your life matters most. When you decide for yourself what kind of future you want, the choices you make give your life purpose, gratitude, and better health.

Some might say it is futile or better to be told what to do, yet creating your own success, staying true to yourself, and taking control of your life are crucial for human development and for each individual to determine their own path.

All these factors drive a person toward great accomplishment. Life is a story, and each person writes a different one; by being yourself in a world that often gives people a script, you always achieve something remarkable.

I agree with Emerson’s idea that “to be yourself in a world that is trying to make you something else is the greatest achievement.” True individuality gives us success, authenticity, and control over our own lives.

First, success matters because society needs people who can make a difference. Philanthropists who help reduce poverty, inventors who create essential tools like cars, the internet, or computers—all of these contributions improve our living standards and help humans thrive. Without such success, progress would stagnate and many would struggle to live healthy, long lives.

Second, being your genuine self is a profound achievement. When you stay true to who you really are, you build honest relationships and live a life that reflects your values rather than merely following what others expect. In doing so, you find deeper meaning and a stronger sense of purpose.

Third, owning your life is essential. When you decide for yourself what kinds of futures you want, you gain a sense of gratitude, freedom, and well‑being. Making choices that fit your own goals rather than following preset instructions creates a richer, healthier life.

Some people might argue that it is better to accept guidance than to forge a path alone. Nevertheless, creating your success, staying authentic, and taking charge of your future are vital for human development. They allow each individual to decide what they want to become and how they plan to live.

In sum, life is like a story, and each person writes their own chapter. Embracing your true self amid a world trying to shape you is a real accomplishment that teaches us all how to live meaningfully.

Use of mobile phones in classrooms is a subject that elicits strong opinions. Some people believe that phones are a distraction, while others see them as useful learning tools. This essay will consider the different attitudes and policies that exist in schools around the world, and why schools should decide based on their own needs.

Many teachers think that phones impede learning. They worry that students will spend time texting, scrolling social media or playing games instead of taking notes. Because of this, they prefer to ban phones in class. Some schools enforce strict rules: if a student uses a phone during lesson, the teacher will inform the parents or the student may be suspended. These halls of discipline emphasize the importance of listening to the teacher and fully engaging with the lesson.

In contrast, other schools allow phones under controlled conditions. Some teachers tell students that they can use their phones if they want, but only for educational purposes. For instance, a class might use a calculator app to solve a math problem or look up a definition quickly. When students have permission to use phones for learning, they often report a higher level of engagement and a better understanding of the material.

Furthermore, the policies differ dramatically from one country to another. In some places—most commonly in some European schools—phones are prohibited entirely, and the penalty for breaking the rule can be severe. In other countries, such as many in Asia, teachers are more flexible. They provide guidance on how to use phones responsibly and even incorporate them into lessons, believing that familiarity with technology is an essential life skill.

If schools decide to allow phones in class, they must set clear guidelines. Students should be expected to use their devices only after the main part of the lesson or for short research tasks. Teachers can also encourage students to switch off notifications and keep the phone out of sight during critical learning moments. By creating a balanced approach, schools can keep distractions to a minimum and still reap the benefits that technology can offer.

In conclusion, whether a phone is a hindrance or a help depends largely on the environment and the policies in place. Some institutions enforce strict bans to protect learning time, while others adopt a more relaxed stance, permitting phones for educational purposes. The best practice is to tailor the approach to each school’s culture, ensuring that the use of mobile devices enriches, rather than disrupts, the learning experience.

It has often been said that a positive attitude is the key to a successful life. I both agree and disagree with this idea.  

On the one hand, a positive outlook can help a person achieve their goals. For example, Michael Jordan was cut from his high‑school varsity basketball team, yet he stayed optimistic and worked hard. His determination turned that setback into success, eventually making him one of the greatest athletes of all time.  

Another case is the rapper Da Baby. People told him he would never make it, but he kept his mind bright and stayed humble. As a result, he now has multiple gold and platinum records and a huge fan base. His story shows that positivity can open doors and lead to achievement.  

On the other hand, positivity is not the only path to success. In situations like war, soldiers cannot simply remain upbeat; they must be alert and prepared for danger. A too‑positive mindset could even be dangerous in such circumstances.  

In conclusion, a positive attitude can indeed be a powerful tool for success, but it is not always the decisive factor. Different situations may require other traits, such as vigilance or determination, to reach one’s goals.

In China we do not share Ralph Waldo Emerson’s idea that one must always pursue what lies beyond what one has already mastered. I believe that people differ, so not everyone can grow only by challenging themselves beyond what they already know. If they stay within what they do best, they may not truly mature. I disagree with Emerson’s claim that seeking new things and learning them is the sole path to growth; small, vital experiences also foster maturity, as do other crucial factors.

People can grow by searching for and learning new things. New ideas are beyond human control, yet students who learn them expand their knowledge and mature in the process. For example, my mother initially came to America with no English. After three years of study, she now speaks basic English. No one could say she did not grow; she learned a language she never knew before. Her story shows that it is not only past mastery that promotes growth, but also new learning.

Even small details matter. In a scientific experiment, a minor mistake can destroy the entire project. Scientists who err might face criticism, and the outcome of the experiment may change. Handling such mistakes is a significant way for scientists to mature. By learning to manage these small problems, they avoid larger failures that could disrupt their lives.

Life presents many opportunities for growth. Society differs markedly from school. At work, you will discover that effort is not the only path to advancement. Understanding this reality turns you into an adult. Marrying your partner can be a pivotal moment that pushes you to grow again. Having a child teaches you the true meaning of responsibility, which is another marker of maturity. Work, a spouse, children, and other life experiences collectively foster growth.

Emerson wrote, “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow.” This may hold true for some, but I disagree. People mature in many different ways; it is not only through perpetually stretching beyond mastery. Studying new subjects expands knowledge. Learning from small mistakes refines skill. Engaging with society also nurtures growth. In China, numerous factors contribute to personal development.

In China we do not share the notion that Ralph Waldo Emerson claimed. Emerson said that people grow only by going beyond what they already know. In my view, people are varied, so not everyone must exceed their current skills to mature. If a person stays within the competence they already possess, they may not truly develop. I therefore disagree with Emerson’s assertion for three reasons: first, seeking new knowledge can foster growth; second, small details can be pivotal; and third, many life experiences contribute to maturity.

Many people can expand their horizons by learning new things, and this is a path to becoming more mature. New experiences are not always within our control, but when students study something unfamiliar they broaden their understanding and therefore grow. For instance, my mother moved to America when she could not speak any English. After three years of study, she can communicate in basic English. Certainly she has matured by acquiring a language she had never known. Her story shows that mastering new skills, rather than relying on old ones, can bring growth.

Small details also matter. In scientific experiments a minor mistake can ruin the entire project. Scientists who overlook small errors may lose credibility and feel ashamed, not realizing how significant those tiny mistakes can become. By paying attention to details, they learn to control outcomes and gain experience. I have learned that tending to minor issues prevents larger problems down the line, and this awareness is a form of growth.

Beyond learning, everyday life offers many opportunities for development. The shift from school to society demonstrates that there is no single path to success. Work requires effort, but there are many routes to advancement. Marriage and parenthood also mark milestones. Experiencing the responsibilities of a spouse and a child forces one to confront meaning and duty, which deepens personal growth. All of these aspects—the job, a partner, children—shape us into adults.

Emerson wrote, “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow.” While this might hold for some, I disagree with his generalization. People mature in diverse ways. Studying new material, learning from small errors, and navigating societal roles all contribute to growth. In China, as elsewhere, there are many reasons to become a better person, and not every path is defined by surpassing one’s current abilities.

Should people make their own decisions or follow the advice of experts and authorities about life's experiences? The author argues that it is better to act independently, especially when one is inexperienced. By making one’s own choices, a person learns from mistakes without external interference. Some people believe that following others’ decisions is safer, but the writer contends that autonomy allows a person to create a "family" of their own rules and become the master of their own life.

First, being alone is better because you learn from your own mistakes. When you make a decision and it leads to a mistake, you gain valuable experience that makes you stronger and more responsible. Others who observe your journey may see you as a future leader, because you have earned your achievements through independence.

Second, you must follow the rules you create yourself. If you adhere to someone else’s rules, you have less control and may not know what will happen. By setting your own guidelines, you can anticipate outcomes and work towards your goals without being constrained by another’s expectations.

Finally, solitude ensures no one else will bother you. You will be in total control of your actions and decisions. Without an external boss, you can become an expert in your chosen fields—work, school, or business—because you are the one setting the standards. If you rely on someone else’s head, they will correct you and impose their ways, which may conflict with your own vision and limit your freedom.

In conclusion, people should make their own decisions and avoid relying on others with more experience. Starting from zero allows you to learn from mistakes, grow stronger, and develop a unique set of rules that guide you. When you are free from external interference, you become the boss of your own life and can inspire others by demonstrating the power of independent thinking.

People must decide for themselves rather than following the advice of others. The idea that being alone leads to personal growth and freedom is convincing because you create your own experiences without external interference. When you are on your own, any mistake becomes a learning opportunity. Instead of simply accepting someone else's conclusion, you evaluate the outcome and develop a deeper sense of responsibility. That process of trial and error strengthens character and builds confidence, so people who face challenges alone are more likely to become resilient and capable.

Another important point is the power of self‑determination. By creating your own rules, you set clear boundaries and goals. Others might impose their expectations or dictate how you should live. Following someone else’s rules can feel limiting, since you do not have full control over the path you choose. In contrast, when you maintain your own guidelines, you know that the trajectory is aligned with your values. Knowing what you expect from yourself gives you a sense of certainty and reduces uncertainty that often accompanies external direction.

In addition, the lack of external interference means you can focus on mastering the tasks that matter to you. When no one is constantly telling you what to do, you have the capacity to become an expert in your chosen field. Whether it is work, education, or personal development, full ownership of your decisions allows you to shape your own future. If you rely on someone else’s authority, you risk being directed in a direction that may not suit your ambitions. The constant adjustments you would have to make can hinder progress.

Being independent also attracts respect. People who choose to live by their own rules are often seen as authentic and self‑confident. Others may admire the courage it takes to go against the grain and learn from their own mistakes. This authenticity can inspire those around them to reflect on their own choices. The statement that “you become a stronger, smarter person” captures this progression: self‑made decisions and self‑imposed rules generate a virtuous cycle of growth.

In conclusion, it is better to construct life through personal decisions rather than heed the counsel of others. Independence equips you with the experience of navigating challenges, the clarity of having your own principles, and the freedom to become a specialist in your area. When you are alone, you are the master of your destiny and the one who ultimately learns from the consequences of your actions. This empowerment will help you to improve yourself, to inspire others, and ultimately to thrive.

This is how our world runs: by doing something in your life, by going to school, by learning, then going to college, and by finding a career for yourself, and all this is by doing something in your life to accomplish your goals and to improve your life, to grow more and more, to gain knowledge and not stop what you want to do. We do accomplish when we always do something. In your life, there are always people pushing you forward, and sometimes you feel like doing nothing, but you should do something because if you do it you accomplish a goal that your parents gave you. For example, during summer break you stay home, doing nothing, playing video games, and eating all the food, and not working while you leave the dishwasher full and did not clean the house, and when your parents come and see you not doing anything, of course they might get mad. Your parents might ask, “Why don’t you leave the video games and start doing something in the house and start washing the dishwashers and getting a job to make money?” and this is when you have to start doing, looking at accomplishing your goals, not in the house wasting your time and not doing anything. Do we accomplish more if we are always doing something? And the answer is yes, and we should not stop doing something, because everyday we are accomplishing it without knowing it.

We should always accomplish something when we do something, so we can do wonderful things. If we undertake more actions, we will reach the goals we set in our minds and keep moving forward. Thomas Jefferson accomplished many things in his life; when he wrote the Declaration of Independence, he did not waste time relaxing or socializing with his buddies. When we begin a project in life, we set yearly goals: what will you do next? Each subsequent goal is pursued because we never stop working toward it, striving to maintain momentum. Many people waste their time and leave their goals unfinished. Every person has a deep motivation that keeps them moving forward and trying to improve their life. Over the years we see new products—phones, shoes, TVs—each driven by individuals who worked hard to improve them. The world continually improves from generation to generation through persistent effort. We act with purpose, because it is wonderful to keep going and never give up. Remaining idle wastes time for both you and those around you. The world runs on people who pursue their lives by attending school, learning, going to college, finding a career, and continuously improving. We accomplish more when we are always doing something. In life, people push us forward, and sometimes we feel reluctant to act, but taking action allows us to achieve the goals our parents set for us. For example, during a summer break, if you stay home playing video games all day, eat without purpose, and leave the dishes full, your parents will be upset. They will ask why you don't put away the video games and start doing tasks like washing dishes or finding a job to earn money. This is when you must begin working toward your goals instead of wasting time at home. We do accomplish more when we are always doing something, and we must not stop; each day we unknowingly accomplish something.

When we set out to achieve something, we must stay focused and keep moving forward. The only way to reach our ambitions is by actively pursuing them. Famous figures such as Thomas Jefferson demonstrate this principle. He wrote the Declaration of Independence and, rather than idly relaxing with friends, he applied himself fully to his work. His dedication allowed him to realise great achievements.

Each year we should set clear goals for ourselves. By checking these goals regularly, we keep ourselves busy, and the work never truly stops. Those who waste time often fail to finish what they set out to do. In contrast, every person has an inner drive that encourages them to keep progressing. Over many years, new inventions appear—phones, shoes, televisions—and behind each innovation is a person who worked hard to create improvement.

Our world moves because people are constantly doing something. New ideas are passed from one generation to the next, each striving to outdo the last. Doing something with a purpose is vital, because a life spent idly gives nothing to the world or the individual. The same principle applies in everyday life: attending school, studying, and eventually entering a career are all steps that help us achieve our goals and grow our knowledge.

It is common for people to feel tempted to do nothing, especially during breaks or free time. For example, a teenager might stay at home, play video games, and avoid chores. When parents observe this inactivity, they are disappointed. They might say, “Why don’t you stop playing and start helping around the house or finding a part‑time job?” This illustrates that progress depends on taking action rather than idling.

In short, the more we actively engage in tasks, the more we accomplish. We continue to build on our achievements without even realizing it. Therefore, we should always be doing something—whether it is studying, working, or helping others—so that we can reach our goals, improve our lives, and contribute to society.

Ralph Emerson’s words can be challenging for adults, and they are even more so for teenagers, because children are still learning what life will be like.

If you grow up in a family that cares about every action you take, you realize how lucky you are, because not everyone has such a family. Teenagers whose families do not care are more likely to face problems than those with supportive families. At this point, the teenager must decide whether to become a good man who makes his family proud by succeeding without their help or to end up in jail. When a person lacks familial support, they do what they can to earn money and put food on the table for their loved ones. Being yourself means caring for your family and giving your younger siblings the opportunities you did not have. Most people reach this decision in their teens, the hardest choice, because it means leaving their past behind and committing to hard work without looking back.

When a teenager is raised in a household that pays little attention to him, he is more likely to face difficulties than one who has a caring family. At that point, the teen must decide whether to become a good person and make his family proud, showing them his achievements without relying on their help, or to fall into trouble and end up in jail.

Without family support, many youths do what they can to earn some money so they can feed themselves and their family. In this sense, being oneself means caring for your loved ones and giving your younger siblings opportunities that you did not get. Most people make this choice during their teenage years, the most difficult decision because it means leaving the past behind and working hard forever.

Those who make the choice early on learn what it feels to be autonomous and to act like a mature person. This world rewards those with strong resolve; the weak cannot survive. To be yourself, you need a strong mind.

I think the best way is to collaborate as a group. You might ask why this is the optimal method for learning. For example, I'm the type of student who enjoys hearing about others’ perspectives. By listening to fellow students, each participant gains insight into how the project or assignment should be approached. When students are given the opportunity to articulate their ideas, they feel confident and unafraid to express themselves.

Many students prefer to work independently, so other classmates seldom interrupt them with too many questions. Most already have a topic and a plan. For example, a student working alone typically progresses at their own pace, which gives them the chance to finish on time.

Collaborating allows the group to divide the workload into distinct sections. For instance, one student would handle this part, another would design the project, and a third would conduct the research. Splitting the project into separate components lets each member focus on a segment that is either straightforward or within their expertise.

Students encounter new people; when working on a group project, one may not choose their collaborators. The professor might assign them a team of classmates they have never met before. Working with unfamiliar peers opens opportunities to discover fresh approaches to working and writing. For example, you might meet a new student who creates a T‑chart, listing the positives and negatives of a topic side by side. After reviewing it, they decide which aspect to emphasize.

You accomplish tasks much more rapidly by working in teams. As I mentioned earlier, collaborating accelerates completion, allowing members to concentrate on their specific responsibilities. Once you finish your portion of the project or assignment, you can volunteer to assist a teammate. For instance, a colleague working alone might need additional time; by stepping in to help, you can ease their burden.

In conclusion, working as a group teaches students to heed other people’s viewpoints, and it is the most effective way for students to function collectively. However, some argue that working alone is preferable, as it cultivates independent decision-making and the ability to write a paper without external assistance.

I believe that working in a group is the most effective way for students to learn. Many students wonder why, but group work offers unique advantages. For instance, I am a student who enjoys hearing others’ viewpoints. When we listen to classmates, we gain fresh ideas and a clearer sense of how to approach a project or assignment. Expressing one’s thoughts in a supportive environment also builds confidence and reduces fear of speaking up.

Some students prefer to work alone, so they are not interrupted by too many questions. They already have a plan and can work at their own pace, allowing them to finish on time. However, working together gives us the opportunity to divide the workload. One person can be in charge of research, another can design the presentation, and a third can write the report. Splitting the tasks lets students choose sections they are comfortable with or are skilled at, which often makes the work more efficient.

Group projects also expose us to people we may never meet otherwise. The teacher might assign a team of unfamiliar classmates, and collaborating with them can uncover new approaches to problem‑solving or writing. For example, a teammate might create a T‑chart, listing pros and cons of a topic; after reviewing it, you decide which side to discuss. Such exchanges broaden our thinking.

Because everyone can focus on their part, the entire project progresses more quickly. Once one completes a task, you can help teammates who may need additional time—someone who is working alone might be struggling, and your assistance can make a difference.

In conclusion, group work encourages listening to others, sharing responsibilities, and learning from new perspectives. It helps students become more collaborative and efficient. Some may argue that working alone fosters independence, but I maintain that teamwork ultimately provides a richer learning experience.

With genuine effort and good intentions, a person can shift another’s view, and actions can transform a bad impression into a good one—or vice versa.

In short, first impressions are hard to change because they determine what others think of me and how they treat me, but change is still possible.

First impressions are hard to change because they become the initial picture that people keep in mind. When someone meets you for the first time, the way they see you is already fixed, and that image influences how they will treat you later. If they first notice you as unfriendly or grumpy, they will tend to remember that even if you’re actually cheerful on subsequent occasions. The initial perception sticks in their mind.

What others think of you depends largely on that first impression. If you behave poorly at first and then try to be kind, people may still hold the earlier view and consider you dishonest. They prefer to stay with their original assessment rather than accept new information that contradicts it. Consequently, your later actions often don’t change their minds easily.

Nevertheless, changing first impressions is not entirely impossible. If a person puts real effort and acts genuinely good, others might gradually see a different side of you. Consistent, sincere behaviour can reshape how people view you—turning a negative first impression into a positive one, or improving an already positive view.

In summary, first impressions are resistant to change because they shape the baseline perception and future interactions. However, with persistent, genuine effort, it is possible to alter the initial image people hold of you.

Everyone eventually asks for advice when they need help with a subject or for an opinion when they feel confused. Advice or an opinion can solve a problem, prevent poor choices, clarify which guidance is accurate, and make a person feel secure in their decisions. Seeking multiple viewpoints can therefore improve the quality of a choice.

First, gathering several opinions can prevent poor decisions. For example, if someone considers stealing, if a desired item is too expensive, if someone gets into a fight, if they encounter a disagreeable person, or if they lie about a mistake, comparing different perspectives can guide them toward a wiser course of action.

Second, evaluating many opinions helps determine which advice is trustworthy. When several people give the same recommendation while others disagree, the consensus often reflects reliability. If someone remains uncertain or receives conflicting information, seeking additional counsel can reveal inaccuracies and help the individual choose the most credible guidance.

Finally, consulting multiple viewpoints can give confidence. Whether one feels confused, lost in a topic, lonely, without a team, worried or afraid, or dealing with the absence of someone close, hearing various perspectives can reassure them and support more confident decisions.

In summary, considering many opinions aids decision‑making by avoiding bad choices, verifying accurate advice, and fostering confidence. While self‑reflection is important, broader input is often more essential for sound decisions.

When we face a problem or feel unsure, we often turn to others for help or hear their opinions. Those suggestions can guide our decisions, prevent bad choices, and give us confidence in what we decide. Asking for several viewpoints instead of relying on one source makes the decision better.

First, hearing many opinions helps us avoid wrong choices. Imagine someone thinking about stealing, buying something very expensive, getting into a fight, dealing with a difficult person, or covering up a mistake. In each of these situations, a single suggestion might lead to a bad outcome. By comparing different voices, we can spot the risky or wrong path and choose a safer alternative. Thus, consulting more than one person helps us make wiser decisions.

Second, multiple opinions let us judge which advice is trustworthy. If many people agree on the same point, it is more likely to be correct. If opinions conflict, we can examine the reasons for the differences or ask for clarification. By filtering out unreliable suggestions, we end up with a clearer, more accurate guide. This makes the final decision more reliable.

Finally, diverse viewpoints give us emotional security. When we are confused, lost, lonely, scared, or worried about something that’s gone missing, hearing several perspectives can help us feel less isolated. Knowing that others have considered the situation too can reassure us that we are not alone and that our decision will be solid.

In short, listening to many opinions is useful because it helps avoid poor decisions, identifies the most accurate advice, and provides comfort in the decision process. While consulting ourselves is also important, gathering several external viewpoints is usually more essential for making a well‑thought‑out choice.

If you imagine a world where students stay home and take online classes, that would be great for many who cannot go to school—whether because they are in the hospital, have cancer, or other severe illnesses. Online learning can help these students continue their education without harming anyone else. Some students say there is no problem with missing school at all, but they do do this because their bodies are too weak to attend in person. These students find it easier to attend classes at home; however, they still have to pay for the courses. Most students do not have the money to cover all their tuition and extra costs, and those who do cannot participate in sports or other extracurricular activities, which can be detrimental to their overall well-being.

At home, students have to manage the challenges and improve their own discipline to attend school online.

When I was five years old, my parents worried about my health when I had a bad cold, but I was scared of going to school because it wasn't comfortable. My grandmother said, “Don’t cry and come to school. If you’re sad, just stay home, but remember we can always return.” She told me stories about when she was young and how her teachers did not use online classes. She worked extremely hard and was determined to succeed despite the lack of technology. In the end, I understood the value of a teacher’s support and the resilience that comes from overcoming hardships.

Now that I am eighteen, I am grateful for everything my grandmother taught me. She helped me learn that education is hard work and that staying home without motivation makes it even harder. I have learned that neither online nor in-person classes are inherently better or worse; what matters is how you approach your studies. You must decide whether to find fun and support with friends, or to take a more independent approach and work later at your own pace. In the end, you will face a choice: live in light or dark, gather your family’s love, and let it nourish you. Whether you attend college or stay home, you can live happily and fulfill your family’s hopes.

If you imagine a world where students could simply stay at home and attend class through the internet, it would be an excellent solution for many. Students who cannot physically travel to school because of illness, a long distance commute, or a family emergency would benefit from online lessons. Those who are hospitalized or dealing with a serious condition would no longer feel forced to miss out on their studies.  

However, some people say it would be fine for students not to go to school at all, whether they are sick or healthy. They argue that learning can happen at home without any problems. Others disagree because they believe that physical attendance is necessary for a strong education. They point out that even healthy students might need the structure and motivation that a school environment offers.  

The fact is that attending school is more than just studying; it also involves social interaction, extracurricular activities, and the disciplined routine that helps many students thrive. While online classes can cover most of the academic material, they usually come at a cost. Families might have to pay for high‑speed internet, a suitable computer, and sometimes for tuition if the school offers a hybrid program. Students therefore cannot enjoy the full benefits of online education for free, especially when they also miss out on sports and clubs that schools normally provide.  

I remember when I was five years old, I was too sick to go to school. My grandfather encouraged me to instead be at home, promising that schooling would still be possible via the new technology. He told me stories of his own childhood, when there were no online classes, yet he managed to succeed through hard work. Those memories stayed with me.  

Now that I am 18, I appreciate the guidance my grandfather gave me. I have learned that while online learning can be convenient, it is not a simple replacement for the traditional classroom. Studies show that students benefit from the personal interaction with teachers and peers, and from the sense of belonging that a school provides. Therefore, even though online classes are a useful backup for times when students cannot attend physically, they should not be seen as a complete substitute. Both formats can coexist, but those used rationally are likely to give the best outcomes for students and their families.

Most people no longer appreciate the simple pleasures of life without digital devices. We can still play outside with friends, visit libraries, and enjoy nature without screens.

Some argue that teenagers should have no limits on their use of computers or cell phones because it helps them learn. I disagree. Adolescents need clear restrictions on screen time, and parents should monitor their online activities. Without limits, kids may develop unhealthy habits and become overly dependent on technology.

Others maintain that unrestricted access benefits teens by preparing them for the future. Still, many find it difficult to complete tasks without constant digital contact. Face‑to‑face conversation builds stronger relationships and teaches empathy. Meeting strangers online can be dangerous; not everyone is trustworthy. Parents may think children are only “playing” online, but real‑world dangers exist. Interaction—whether through chat or gaming—should be limited until a trusted bond has formed.

In addition, the temptation to shop online is huge. Many people buy items from unknown sellers, exposing themselves to fraud. E‑commerce sites sometimes promise authenticity, yet some sellers are merely scammers. Before purchasing anything online, make sure the website is reputable. The ease of acquiring goods through platforms like Amazon and eBay has made people reluctant to spend time with family, harming social bonds. Fraudsters exploit this by creating fake sites to fleece consumers.

To counteract these problems, parents can encourage activities outside the digital realm. Spending time with friends, engaging in outdoor games, and avoiding excessive social media use help children stay grounded. Whenever a child interacts with a new online contact, parents should supervise and ensure safe communication.

Consequently, children should not be given unrestricted access to devices. If parents do allow a cell phone or computer, strict boundaries must be set. Technology alone cannot enable people to complete tasks without human contact, and this isolation is harmful. Online scams abound, and without vigilance, families risk losing valuable time together. Technology’s benefits come at a cost, and careful supervision is essential to protect children’s wellbeing and preserve their childhood.

I believe art, music and drama courses should be offered as electives rather than core subjects. Many students already take them as optional classes, which helps them finish on schedule while still enjoying creative pursuits. By keeping these courses elective, schools allow students to choose whether they want to add a fun, exploratory element to their education instead of being forced to take them as mandatory.

Students who think music, art or drama should be required often argue that exposure to the arts is important. Yet, these subjects are less essential than core academic classes, and obligating them could overload students who must meet graduation requirements. Making them electives preserves the purpose of core courses—to ensure that every student gains a solid foundation in essential skills—while still offering the option for those interested in the arts to enjoy these experiences.

Electives also bring practical benefits. Students who pick an art or music class often meet peers with different interests and talents, creating a richer social environment. They get to try something new, discover hidden strengths, and sometimes even find a passion that could guide future study or career choices. In this way, elective arts classes add value without constraining students to a curriculum that may not fit their interests.

Many people say that only being an expert guarantees a bright future, but others worry that spending too much time on one thing wastes life’s time. The truth is that the only thing that truly matters is what you really want.

Some people keep trying and fail, eventually giving up; others keep pushing forward and improve with each attempt. You should always give your best and never quit. When family or friends say you won’t succeed, don’t let them convince you otherwise; you are stronger than you think. If you become skilled at something you love, you can prove to everyone your capabilities. Hold on to that faith. I disagree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s claim that failing at a familiar task ends your growth; keep challenging yourself, and everything will depend on your effort.

Some people believe that students’ confidence should come from external praise, especially before exams or when they need to pass a subject. However, I disagree with this view. I think that students’ self‑esteem should not rely mainly on achievement. The reason is that young people already work hard to produce their best work, they put energy into being successful, and they constantly strive for excellence, so their confidence should stem from their own effort and persistence rather than from the marks they receive. 

Students invest a lot of effort into their studies. When they miss a lesson, they stay after class to catch up. Even when they receive praise, it is usually a reward for something they have already worked hard on. Many students prefer to focus on doing their homework rather than taking breaks, because they know that their diligence will pay off. These behaviours show that their self‑respect comes from putting in effort, not merely from awaited compliments.

Moreover, students try to generate the energy needed for learning. They eat breakfast, bring snacks to school, and believe that confidence is a prerequisite for learning. When a teacher offers help, they accept it, and they organise their tasks when assignments are handed out. These habits reflect a personal drive, which is the real basis for believing in themselves. Relying on external praise would undermine this individual motivation.

Finally, students continually work to achieve the best results. They study after school, complete homework, and practise exercises during short breaks. Some visit the library to read extra material because they want to pass, not because they are looking for compliments. This continuous effort and perseverance reinforce their self‑esteem. It shows that genuine confidence comes from the knowledge that they have done all they can.

In conclusion, while praise has its place, students’ self‑confidence should be built on their own hard work, energy, and continuous striving. Only by recognising their personal effort can they develop a true, lasting sense of worth.

People should make their own decisions because each individual must take responsibility for their own life. When we decide for ourselves, we learn what works best for us and gain confidence in our choices. This autonomy makes our lives simpler and more meaningful.

Choosing for ourselves gives us greater freedom. Freedom means we can pursue the goals that genuinely matter to us, rather than following someone else’s plan. If we listened only to external opinions, we would miss the chance to discover what truly fulfills us. The ability to act on our own judgment allows us to build a life that reflects our values and aspirations.

Furthermore, relying on others’ decisions can be confusing. Different people think differently, and what may suit one person might not suit another. When we depend on others’ choices, we often end up with dissatisfaction because those choices clash with our own needs and desires. By making our own decisions, we avoid the constant tension that can arise when we try to align our lives with others’ expectations.

When we make our own decisions, we also become more adaptable. If we encounter obstacles, we have already learned how to evaluate options and choose the best course of action. This skill improves our ability to handle future challenges. Rather than simply following a set of instructions, we develop critical thinking that benefits all areas of our lives.

Another advantage of personal decision‑making is that it deepens our self‑understanding. Deciding for ourselves forces us to reflect on our preferences, strengths, and weaknesses. This introspection helps us set realistic goals and develop the perseverance needed to achieve them. In contrast, if we always let others decide for us, we risk never discovering our true potential.

It can sometimes feel intimidating to choose alone, especially when faced with a difficult decision. Yet this difficulty is a small price to pay for the long‑term benefits. By practicing independent decision‑making, we build trust in our own judgment and reduce the anxiety that comes from relying heavily on others.

In the end, life becomes smoother when we decide for ourselves. Not only does it align our actions with our personal goals, but it also frees us from the frustration of constantly negotiating with others who may have different priorities. When we live life on our own terms, we are more likely to experience fulfillment and personal growth.

Therefore, people should make their own decisions. Doing so respects their individuality, enhances their freedom, and creates a life that truly belongs to them. Making personal choices is an essential part of living a meaningful and autonomous life.

Students use cell phones in the classroom for educational purposes.

When teachers allow us to use cell phones in class, they give us an opportunity to focus on our work without wasting time on other distractions.  

Sometimes, however, students do not use their phones for the intended purpose. When a teacher says, “Feel free to use your phone to search for information or complete a task,” some students play video games or scroll through Facebook and Instagram instead of listening. This diversion affects both the student’s learning and the classroom environment.  

For example, I once knew a student who, when the teacher asked everyone to search for a story on the internet, used his phone in math class as a calculator. Another girl, who often ignored the teacher’s instructions, spent the entire class time on Facebook, sending messages to classmates. Such behavior can negatively impact others.  

On the other hand, using a phone can be very useful. When I lack the time in my country, I sometimes need to look up a word or phrase in my English class. I also need to translate math symbols in class. In those cases, the phone helps me learn more quickly and perform better. The school’s permission to use phones can therefore be a great aid for both students and teachers.  

Ultimately, the impact of cell phones depends on the student. If used responsibly for work, they can enhance learning; if misused, they can lower grades. We should therefore be grateful for the opportunity and use our phones only for academic purposes.

Students can use cell phones in the classroom for educational purposes.

When teachers allow us to bring our phones into class, they give us a valuable resource. The opportunity to access information instantly helps keep us focused on the lesson rather than wasting time on unrelated things.

I remember a friend who was assigned to research a historical topic on the internet. While the teacher expected him to browse, she was disappointed to see that he was instead chatting on Facebook and sending photos to a friend. This distraction prevented him from completing the task and set a bad example for others.

On the other hand, when used responsibly, phones can enhance learning. In my own experience, I’m often short on time in this country, and when I’m reading a text in English class and encounter an unfamiliar word or phrase, I quickly search the meaning. In math class, if I’m unsure how to interpret a symbol, a quick online lookup clears things up right away. These practical uses demonstrate how phones can be instrumental in deepening understanding.

Ultimately, the effect of phone use depends on the student. Schools give us the privilege to use these devices for learning, and we should be grateful. By focusing on academic tasks and refraining from distractions, we can improve our grades and make the most of this technology.

When someone is constantly told they are unimportant, they may believe there is no point in living, and this can drive them toward despair.

Conversely, whenever we speak harshly to someone, we do ourselves a disservice as well. We only learn to be hurt when we care about others’ opinions of us; this mindset can breed cruelty.

Listening, being there in both good times and bad, and giving unconditional support are the hallmarks of real friendship. Those programs force students to take extra classes after normal school hours or during the summer, and often they cut out elective courses. They also miss out on valuable electives in subjects such as foreign languages, nutrition, music, computer skills, or health‑and‑physical education.

Here are three reasons why students should not do their classwork online from home.

First, studying from home can be difficult. When you work at school you can readily ask the teacher for help, which is not possible at home. Because you don’t know what the teacher will provide in an online setting, it may be easier to solve problems at school where the teacher can offer immediate assistance. Trying to do classwork online at home can therefore be a hard and confusing experience.

Second, students who perform well might prefer to study online. Those who pass the SOL and other assessments can leave school earlier, and those who maintain a high GPA will have better opportunities when they graduate. However, many intelligent students believe that they need not attend school because they already know the material. This view ignores the benefits of a structured learning environment.

Even middle schoolers would benefit from online lessons, as it is easier to complete assignments and earn higher grades, giving them an advantage when they move to college. College students should also be able to complete coursework online to free up time for study or other responsibilities.

I disagree because I think knowledge is more important than imagination.

I think knowledge is more important because, after you imagine, you must know what you have imagined. For example, you can think of something well, but you cannot understand it fully if you lack the knowledge to explain it.

For instance, if you have no knowledge, you will not even know where to place objects in a scene, which could be detrimental to clarity.

Knowledge is essential because it allows you to search for information and determine what to do. If you rely only on imagination, it may not be enough.

For example, when you go to work, you need the knowledge of what tasks to perform that day. In school, when studying a plant, you must know its characteristics before you can observe it properly.

Sometimes you need to be aware of the situation, such as when a suspect is questioned by the police. They must know the scene, identify the suspect, and understand how the incident occurred.

Some people think that imagination comes first and is more important. I understand why some might feel that way because imagining can create vivid images in your mind.
